f08c722676.post: Some people were unemployed, some were told their state had high unemployment, and some were asked to think about past and future economic insecurity. Others had none of these experiences. Everyone then reported how much physical pain they felt. People who had these experiences reported more pain.

f0af0cf0ba.post: Seven-month-old babies listened to made-up sentences that all followed one pattern. Then they heard new sentences, some with the same pattern and some with a different one. The babies listened longer to the sentences with the unfamiliar pattern.

f196ce5262.post: People read an object and a property, such as cranberries and tart, and judged whether the property fit the object. Then they did the same for another pair, such as blender and loud. They were slower to judge when the property involved a different sense than the one just before, like sound after taste.

f1bab4aca3.post: People compared prices that were one cent apart and rated how big the difference felt. In some pairs, such as $2.99 and $3.00, the first digit changed. In others, such as $3.00 and $3.01, it did not. People rated the first kind of pair as a larger difference.

f1c53f4309.post: People unscrambled jumbled sentences. For some, the sentences contained God-related words, and for others, neutral words. Then everyone said how willing they were to take risks. People who had seen the God words were more willing to take risks that had nothing to do with morality.

f1c8a90d47.post: Men chose between a smaller sum of money tomorrow and a larger sum at a later date. Then they rated how appealing 12 photographs of women's faces were, attractive faces for some and unattractive for others, and chose again. Men who saw attractive faces then favored the money tomorrow more than men who saw unattractive ones.

f1f873e260.post: Crows watched a stick move inside a hide. Sometimes a person went in before it moved and left after. Other times no one went in or out. The crows inspected the hide and gave up fishing for food with a tool more often when no one had been in the hide.

f243d1dbc4.post: People saw one serving of ice cream on its own and said how much they would pay for it. For some it was 7 ounces in a cup that overflowed, and for others 8 ounces in a cup that was not full. People valued the overfilled 7 ounces more than the underfilled 8 ounces.

f2e52468a2.post: People assembled IKEA boxes, folded origami, or built Lego sets. Then they said how much they would pay for what they had made and for a similar product they had not made. People would pay more for their own creation.

f2fa4623bb.post: Some people were given an object to keep and others were not. Everyone then rated the object. The people who owned it rated it more favorably.

f324c2ec6a.post: Some people were reminded that resources can be scarce, and others were not. Then everyone played a game where they could keep resources for themselves or share them. After the reminder, people who cared less about others' outcomes shared less and kept more for themselves.

f383b1084d.post: Adults pressed a button whenever a go signal appeared, but tried to hold back when a stop signal came. The stop signal was a picture of a face that was fearful, happy, or neutral. People were better at stopping when the face was fearful or happy than when it was neutral.

f3bf8206bf.post: During the 2008 U.S. presidential election, people took an online study. Some were briefly shown an American flag and others were not. Then everyone reported their political beliefs, attitudes and voting intentions. People who saw the flag reported more Republican beliefs, attitudes and voting intentions.

f480eb0da6.post: People rated how much they and others are swayed by various biases in thinking. The others were the average American, classmates in a seminar, or fellow airport travelers. People rated themselves as less susceptible to biases than they rated other people.

f4832b45d4.post: Jays could hide food either behind a solid barrier or behind a see-through one. Sometimes another jay was watching, and sometimes the jay hid food in private. The jays hid more of their food behind the solid barrier when another jay was watching.

f4c18c1937.post: People saw a series of striped patterns one after another and reported the tilt of each one. Their report was pulled toward the tilt they had reported on the previous pattern.

f51e802051.post: People were randomly given a rank among other participants. Then each chose whether to give money to the person one rank above them or one rank below. People ranked second-to-last were the most likely to give to the person above them rather than the one below.

f52e778cfb.post: Some people were asked to eat radishes while chocolates were nearby, and others had no such demand. Then everyone tried puzzles that could not be solved. People who had to resist the chocolates and eat radishes quit the puzzles sooner.

f55bce5fcc.post: A nationwide group of adults said how they spent their income and how happy they were. People who spent more of their income on others were happier than people who spent more on themselves.

f6395d9d4a.post: People saw a word such as mother, father, nurse or doctor, and then a pronoun such as she or he. They said whether the pronoun was male or female. They answered faster when the pronoun matched the gender suggested by the first word.

f6444e0b43.post: Children and adults read a sentence suggesting an object was large or small. Then they saw a picture of the object, shown either large or small, and responded to it. They responded faster when the size in the picture matched the size the sentence suggested.

f64b86590c.post: Students, some of them depressed and some not, could press a button or leave it alone, and a green light sometimes came on. Afterwards each one guessed how much the light depended on what they did. The depressed students guessed more accurately than the others.

f664e5cc80.post: Voters read about two candidates in a pretend race for mayor. One was always a middle-aged white man, and the other varied in gender, race or age. Voters tended to favor the candidate who shared their own gender or race.

f6819db591.post: People reported how much television they watch each day by picking from a list. One list ran from 'up to half an hour' to 'more than two and a half hours'. The other ran from 'up to two and a half hours' to 'more than four and a half hours'. People given the first list reported watching less television.

f701ed7e9c.post: People heard two voices at once, one in each ear. They repeated one voice out loud and ignored the other. They noticed almost nothing from the ignored voice, except their own name.

f71d96ee8a.post: People read about an outbreak expected to kill 600 people and chose between a sure outcome and a gamble. For some the outcomes were described as people saved, and for others as people dying. When it was about lives saved people picked the sure option, and when it was about lives lost they picked the gamble.

f7baeacb41.post: People recalled personal events from their past, some positive and some negative, and rated how far away each event felt. People felt farther from their negative events than from their positive ones, and the gap was larger for people with high self-esteem.

f8224c7654.post: People unscrambled sentences, some full of hostile words and others with neutral words. Then they rated how hostile some behavior seemed, behavior that could be read either way. The people who had seen more hostile words rated the behavior as more hostile.

f8a1007f2e.post: People chose between consumer products, from simple ones like towels to complex ones like cars. Some thought carefully before choosing and others were distracted first. Afterward they rated their choice. For complex products, the distracted people rated their choice more favorably than the people who thought carefully.

f92c2f6310.post: People unscrambled jumbled sentences, some containing God-related words and others neutral words. Then everyone chose between a safe way and a risky way to get money. People who had seen the God words took more risks.

f9b9a16f2b.post: People unscrambled sentences that contained religious words, or neutral words. Then they decided how much money to give to an anonymous partner. People who unscrambled religious words gave more money.

f9c8f36b69.post: People read a sentence that hinted an object was standing up or lying flat. Then they saw a picture of that object, either standing or lying. They recognized the object faster when its position matched the sentence.

fa07252cce.post: Half the people were given a coffee mug and half were not. Then everyone could buy and sell mugs. The people who had a mug asked for more money to sell it than the others were willing to pay to buy it.

fa29f6606d.post: Consumers saw an ad for a product available only in limited quantity, or a control ad. Then researchers measured how they saw other shoppers and how aggressively they acted. People who saw the limited-quantity ad saw other shoppers as competitive threats and acted more aggressively.

fabc453a9a.post: People saw a target letter in the middle of a row, with other letters on each side, and pressed one key or another depending on the target. Sometimes the side letters called for the same key and sometimes for the opposite key. People were slower when the side letters called for the opposite key.

fadf643df9.post: Adults were randomly given one of two tasks for a month. Some tried to live the month as if it were their last in their current city, and others just kept track of their daily activities. Everyone reported their well-being. People who imagined their time in the city as limited were happier than people who tracked their activities.

fafd1b8078.post: Some people were asked the least money they would accept to spend a given number of hours on something. Others were asked the most hours they would spend for a given amount of money. Researchers worked out the hourly wage each answer implied. People asked about hours demanded a higher wage than people asked about money.

fb6e31b775.post: People did a real task twice, once paid for their own work and once in a competition against others. Then they chose which of the two pay schemes to use for their next try. Twice as many men as women chose the competition.

fb71bc850e.post: Adults were shown pictures of objects and wrote down each object's name. Some of the names are learned early in life and others late, but the words are used equally often. Names learned early were written faster and more accurately.

fba1a0e853.post: Students who had learned French as a second language translated 145 words, in both directions between English and French. Words people had learned early in life were translated faster than words they learned later.

fbc2fb5ef9.post: Adults read a story about a sudden change to their imagined future income. For some it got worse, for some better, and for some it stayed the same. Then they did a task that measured how much they valued money received or lost later. People whose imagined income dropped valued delayed gains and losses less.

fc461d1fee.post: People saw a person repeatedly gaze toward some objects and away from others. Then they rated how much they liked each object. People rated the objects the person had gazed toward as more likeable.

fc945016a7.post: The death tolls of 92 past hurricanes were compared. Some hurricanes had girls' names and some had boys' names. Hurricanes with girls' names caused more deaths than hurricanes with boys' names.

fd036c40ff.post: Turkey changed its law to make students stay in school longer. Researchers compared rural women who had to stay in school longer with those who did not, and asked about violence at home. The women who stayed longer reported more psychological violence and financial control at home.

fd16a30172.post: Over 10,000 students in China were surveyed about learning English. They were asked whether they picture themselves using English well in the future, and how motivated they were to learn it. The students who did picture it were more motivated.

fd1b270a90.post: People read sentences about an object that was either near or far from a person in the scene. Then they saw a picture of the object, either big or small, and responded to it. When the object was far, people responded faster to small pictures, and when it was near, faster to big ones.

fd3427630b.post: Adults received a nasal spray containing oxytocin or a placebo. Then they played a game in which they decided how much money to hand to a stranger. People who got oxytocin trusted the stranger with more money.

fd40b47904.post: People watched words appear one after another in rapid succession and tried to spot two target words. Sometimes the second target came right after the first, and sometimes later. People often missed the second target when it came 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first.

fdc13a9763.post: Adults watched either a video that put them in a mildly positive mood or a neutral video. Then they chose between smaller amounts of money now and larger amounts later. People who watched the positive video were more willing to wait for the larger amounts.

fdefe06619.post: People read a sentence about an animal in a certain place, such as an eagle in the sky or an eagle in a nest. Then they saw a line drawing of the animal and said whether it had been mentioned. They answered faster when the drawing's shape matched the shape the sentence implied.

fdff112db8.post: People answered political knowledge questions in an online experiment. Before that, some were reminded of gender stereotypes about political knowledge and others were not. Women who were reminded did worse on the questions than women who were not.

fe196cafe8.post: People filled in a form reporting information about themselves, with a chance to cheat. Some signed a statement of honest intent at the beginning, before reporting, and others at the end, after. People who signed at the beginning were less dishonest.

fe40578263.post: U.S. residents were asked to write an essay arguing against their own view on who made a better president. Some preferred conservative presidents and some liberal ones. Researchers recorded who went along with it. Conservatives were more likely to avoid writing it than liberals.

fed1e7d99b.post: Students briefly held a cup of hot coffee or iced coffee. Then they read a description of a person and rated the person's personality. Students who held the hot coffee judged the person as warmer and more caring.

feffdf75c7.post: People said how lonely they felt and how often they took warm baths or showers. The lonelier people were, the more warm baths and showers they took.

ff4e922ade.post: Some people chose between a sure gain and a gamble. Others got the same problem with the gains turned into losses. People avoided risk when the choice was a sure gain and took risks when it was a sure loss.

ff6afe4e5a.post: People saw strings of letters and had to say, as fast as they could, whether each one was a real word. Some of the words are ones people learn early in life, and others they learn later. Words learned earlier were recognized faster and more accurately.

ff773a7b5c.post: Students studied a list of words and then took a recall test. After the test, they restudied some of the words. On the test, they had recalled the restudied words better than the words they did not restudy.

ffb4c9e0bd.post: Adults read sentences while their eye movements were tracked. Some words in the sentences are ones people learn early in life, and some are ones they learn later. Words learned early got shorter looks than words learned later.

g00bb75770.post: People read about a crime. Some were told it was explained by the offender's genes and others by the offender's environment. Then they rated how well an insanity defense applied. People given the genetic explanation said the insanity defense applied more.

g00d70652a.post: People looked at pictures that got clearer the harder they squeezed a hand grip. Researchers wanted to see whether people squeeze harder for pictures of things they like. Most people squeezed hardest for the kind of picture they liked best.

g01c78ad40.post: People thought about their own regrets, both things they did and things they didn't do. They did this for two different stretches of time, and one was their whole life so far. Looking back over their whole lives, most people (84%) regretted things they failed to do more than things they did.

g0279d7097.post: People saw digits appear at irregular times and later recalled either their order or their timing. Some were told to split the list into groups. People paused between the groups when they recalled, whether they were recalling order or timing.

g02df90a5b.post: People were first led to think about space in one way or another, depending on their group. Then everyone answered a question about time. Most of them, 71.3%, answered in a way that matched how they had just been led to think about space.

g034e5d76e.post: People read someone's description of a Democrat. Some read it with the good deeds described in broad terms and the bad deeds in specific detail, and others read the reverse. People who read the first version were more likely to think the writer was also a Democrat.

g04f1e1a9a.post: Some people read an essay saying that behavior is shaped by genes and environment, and others read a neutral essay. Then everyone solved math problems on a computer that could show the answers if they let it. People who read the essay about behavior being determined cheated more.

g0564da8de.post: People read about someone whose actions led to a person's death. In one version the person who died was a police officer, and in the other a thief. Then they rated whether the death was brought about intentionally. People rated it as more intentional when the victim was a police officer.

g0669aacf9.post: People looked at a seesaw logo. For some the bar was tilted to suggest movement, and for others it was left flat. Then they rated how they felt about the brand. People who saw the moving logo felt more favorably toward the brand.

g06b0efcd8.post: People named the ink color of color words, some spelling a different color than the ink and others the same, once while sitting and once while standing. When seated, people were slower on the mismatched words. When standing, they were not.

g0749ca15c.post: College students did a quick attention task over many rounds. Each round showed images, some threat-related and some neutral, and people responded to a probe on the screen. Sometimes the probe was where a threat image had been. After responding to a probe at a threat image, people's attention was pulled toward threat on the next round.

g07bc1e61d.post: Students said whether they think interests are fixed or can be developed. Then they read an article on a topic that fit their existing interests or one that did not, and rated how interesting it was. Students who see interests as fixed lost interest in topics outside their existing interests.

g08f177485.post: People imagined eating a food, such as cheese, many times, or only a few times, or imagined eating a different food. Then they were given the food to eat. People who imagined eating the food many times ate less of it.

g0a1df3a6c.post: People played buyers and sellers in a market where only the seller knew what fix the buyer needed. In some games sellers had to pay if they prescribed the wrong fix. In some, buyers could check what was done. Markets worked better when sellers were on the hook, but letting buyers check did little.

g0a6c73ab7.post: Senior police officers did realistic video shoot or don't-shoot scenarios before and after a training. Some were randomly given a video-based training on situational awareness and where to look, and others a training like traditional police training. Officers who got the video-based training responded faster and hit the target sooner.

g0beacb169.post: People rated how much they agreed with comparisons such as 'men earn more than women' or 'women earn less than men'. The two kinds of wording say the same thing. People agreed more with the 'more than' wording.

g0ca48084e.post: European Americans and Koreans looked at abstract figures and rated how much they liked the different parts of each one. Some parts were one of a kind within their figure. European Americans liked the one-of-a-kind parts more than Koreans did.

g0f360ff07.post: People imagined two people. One knew what experiences they had paid for, like vacations and concerts, and the other knew what things they had bought, like clothes and gadgets. They rated how well each would know them. People said the person who knew their experiences would know them better.

g0f88c1df1.post: People marked points on graph paper, with the points either close together or far apart. Then everyone rated how close they felt to their family and their hometown. People who had marked far-apart points felt less attached.

g1013df2ef.post: People viewed everyday objects, each shown in a state such as open or closed. After a short or a long delay, they were asked which state and which particular object they had seen. After a long delay, people often remembered one of the two without the other.

g119401406.post: People read about a person who acquired a moral deficit, or lost their memories, or lost their desires. Then they rated how profoundly the person had changed. People rated the person who lost their morals as more profoundly changed.

g119f7b623.post: People chose a mutual fund to invest in. One option was the fund recommended by a robo-advisor, a computer program that gives investment advice. Some people were led to think about God, and others were not. Of those who thought about God, 50.5% picked the robo-advisor's fund, compared with 35.7% of the others.

g11aac6f31.post: People saw colored pictures of animals, and a cue told them each time whether to say the animal or its color. Some spoke one language and some spoke two. When the two tasks were mixed together, the people who spoke two languages slowed down less.

g11c290e3b.post: People were asked what share of the smartphones sold in the US came from one particular phone. Some saw its model number as P97 and others as P17. The people who saw P97 guessed a higher share.

g15a3983f2.post: Pairs played a money game for 60 seconds. In some games each player could switch between cooperating and not at any moment. In others they could only choose eight times. The pairs who could switch at any moment cooperated far more.

g1792158a3.post: Each person was given some money and could split it between two pools. One pool helped only their own group. The other helped their group and also hurt a rival group. Almost all the money went to the pool that helped only their own group.

g19a89a81e.post: Some people wrote about the limits on their money, and others wrote about something else. Then everyone chose between buying things and buying experiences. The people who had written about their money limits leaned more toward buying things.

g1ad536699.post: People imagined they were about to buy a calculator and could drive to another store to save $5 on it. For some, the calculator cost $15. For others, it cost $125. Most people would make the extra trip to save $5 on the $15 calculator (68%), but far fewer would for the $125 one (29%).

g1afd7f006.post: Women estimated the weight of 120 other women who varied in body size. They underestimated the weight of overweight and obese women, and the heavier the woman was, the bigger the underestimate.

g1c168a5cd.post: Children and teenagers, some with anxiety disorders and some healthy, viewed faces while their eye movements were tracked. Researchers measured how long they looked at negative faces compared with other faces. Those with anxiety disorders looked longer at negative faces than healthy peers did.

g20159a32d.post: Adults online did a quick task that brought to mind either cleanliness or a neutral idea, and were told to respond fast without paying much attention. Then they rated how wrong the behaviors in several stories were. People who had cleanliness on their minds judged them as less wrong.

g226ba5776.post: Lists of real and made-up words flashed by very fast, and some lists had one word repeated. People wrote down what they saw. They reported the repeat less often than the first showing.

g22830c464.post: Consumers read persuasive messages from sources described as either experts or non-experts. Some sources sounded certain and others uncertain. Non-experts persuaded more when they sounded certain, while experts persuaded more when they sounded uncertain.

g22da4a617.post: White people in the US said how fair they think the country's racial order is. Then some read about progress in racial equality and others did not, and everyone said how much Whites face discrimination. Among people who saw the racial order as fair, those who read about progress said Whites face more discrimination.

g2358b523e.post: Adults answered questions about how often they feel inspired and about their personality. People who scored higher on inspiration also scored higher on extraversion.

g23d9ebffd.post: People had to say whether they had seen a face or a house before. Sometimes they were shown the whole thing, and sometimes just one part of it. People were more accurate when they saw the whole face or house than when they saw a part.

g23e487f3d.post: People got a message that came either from friends and family or from an organization. Then they said how willing they were to join in on social media, for example by commenting or liking. They were more willing when the message came from friends and family.

g24edf60c2.post: People said how long they would be willing to work to get either cash or a music book, priced at $30 or $60. For cash, people would work much longer for $60 than for $30. For the book, the price made less difference.

g2566717e4.post: Women looked at a photograph of a man shown on either a red or a gray background and rated how attractive he was. They rated him as more attractive on the red background.

g25edd4513.post: People were asked the average price of a middle-class car. Before answering, they saw a number flashed too briefly to notice, either high or low. People who had seen the high number gave higher price estimates than people who had seen the low number.

g26275b33f.post: People saw a row of objects from smallest to largest and marked where 'big' starts. The stretch they called 'small' was longer than the stretch they called 'big'.

g2676fc3b9.post: People were asked to think about regrets in their own lives. They said whether they felt more regret over things they had done, or over things they had not done but wished they had. Three out of four said they regretted the things they did not do more.

g2789384ad.post: Some people looked at pictures taken from high up and others at pictures taken from down low. Then everyone said how likely they were to buy new products. The people who saw the high-up pictures said they were more likely to buy.

g27dce03de.post: Some people read a passage of literary fiction and others a passage of popular fiction. Then everyone looked at photos of eyes and guessed what each person was feeling. The people who read literary fiction did better.

g290dcb2e5.post: People were given a high-ranking or a low-ranking role and recorded talking. Other people listened and rated how likely each speaker was to act like a boss. Speakers who had been given the high-ranking role were rated as more likely to act like a boss.

g29456dbf6.post: People viewed random patterns of dots or shapes and estimated how many items each pattern contained. Some patterns were all identical in color and shape, and others had several colors or shapes. People estimated more items in the identical patterns.

g294c0c989.post: People watched videos of eight job interviews. Half the job candidates told the truth and half lied to look better. People who trust others in general were better at spotting the lies than people who don't.

g2a92fbc8c.post: People looked at angry, fearful and other faces while researchers measured how quickly their attention could move away from them. Some people had a diagnosed anxiety disorder, some were healthy volunteers, and some were very anxious without a diagnosis. People with the anxiety disorder pulled their attention away from angry and fearful faces faster than the comparison groups.

g2bb855678.post: Adults looked at an image of Rodin's sculpture The Thinker, or at a control image. Then they reported how much they believed in God. People who saw The Thinker reported less belief in God.

g302bafbb9.post: People rated how closely different traits go with creativity. Some traits are ones we think of as masculine, like daring and self-reliance, and some as feminine, like cooperative and supportive. The masculine traits were linked to creativity more than the feminine ones.

g33fe2976b.post: People were made to feel either unsure or sure about who they are. Then they chose whether to keep or cancel a subscription that fit their identity. People made to feel unsure were more likely to keep it.

g346d8bde2.post: People held a cold pack, a warm pack, or a neutral one, and then rated how lonely they felt. People who held the cold pack felt lonelier than the others.

g36ebff528.post: People were shown a sample amount of candy and poured out candy to match it. Some poured candy of mixed colors and others poured candy of a single color. People who poured mixed colors poured more.

g36efffd81.post: Hindi speakers read a story about a chairman. In one version what he did harmed the environment and in the other it helped. They judged whether he acted 'jaan-bujhkar', a Hindi word for intentionally. They were more likely to say he acted intentionally when his behavior caused harm.

g3c08e9f10.post: People studied pictures of objects on plain backgrounds. Some objects were positive, some negative and some neutral. Later, people were shown either the object or the background and had to recall the other one. Emotional objects were more likely than neutral ones to bring back their background.

g3d1e2653f.post: Students learned about Bayesian reasoning. Some tried to solve problems before being taught the solution, and others were taught first. Then everyone took a test of conceptual knowledge. Students who tried the problems first scored higher.

g3e562f91c.post: Some people were put in a condition that gave them high standing, meaning lots of respect and admiration from others in a small group. Others were put in a low-standing condition. Then everyone rated their well-being. People in the high-standing condition reported higher well-being than people in the low-standing condition.

g3f0139c85.post: People were told they would play either a confrontational game or a nonconfrontational one. Before playing, they chose which activities they would prefer: ones that would make them angry, ones that would excite them, or neutral ones. People who expected a confrontation preferred activities that would make them angry, but people who expected a nonconfrontational game did not.

g3f8d8ff6e.post: While their eyes were tracked, people judged whether faces were happy, fearful or neutral. The faces appeared at increasing distances from the point where people were looking. Judging happy faces stayed accurate farther from the center of gaze than judging fearful faces.

g402c3db28.post: People chose between two laptops. One was better overall, and the other was better on more of the separate features. Some people read descriptions that made both laptops sound human, and others read plain descriptions. The people who read the human-sounding descriptions picked the better-overall laptop more often.

g4250a6010.post: People heard lists of words to remember while a stream of other words that rhymed with them played in the background. Some had to recall the words in any order and some in the order they were heard. The rhyming stream hurt recall in any order but not recall in the order heard.

g43fb642cf.post: People studied a list of words. Some controlled how long to spend on each word, and others saw the words at a fixed pace with the same total study time. Then everyone took a memory test. People who controlled their own study time did better.

g442483f76.post: Young and older adults described events from their past and imagined events in their future. Each description was split into details about the event itself and other kinds of details. Older adults gave fewer details about the event itself than younger adults, for both past and future events.

g4455a836a.post: People copied out a story about themselves, a story in which they did something either unethical or ethical. Then they rated how much they wanted cleansing products. Those who had copied the unethical story wanted cleansing products more.

g458b75829.post: People were given a comparison about the environment. For some it looked back at the past, and for others it looked ahead to the future. Then they gave their attitudes about climate change. With the future comparison, conservatives were less favorable than liberals, but with the past comparison that gap was much smaller.

g462fe3aff.post: People read about someone doing something wrong. In some stories the person came from the reader's own culture, in others from a very different one. The more different the person's way of life, the less people said there was one right answer.

g46817d4c1.post: Drivers were watched to see who broke traffic laws, and in lab tests people could lie, cheat or take things from others. Upper-class people did all of these more often than lower-class people.

g47a0c89e6.post: People could donate money to help a sick child, or to help a group of eight sick children. Some saw a photo of the child or children and some did not. A photo made people give more to the one child, but made no difference for the group of eight.

g4843bef5c.post: Some Americans were prompted to think in terms of choice, and others were not. Then everyone read facts about wealth inequality in the United States and said how disturbed they were. The people prompted to think about choice were less disturbed.

g4a151ef2f.post: People tried to get a reward but were sometimes blocked from getting it. Some were closer to the reward, and some had put in more effort trying. The closer people were and the more effort they had put in, the more they said they wanted the reward, and the faster they responded.

g4b61c0dcb.post: People aged 10 to 20 filled out a personality questionnaire online. The younger ones differed more from each other in how often they just agreed with a statement, whatever it said.

g4c56a436d.post: People read made-up words, company names, or person names and rated how much they liked them. In some the consonants move from the front of the mouth to the back, like BENOKA, and in others from the back to the front, like KENOBA. People liked the front-to-back words more.

g4c60f12bb.post: People rated how much their personal goals conflicted with each other. Then they browsed a set of books that was described as work. People who felt more conflict between their goals spent more time browsing.

g4d86fee69.post: College seniors reported their emotions on graduation day. Some of them were first reminded that graduation was an ending. Those who were reminded felt more mixed emotions than those who were not.

g4f043273e.post: People were asked about their own regrets, and about the regrets of people in short stories. Things people did hurt more at first. Over the years, people regretted the things they never did more.

g4f1039da2.post: Some people repeatedly checked a virtual stove, some just repeatedly used it, and others did the same with a light bulb. Then they rated how well they remembered the object. People were less accurate, confident and clear about their memory of the stove than of the light bulb.

g4f6062772.post: People read about a negotiation. In one version the buyer used true statements to give a misleading impression, and in the other the buyer answered honestly. Then they rated the buyer's behavior. People judged the buyer who used true statements to mislead as more unethical.

g4ff55b0de.post: People first said how much their view on an issue rested on moral concerns. Then they read a message arguing against their view, framed either as a moral appeal or as a nonmoral one. A moral appeal persuaded more than a nonmoral one when the person's view rested on moral concerns, and less when it did not.

g517d260a2.post: Adults recently diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes were randomly given a five-step course on managing their condition, or no course. Afterward researchers measured how well they planned ahead for problems, how well they reached their goals, and how confident they felt. Those who took the course did better on all three.

g5244df747.post: Dogs were observed with their owner, who either cried, hummed, or talked. Observers recorded how often each dog looked at, approached, and touched the owner. Dogs looked at, approached, and touched a crying person more than a person who was humming or talking.

g55c71d874.post: People read about a world where everything that happens is determined by earlier events. In it, a man robs a bank. Then they judged whether he robbed the bank of his own free will. Most people said he did.

g55d4d3605.post: People saw two foods side by side, one healthy and one unhealthy, and chose which they preferred. For some people the healthy food was on the left, and for others it was on the right. People chose the healthy food more often when it was on the left.

g564cfd00c.post: Registered voters received a survey before a statewide election. Some survey questions asked about 'being a voter' and others about 'voting'. Official state records later showed who voted. People asked about 'being a voter' were more likely to vote.

g564ea117b.post: Adults judged where a sound came from, sometimes while a flash of light appeared at the same time. Researchers also tested how well they located the sound alone and the flash alone. Adults located the source more precisely when they heard and saw it together than from sound alone or sight alone.

g572fc4c3c.post: People looked at photos of government officials they did not know and rated each on traits such as corruptibility, honesty, selfishness and aggression. Some of the officials had been convicted of corruption and others had clean records. People rated the convicted officials as more corruptible, dishonest, selfish and aggressive.

g57ab6852e.post: People guessed the values of several things they couldn't know exactly. Before guessing, some were asked whether a given number was higher or lower than the true value. That number was set either low or high. Compared with a group given no number, both kinds pulled guesses toward them, but high numbers pulled more.

g57b45003a.post: People held digits in mind while switching between tasks, with some people switching more often than others. Then they recalled the digits. The more often people switched tasks, the fewer digits they recalled.

g5830c2474.post: People looked at upsetting pictures, each with an object in front of a background. Then some stayed awake for 12 hours and others slept. People who slept still remembered the upsetting objects but not their backgrounds, while people who stayed awake forgot the whole scene.

g593f64594.post: People looking for dates flipped through photographs of potential partners and chose those they wanted to meet. Some photos showed an expansive posture, taking up more space, and others a contracted one. People were more likely to choose the photos with an expansive posture.

g5944b0c41.post: People rated things as pleasant or unpleasant right after a pleasant or unpleasant item flashed by. Some could pass on any trial where they felt that first item had influenced them, and others had no pass option. Having the pass option did not reduce how much the first item swayed their ratings.

g595242176.post: Groups harvested from a shared supply that could run out, over several rounds. Some groups could talk to each other, and others could neither talk nor punish. The groups that could talk earned more.

g5b6f01eab.post: People with PTSD and trauma survivors without PTSD were shown reminders of upsetting scenes and told to push the memory away. People with PTSD were worse at forgetting the scenes they tried to push away.

g5c2a0282b.post: People rated how much they agreed with claims that one thing causes or explains another. In some cases the relationship held only under certain background conditions, and in others it held across conditions, with the overall strength the same. People agreed less with the claims when the relationship held only under some conditions.

g5c96bc515.post: Groups played a money game over many rounds. Some groups could pay to punish each other, and some could not. When players couldn't see exactly what the others had given, the groups that could punish ended up earning less.

g5d6c1fb8c.post: European Americans and Asian Americans were reminded of death, or of another topic. Then they rated someone who breaks cultural norms. After the death reminder, European Americans defended themselves, while Asian Americans defended other people.

g5edad51fe.post: People from China and from Western countries read made-up stories and said who a name refers to. One kind of answer follows the chain of people who passed the name along. Another follows whoever fits the description. In the Gödel story, Westerners gave the chain answer more often than Chinese participants did.

g5fb4717ab.post: Researchers made some people feel unsure about who they are, and others feel sure. Everyone then said how interested they were in adding new traits to themselves, and rated themselves on the traits of a possible romantic partner. The people who felt unsure were less interested in adding new traits, and less likely to pick up the partner's traits.

g61b50aceb.post: People judged whether two letters were the same or different. Some pairs of different letters were mirror images of each other, like b and d, and others were not, like a and h. People took longer and made more errors telling apart the mirror-image letters.

g62dc2932d.post: People's friend counts on a social networking site were recorded, and their brains were scanned. Some people had few online friends and others had many. The number of online friends predicted how much grey matter, the brain's working tissue, people had in three areas, including ones tied to social perception and memory.

g6306bc101.post: People read information about hazards such as nuclear power. The information was written to make people feel more favorable or less favorable toward each hazard. Then they rated how risky and how beneficial it was. When people felt more favorable, they saw less risk and more benefit.

g6529ad286.post: People wrote about their own death or about dental pain. Then they filled in the missing letters of word fragments, some right away and some after a delay. People who had thought about death and filled them in right away made more death-related words than those who waited.

g6655914b3.post: People saw items flashed one after another very quickly and had to pick out two targets. Some of the adults spoke one language and some spoke two. Bilingual adults were worse than monolingual adults at noticing the second target when it came soon after the first.

g665934120.post: People read about scientific studies and guessed how likely it was that the results would come out the same way again. Some were told how the study came out, and others were not. People who were told the result thought it was more likely to happen again.

g66f677083.post: Seventh graders said whether they thought intelligence can grow or is fixed. Then their math grades were followed for two years. Students who thought intelligence can grow saw their grades climb, while students who thought it is fixed stayed flat.

g672f1c2af.post: Babies were shown things to look at while a sensor measured blood oxygen in the sides of their brains, using light that passes through the scalp. Blood oxygen rose in two spots toward the back on each side, areas the researchers linked to the social brain network.

g679faa6d9.post: People read stories about someone who acted against their own better judgment. In some stories the action was bad and in others it was neutral. Then they rated how much the person showed weakness of will. People were more likely to say so when the action was bad.

g68d204b37.post: People read descriptions of a person's behavior, written either as what the person was doing or as what the person did. Then they rated how intentional the behavior was. People who read what the person was doing rated the behavior as more intentional.

g68e6d6c15.post: Employees chose between helping a colleague, a career-advancing project, or a project taking the company in a new direction. Some were first prompted to think of a long future at work, some a short one, and some not at all. Those prompted to think long were less likely to choose helping a colleague.

g6a11f9966.post: People saw products with either a round logo or an angular one. Then they rated how comfortable and how durable each product seemed. Products with round logos were rated as more comfortable and less durable than products with angular logos.

g6a77908a7.post: People quickly judged whether five-word sequences were grammatical. Some wrong ones were made by swapping two neighboring words in a correct sentence, like 'The white cat was big' becoming 'The white was cat big'. People were slower to call those wrong than wrong ones made from an already wrong sequence.

g6b000ff80.post: People chose whether to receive health-related information. For some they had to opt in to get it, and for others they had to opt out to avoid it. More people agreed to receive it when they had to opt out.

g6b12ac86b.post: People chose whether to enter a competition based on solving calculations. Under one rule nothing changed, and under another one extra correct calculation was added to every woman's score. Women entered the competition more often under the rule that added to their score.

g6b7e4fd72.post: People were asked to think about either a big secret they were keeping or a trivial one. Then they did a throwing task, and researchers measured how far their throws went past the mark. People thinking of big secrets overthrew more than people thinking of trivial secrets.

g6bf6b8afe.post: People chose between two options. In some conditions a third, clearly worse option was added. Some people were also asked to think about how much they might regret their choice. Thinking about regret stopped the worse third option from pushing people toward the more expensive choice.

g6c1701060.post: Some people planned how they would carry out a decision. Others weighed up a decision, and others did neither. Then everyone said how they felt about several things unrelated to the decision. People who had planned how to carry out their decision had less mixed feelings about those things.

g6c6f2a3ab.post: People responded to letters shown on a screen while hearing a letter spoken at the same time, which they were meant to ignore. Sometimes the spoken letter had the same name as the one on the screen, and sometimes it was a different letter. People responded faster when the names matched.

g6f454777f.post: Adults read a short literary fiction story or a nonfiction article. Then they took a test of how well they understand other people's emotions. People who read the literary fiction story did better than people who read the nonfiction article.

g6f82cebed.post: People did tasks that tested attention and memory with their own smartphone on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. People did worse when their smartphone was nearby than when it was in another room.

g6f8394118.post: Adults received money offers, some fair and some unfair, that were worth the same amount of money. They rated how happy each offer made them while their brain activity was recorded. Fair offers made people happier than unfair offers of the same value.

g70cae8571.post: People held either a heavy clipboard or a light one while they rated job candidates on how important they seemed, from 1 to 7. People holding the heavy clipboard rated the candidates as more important.

g70fbb0cff.post: People tried to recall the same list of items in order, over and over, with new lists mixed in. The more often they had given a particular answer before, the more likely they were to give it again, whether it was right or wrong.

g735e3d716.post: People played a golf putting game. Some were told the ball they were using was lucky, and others used a neutral ball. People did better with the ball they believed was lucky.

g7403844c5.post: People read a story that contained a morally odd statement. Some read it as a police story and others as an Aztec myth, with the same statement in both. People resisted going along with the statement more in the police story than in the myth.

g744e4cb3a.post: Adults chose between completing a task alone or together with a partner. Doing it alone was the more effective way to reach the goal. Adults preferred to do it together anyway.

g7571d43b7.post: People read climate information from NASA online and shared what they thought it showed in small groups. Some groups had only liberals or only conservatives, and others had both. When liberals and conservatives shared their views with no party labels showing, both got better at reading the data, and the gap between their beliefs disappeared.

g7668ae1fa.post: Adults said whether they owned each of 52 things and how much they wanted each one. Then they rated how happy they were. The more of the things they wanted that people had, the happier they were.

g76da92b99.post: People studied words, some shown once and some shown twice. Then they were told to forget some of the words before recalling them. When told to forget, people forgot the words they had seen twice more easily than those they had seen once.

g7861778bc.post: People read descriptions of decisions that were identical except for how things turned out, a success or a failure. Then they rated how good each decision was. People rated the decision as better when it turned out well.

g788a58218.post: People recalled something unethical they did, something ethical they did, or a neutral event. Then they rated how human they felt. People who recalled the unethical act felt less human than people who recalled the ethical act.

g794cc8ebf.post: Children played a game where two puppets, each starting with a different number of chips, gave some chips to the child. Then the child picked which puppet was nicer. Four-year-olds picked the puppet that gave more chips, while five-year-olds started to look at what share of its chips each puppet gave.

g79e116167.post: Students read science texts. Some then practiced recalling what they had read, and others studied the texts by making concept maps. One week later everyone took a final test. Students who practiced recalling did better.

g79ea71c65.post: Hiring managers read about job candidates who were either highly capable or capable enough. They rated how committed each candidate would be to the organization and decided whether to offer a job. Managers saw highly capable candidates as less committed and were less likely to offer them the job.

g7a228798d.post: Some people were told they would probably get a mug, and others that they probably would not. Then everyone named the lowest price they would sell the mug for. The people who expected to keep the mug asked for more money.

g7a69bfa12.post: College students answered questions about how often they look for reassurance about tests. Researchers then looked up their ACT college entrance test scores in their academic records. Students who sought more reassurance scored lower on the ACT.

g7acb4c9b7.post: People read about a stranger, described either in words that made him seem less than human or in words that made him seem fully human. Then they said how willing they would be to break his thumb for money. People were more willing when he was described as less than human.

g7b69cf6d1.post: People rated words for how useful each would be in a survival situation, or in a richly described scenario that was not about survival. Then they recalled the words. People remembered more of the words they had rated for survival.

g7c8fefa08.post: People chose between two programs where lives were at stake. One group read: 200 saved for sure, or a one-in-three chance of saving 600. Another read: 400 die for sure, or a one-in-three chance nobody dies. Most took the sure thing when it was about lives saved, and the gamble when it was about deaths.

g7de19e633.post: People were grouped by how they weigh other people's outcomes: caring about others, caring only about themselves, or wanting to beat others. Young, middle-aged, and older adults were compared. Middle-aged and older adults had more people who care about others than young adults did, and fewer of the other two types.

g7e2f508b1.post: Some people were subtly exposed to the word red, and others to the word gray. None of them guessed what the study was really about. Then everyone took a test. People who got the word red scored lower than people who got the word gray.

g7f1c9c81e.post: Right-handed and left-handed people looked at each of their arms and hands one at a time and judged how long they were. Right-handed people judged their right arm and hand to be longer than their left. Left-handed people judged both arms accurately.

g7fa992dfe.post: People looked at ads that promised a change. Some ads showed just the before and after pictures, and others also showed pictures of the steps in between. People found the ads with the in-between steps more believable.

g7fd2d48bd.post: People made a numerical estimate after seeing a starting number. For some the number was precise, and for others it was rounded. People adjusted less away from the precise number than from the rounded one.

g8156193d1.post: Some people wrote about the role of God in their lives, and others wrote about their day. Then everyone chose whether to follow advice from a computer or from a human. The people who wrote about God leaned more toward the computer.

g818de5171.post: People who use social media a lot and people who use it less saw social media images and other images. After each image they rated how pleasant an unrelated Chinese character looked. Frequent users rated the characters as more pleasant after social media images than after the other images, while less frequent users rated them the same.

g82018052d.post: People worked on two different visual tasks. They believed they would probably do one of the tasks again later, and probably not the other. Which task was which varied across people. People did better on the task they thought they were unlikely to complete later than on the one they thought they were likely to complete.

g84bb5cd65.post: Preschool children and adults looked at eight pictures at once and had to find one particular picture. Sometimes the picture they were looking for was a snake, and sometimes a flower, a frog or a caterpillar. Both children and adults found the snake faster than the others.

g84dd89e40.post: People were randomly asked to think about a recession or about architecture. Then they rated how much meaning they felt in their life. People who thought about a recession felt their life had less meaning.

g85938cde3.post: People saw a word like 'farmer' in the middle of the screen with a word on each side. They had to decide whether the middle word was a real word. They were faster when the side words were 'farm' than when the side words were unrelated.

g885a60293.post: People looked at ads that put either a sexually charged scene or a neutral scene next to an expensive or a cheap product. Then they rated how they felt about the imagery. Women reacted less negatively to the sexual imagery when the product was expensive than when it was cheap.

g88d673018.post: A public attitudes survey asked Londoners about their police, and the day each person was surveyed was random. Black Londoners surveyed after the police killing of Eric Garner in New York were less satisfied with London's police than those surveyed before. White and South Asian Londoners changed little.

g8a51cb052.post: People looked at photographs of tennis players at their peak emotional moments. Some saw only the body, some only the face, and some the face with the body. They rated how positive or negative the player felt. People could tell positive from negative by looking at the body alone, but not by looking at the face alone.

g8a82e2f67.post: People imagined working on a team project and read a greeting from a teammate. Some greetings had smileys and some didn't. Then people rated the sender. In formal work messages, the sender who used smileys seemed less competent.

g8add51e26.post: Poorer and richer people were asked to think about a money problem. Then they did a test of how well they could focus their attention. The poorer people did worse on the test than the richer people.

g8af3c94ff.post: People played an online game as a fake news producer and learned six tricks used to spread misinformation. Before and after playing, they rated their ability to spot and resist misinformation. After playing, people rated their ability higher.

g8b8569b99.post: People read a statement from a made-up government official that set low or high expectations for the city's services. Then they looked at photos of streets that were cleaner or dirtier and rated how satisfied they were with public services. People who saw the cleaner streets were more satisfied than people who saw the dirtier ones.

g8d0439b1d.post: People drank a sweet drink, a bitter drink or water. Then everyone rated how wrong various moral misdeeds were. The people who drank the bitter drink judged the misdeeds more harshly than the people who drank water.

g8f84ec622.post: People negotiated a simulated deal after being given a weak alternative, a strong alternative, or no alternative. Researchers recorded each person's first offer. People with a weak alternative made lower first offers than people with no alternative or a strong one.

g90547626e.post: People watched a series of actions and split it into separate segments. Some believed they would probably go on to the next part of the experiment and do those actions themselves. Others believed they probably wouldn't. People who thought they were unlikely to continue split the actions into fewer segments than people who thought they were likely to.

g9172d5ab7.post: People decided how much more to invest in a project that was failing. Some were told they would be judged on how they made the decision, and others had no such evaluation. People judged on their decision process committed fewer resources to the failing project.

g94b52f3ad.post: Arabic speakers who use two sets of number symbols saw pairs of digits, written in the same set or in different sets. They only had to say whether the two digits looked identical, whatever their value. They still answered faster when the numbers were far apart in value than when they were close.

g959d1a09f.post: People read either neuroscience articles about the brain basis of human behavior or other science articles. Then they recommended a prison sentence for a wrongdoer and said how much to blame the wrongdoer. People who read the neuroscience articles recommended shorter sentences and blamed the wrongdoer less.

g95ad01eb6.post: Some people were first led to think about God and others were not. Then everyone chose whether to follow a song recommended by artificial intelligence. People who had thought about God were more willing to follow the AI's recommendation.

g965daa634.post: Adults got 25 painful electric shocks to the arm and rated how much each one hurt. Some shocks came alone and some came a split second after a weak electrical pulse. Shocks that came after a weak pulse were rated as less painful.

g9706097f8.post: People studied pairs of words, then practiced recalling some of them, which made them forget other related pairs. After that they studied some of the forgotten pairs again, along with some they hadn't forgotten. Relearning helped more for the pairs they had forgotten.

g974c7f1c7.post: People chose between a kiss from their favorite movie star and $50 in cash. For some the choice was between getting each for sure, and for others between a tiny chance of each. When both were certain, people preferred the cash, but when each was only a tiny chance, they preferred the kiss.

g988316a54.post: People in Hong Kong and in the US were asked where rich and poor people live in an imaginary city. Hong Kong people put the rich people in the south and the poor people in the north. People in the US did the opposite.

g9b5613ee7.post: People read about unfamiliar natural events, with no explanation of how they work. Some were told that scientists understand the events, and others that scientists don't yet. Then everyone rated how well they understood the events themselves. Those told that scientists understand rated their own understanding higher.

g9b7ac8e03.post: People watched videos of people lying or telling the truth, then judged which statements were lies. Some were distracted before deciding, some were told to deliberate, and some decided right away. The distracted people spotted lies and truths more accurately than the others.

g9e69b4db0.post: Students took a math pretest. Later they took a high-pressure math test, and some wrote about their thoughts right before it while others did not. Students who wrote about their thoughts improved more from the first test to the second.

ga040598b9.post: People looked at a series of still photographs that implied movement in one direction. Then they judged which way patterns of moving dots were going. After the photos, people saw real motion as heading in the opposite direction.

ga0e986d3f.post: People looked at packages of snack foods that showed different numbers of product units on the front, and judged how many items each package contained. People thought a package held more food when it showed more product units.

ga2768bdc1.post: People in 17 countries watched real news clips while their bodies were monitored and they reported their feelings. Some clips were negative, some neutral and some positive. Negative news set off stronger bodily and emotional reactions than the other clips.

ga2d094579.post: People read about a virtual reality machine that provides pleasurable experiences. Some read that their life was going badly and others that it was going well. Then they chose whether to stay connected to the machine or return to reality. People whose life was going badly were more willing to stay connected.

ga2d2a169e.post: Canadians read about a made-up Olympic athlete. He was either Canadian-American or Belgian-American, and he either won or lost. Then they rated how Canadian he was. The Canadian-American athlete was seen as more Canadian when he won than when he lost.

ga37baefbb.post: American adults read information about rising economic inequality in the United States, or read control information. Then they rated how important being born wealthy and how important hard work are for getting ahead. People who read about rising inequality said being born wealthy matters more and hard work matters less.

ga5eb8a37f.post: Some people ate soup from bowls that slowly and secretly refilled as they ate, and others ate from normal bowls. The people with the refilling bowls ate about 73% more soup. They did not think they had eaten more, or feel any fuller.

ga8fbea240.post: People read messages urging them to protect the environment. Some messages talked about harm and care, and others about keeping nature pure and clean. Conservatives who read the purity version cared more about the environment.

ga942ab3cf.post: People played firms and workers in a lab job market. Some firms could check an applicant's work attitude before hiring, and some could not. The firms that could check produced more total value.

ga97d8cb70.post: People watched two flashes of light appear one right after the other in the same spot and said whether they saw one flash or two. Sometimes a cue pointed to the spot just before, and sometimes not. People were worse at telling the two flashes apart when a cue pointed to the spot.

gac8c2880b.post: White Americans read about the projected shift toward a nation where racial minorities are the majority, or read a control passage. Then they reported how much they supported conservative policy positions. Those who read about the demographic shift supported conservative positions more strongly.

gaf2f5a5ed.post: Some people were put in a situation where they had no control over what happened, and others in one where they had complete control. Then everyone said how much physical pain they felt. The people with no control reported more than double the pain.

gb0ab41308.post: People received a greedy, an equal or a generous split of money or work from an anonymous person. Then they divided more resources with a different anonymous person. People treated greedily passed on more greed than people treated generously passed on generosity.

gb0bff7869.post: People were taught to fear two signals, and then one of the two was unlearned. The next day both signals were shown again while their sweat and brain waves were recorded. The signal that had never been unlearned set off a bigger sweat response and more of one kind of brain wave at the front of the head.

gb1de46812.post: People answered reasoning questions. For some, the questions were printed in a degraded, hard-to-read font, and for others in a normal, easy-to-read font. People did better on the questions when they were hard to read.

gb36500073.post: People finished a survey, were paid five one-dollar bills, and could donate any of it to Save the Children. Some read about one little girl with her picture, others read facts about hunger in Africa. Half also read a short lesson on how people give more to a single person than to statistics. The lesson lowered giving only for people who saw the girl.

gb38550e49.post: People read about a chairman whose pursuit of profits also harmed or helped the environment. Then they rated whether he brought about that side effect on purpose. People said he did it on purpose more when the side effect was harmful than when it was helpful.

gb3c4b9096.post: Some people solved a set of tricky puzzles before judging some moral dilemmas, and others solved them afterward. People who did the puzzles first judged actions that harm some people to help others as more acceptable.

gb3f92eda2.post: Six teachers ran a new extra-help program with second graders for 6 to 8 weeks. It worked on reading aloud smoothly and on staying engaged in class, together. Students were measured on both before and during the program. Their reading and their classroom behavior both improved from before the program to during it.

gb44fa3145.post: People answered 18 questions about how open they are to opposing views. Then they chose how much to read from U.S. senators of their own party and from senators of the other party. The more open people were, the bigger the share they chose to read from senators of the other party.

gb52ce49fe.post: People looked at webpages with ads on backgrounds that were simple or complicated. Then they rated how they felt about the ad, the brand, buying the product and the website. Simpler backgrounds led to more positive feelings on all four.

gb83f6a371.post: White people watched videos of Black and White speakers talking about their relationships. Some of the speakers told the truth and some lied, and the viewers judged which. The White viewers said 'truth' more often for the Black speakers.

gbcc2322ec.post: Adults played an exercise video game in which they held an abdominal plank as long as they could. Then some exercised alone and others with an Internet partner, and everyone held a plank again. People with an Internet partner held the plank longer than people alone.

gc2877ee3c.post: Some people were put in a frame of mind of having a lot of power, and others of having little. Then everyone rated how sarcastic a message would seem to a reader who lacked the sender's inside knowledge. People in the high-power group rated it as more sarcastic than the low-power group did.

gc2a9660bc.post: Some people were reminded of scarcity and others of plenty. Then everyone had to come up with uses for a given product. The people reminded of scarcity came up with more novel uses.

gc2ed93a6d.post: Drivers rated how safe and how skillful they are compared with the average driver. People rated themselves as safer and more skillful than the average driver.

gc4e84cffd.post: People traded assets in a market. In some markets what the asset was truly worth stayed the same over time, and in others it went down. Prices moved farther away from the true worth when it went down.

gc56d9f446.post: African American and White professionals read about workplaces that varied in how many minority employees they had and in whether they valued diversity or were colorblind. They rated how much they would trust each one. African American professionals distrusted a workplace with few minorities that was colorblind rather than valuing diversity.

gc5e0ea304.post: People recalled either an unethical deed or an ethical one. Then they were offered a choice between an antiseptic wipe and another product. People who recalled the unethical deed were more likely to take the wipe.

gc5ef78cc0.post: Adults spent 90 minutes either doing a demanding mental task or watching emotionally neutral documentaries. Then they cycled at high intensity until they could not continue. After the demanding mental task, people gave up cycling sooner.

gc6d419676.post: People looked at objects and products in colors that were either vivid or dull, and rated how big each one looked. People rated the products in vivid, highly saturated colors as larger.

gc79a4053c.post: People thought about personality traits, either ones about being friendly and close to others or ones about being capable and getting things done. Then they estimated how warm the room was. Those who thought about the friendly traits guessed the room was warmer than those who thought about the capable traits.

gc81bb12a2.post: People were told something negative about a health risk, a risk described as either changeable or unchangeable. Some were asked to think about it in broad, big-picture terms, and others in concrete detail. When the risk was changeable, big-picture thinking made people more eager to find out more.

gc8c561191.post: Men and women judged whether women's nonverbal cues showed friendliness or sexual interest. Men were worse than women at telling the two apart.

gc985a4195.post: People looked at a series of objects and said whether each was new, seen before, or similar to one seen before. Right after seeing a new object, they were better at noticing a subtle change in a similar object than right after recognizing an old one.

gc99e8664e.post: Thousands of German adults who had jobs rated their personality, and then rated it again four years later. In between, some of them lost their jobs. The people who became unemployed changed more in agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness than the people who kept working.

gc9ea607b2.post: People unscrambled sentences, some of which brought analytic thinking to mind and others not. Then they rated how much they believed in conspiracy theories. People primed to think analytically believed in conspiracy theories less.

gca7778a7b.post: Countries were compared on how many of their people become organ donors. In some countries people are donors unless they opt out, and in others they are donors only if they opt in. Donation rates were higher where people were donors unless they opted out.

gcc95fcb04.post: White people expected to have a conversation with a Black partner, about either racial profiling or love and relationships. Then the researchers measured how far apart they sat. The ones who feared seeming racist sat farther from the partner.

gcebe7f064.post: Groups played a trading game in a lab. Some groups had a money object to trade with and some did not. The groups with money got more out of their trading.

gcf7531c11.post: People read short stories about a person who thought something was true. In some stories the person would lose a lot if they were wrong, and in others very little. People were less likely to say the person knew it when the stakes were high.

gd0c94c9b9.post: People did a task in which some were in a poor group and others in a rich group. Within each group, some got a preview and some did not. Poor people did about the same with or without a preview, while rich people did better with a preview than without.

gd197285cf.post: People faced mild or intense upsetting pictures or electric shocks. Each time they chose between two ways to handle their feelings: thinking about the situation differently, or distracting themselves. People preferred thinking about it differently for the mild situations and distracting themselves for the intense ones.

gd1bd22fa0.post: People watched letters flash by very fast, and two of the letters had a ring around them. They had to name both ringed letters. When the second ringed letter came soon after the first, people picked it out less often, more slowly and less precisely.

gd23779534.post: People played an economic game in which they chose how much of their own money to contribute, at a cost to themselves, to benefit others. Before playing, some were nudged to trust their gut feelings and others were nudged to think things over carefully. People nudged to trust their gut contributed more than people nudged to reflect.

gd2eae5db4.post: Before a speed-dating event, people rated what they wanted in an ideal partner. At the event they met partners and rated their romantic interest in each one. Researchers compared those ratings with each partner's attractiveness and earning prospects. Attractiveness and earning prospects shaped romantic interest no differently for men than for women.

gd3a6c2164.post: High school students, some Asian American and some European American, experienced a failure. Then they reported how motivated they felt by their mothers. Asian American students were more motivated by their mothers than European American students were.

gd5137e011.post: Researchers compared the criminal records of incarcerated men who had antisocial personality disorder, antisocial personality disorder plus psychopathy, or neither. Men with antisocial personality disorder alone had committed more types of crimes than men with neither.

gd5ff42d8e.post: People searched displays of four or eight items for a target, once while sitting and once while standing. People searched more slowly while standing than while sitting.

gd6109585a.post: People read a custody case about two parents. Some were asked which parent should be awarded the child, and others which should be denied the child. The same parent was the more popular answer to both questions.

gd6b425692.post: People saw some die rolls: three 6's, two 6's, or two 6's and a 3. Each person guessed how long the whole sequence of rolls had been. People who saw three 6's guessed a longer sequence than people who saw two 6's or the mix.

gd6b51f068.post: People read stories in which a harmful outcome could come from doing something or from doing nothing, with the person's intentions, motives and the outcome the same. They rated how immoral the person's choice was. People rated harm from doing nothing as less immoral than harm from doing something.

gd7bd1cb0b.post: People saw two curtains on a screen and guessed which one hid a picture. Only after they guessed did the computer randomly pick which side the picture was on. When the hidden picture was erotic, people picked the right curtain more often than chance.

gd7c57f93a.post: People took a perspective-taking test. Some were told it measured spatial ability, and others that it measured empathy, with human figures added to the empathy version. Men outperformed women when the test was framed as spatial but not when it was framed as social.

gd889e2c02.post: People briefly viewed a display of colored circles of different sizes, then reported the size of one circle they were asked about. People remembered a circle as larger when it was among larger circles of the same color, and smaller when it was among smaller ones.

gd8dd1a053.post: People drank a soft drink that had either sugar or artificial sweetener. Then they chose again and again between a smaller amount of money now and a larger amount later. The people who drank sugar valued the larger, later amount more than the people who drank artificial sweetener.

gd9409ebf3.post: Children with autism either got 35 to 40 hours a week of early intensive behavioral treatment from a community agency or went to special education classes, as their parents chose. Researchers tested their IQ and adaptive behavior over three years. The treated children had higher IQ and adaptive behavior scores than the children in special education.

gda118e382.post: People chose between less money soon and more money later. Some were nudged to line the two offers up and compare them side by side. Others were nudged to look at one offer at a time. The people nudged to compare were more willing to wait.

gda60c1911.post: People watched a film clip that wasn't very funny. Some were told beforehand that it was good, and others were told nothing. People who like thinking hard enjoyed it less after being told it was good, while people who don't enjoyed it more.

gdab919b48.post: People answered a series of difficult trivia questions. Then they named the ink color of words as fast as they could, some about computers and some not. After the hard questions, computer-related words came to mind more readily than other words.

gdad375184.post: Younger and older adults imagined donating money and time to relatives and to people they were not related to, at different levels of closeness. Older adults donated less to people they were not related to than younger adults did, but gave more time to relatives.

gdcd682156.post: Some people were asked to recall a time they were treated with disrespect, and others to recall an ordinary experience. Then everyone rated how selfish and untrustworthy they think people are. Those who had recalled being disrespected were more cynical.

gdced4f949.post: Some people were made to feel lonely, some scared and some neither. Then everyone rated how much they believed in supernatural beings, and how many social traits their pets had. The lonely people believed more in supernatural beings and saw more social traits in their pets.

gdd7b2a1ee.post: People watched an upsetting movie. Some were told just to watch it, some to feel less, and some to feel more. Afterwards, the ones who tried to change their feelings said it took more effort than just watching.
