ge13b33391.post: German speakers read words for groups of people, either in the usual masculine form or in forms that also name or include women. Then they named their favorite musicians. Those who read the masculine-only form named fewer women than the others.

ge2247dfb2.post: People took the role of a buyer choosing between three suppliers. They read a few customer comments about each one, then guessed how many of all its comments were good and how many were bad. They guessed too few were good and too many were bad, and the more comments a supplier had, the bigger the mistake.

ge290113ed.post: People were led to think about an economic recession or an economic upswing. Then they decided how to split resources between girls and boys. People who thought about a recession gave more to girls than people who thought about an upswing.

ge6f20433e.post: Some people were made to think about God, and others were not. Everyone then said how willing they were to consider advice from artificial intelligence. People who had thought about God were more willing to consider AI advice than people who had not.

ge80af4395.post: People guessed something they did not know, then guessed again after a delay. Researchers averaged each person's two guesses. The average of the two guesses was closer to the truth than the first guess alone.

gea051ba4e.post: People agreed or disagreed with statements by moving a handle toward one of two answers, while the path of the movement was recorded. Some statements seemed clearly true, some clearly false, and some partly true and partly false. People's hand movements wavered more on the partly true, partly false statements.

geb693aff5.post: People in Calgary listened to recordings of workers speaking English. Some of the speakers were native English speakers and some were native Tagalog speakers. The listeners rated the Tagalog speakers as less competent and harder to understand.

gec15e0bd3.post: Two people sat in the same room, each doing half of a reaction-time task by responding to just one of two possible signals. They sat farther apart than arm's reach. Sitting close, people usually respond faster when a signal appears on the same side as their response. At this distance, that speed advantage did not show up.

gec7677bff.post: People read about someone giving a gift, either a $45 scarf or a $55 coat. Each person read about only one of them and rated how generous the giver was. The giver of the cheaper scarf was rated more generous than the giver of the coat.

gecd6d761d.post: Some people were asked for a small favor. Others were first asked for an extreme favor, which they refused, and then asked for the small favor. People who had first refused the extreme favor were more likely to agree to the small one.

gedf602d20.post: Women rated their mood while thinking about their next menstrual period, and again while remembering their last one. They reported stronger emotion while looking ahead to it than while remembering it.

geeed8bb26.post: People made plans for managing a limited resource when it was more or less tight. Some plans stretched the resource to make it last, and others gave up less important goals to save it. The tighter the resource, the more people gave up less important goals instead of stretching it.

gef528c7da.post: People read statements and rated how likely each was to be true. Each statement had the same content but was written either in concrete language or in abstract language. People judged the concrete wording as more likely to be true.

gefa13784d.post: People were put in a situation that made them feel either lower or higher in social standing compared with others. Then they did a task that measured their automatic, gut-level liking for calorie-packed foods versus fruits and vegetables. Those made to feel low in status showed a trend toward a stronger automatic preference for the calorie-packed foods than those made to feel high.

gf0aab7478.post: People viewed an advertisement for lamb. In one version the lamb was shown as a living animal, and in the other as meat. Then they reported how much empathy they felt. People felt more empathy when the lamb was shown as a living animal.

gf0f4e464b.post: Pairs of people watched a film, each seeing a different version, and then discussed it. Afterwards each person recalled details alone. People remembered the details they had not discussed better than the details they had.

gf15632d5b.post: In a game, two sides had to pick a judge for a dispute. In some games both sides struck out names at the same time. In others they took turns narrowing down a list. The turn-taking games gave the two sides higher payoffs.

gf1de109ef.post: People in a public place reported their political attitudes. For some, a hand-sanitizer dispenser was nearby, and for others it was not. People near the hand sanitizer reported more politically conservative attitudes.

gf2a93cafc.post: Some people took part in a racist task and others only watched it. Then they rated a person who refused to go along with it. People who had taken part disliked the person who refused, but people who had only watched did not.

gf368bfa75.post: Women rated how attractive they found men who were described as either single or already in a relationship. Women who already had a partner favored the attached men at times in their cycle when they were least likely to conceive. At times when they were most likely to conceive, they favored single, masculine men.

gf42fa8bd7.post: People played a money game where they could cooperate with another player. They could choose whether to see exactly what cooperating would cost them. For some, others could see whether they looked; for others, it stayed hidden. Fewer people looked at the cost when it was observable (59%) than when it was hidden (70%).

gf4738c406.post: People looked at spiky shapes and rounded shapes and rated how emotionally arousing each one was. People rated the spiky shapes as more emotionally arousing than the rounded ones.

gf529ea20e.post: People read about an organization that had either many levels of bosses or few. Then they rated how much corruption they expected from its employees. People expected more corruption in the organization with more bosses over workers.

gf83e798d8.post: People saw photos of the crowds at the 2017 Trump inauguration and the 2009 Obama inauguration and picked which crowd was larger. Trump supporters were more likely than other people to wrongly pick Trump's crowd.

gf8f10b3cf.post: Adults listed who they spent each part of yesterday with. Some had spent time with a wide mix of people, such as a partner, friends, coworkers and family, and others with fewer kinds of people. The people with the wider mix said they felt better about their lives.

gfaf524330.post: People evaluated leaders who acted either dominant or communal. The leaders were Black or White, women or men. White female leaders were given lower status when they acted dominant rather than communal, but Black female leaders were not.

gfb894d68f.post: People read about someone making a moral or an immoral decision, either quickly or slowly. Then they rated the person's moral character. Quick immoral decisions made the person look worse than slow ones, and quick moral decisions made the person look better than slow ones.

gfc9f764ec.post: People rated how much they liked four vegetables. Then some were led to think the vegetables were scarce and others plentiful, and everyone chose six pieces from the set. People who saw the vegetables as scarce chose a bigger share of their favorite than people who saw them as plentiful.

gfd42786a8.post: People were told a study was about vigilance and watched several hundred words and images go by. Mixed in, one unfamiliar object kept appearing with positive items and another with negative ones. Later people liked the object paired with positive items more, though they did not remember the pairings.

gfd6537bed.post: People read about someone from a harsh, unpredictable place or from a secure, stable one, rich or poor. Then they guessed how impulsive and short-sighted that person was. People from the harsh places were judged as more impulsive and short-sighted, whether rich or poor.

gfd8847805.post: People made number estimates, starting from a number they had come up with themselves. Some were kept mentally busy while they adjusted their guess. The people who weren't busy moved their estimates further away from the starting number.

gfd8fe4bc1.post: Rats were trained with delayed rewards, with immediate rewards, or not at all. Then they chose between a smaller immediate reward and a larger delayed one. Rats trained with delayed rewards chose the larger, later reward more often than rats trained with immediate rewards or no training.

gff92ccfc2.post: People saw a word for something usually up high, like head, or down low, like foot. Then they tried to identify a target that appeared at the top or the bottom of the screen. They made more errors when the target appeared where the word's object usually is than when it appeared in the opposite place.

gffc4447be.post: American students wrote about their own death or about watching television. Then they read two essays, one praising the United States and one criticizing it, and rated how much they liked each author. Students who wrote about their own death liked the author who praised the country more than the one who criticized it.

p0016cde7f.post: Eight of the most disruptive children in a third grade class were watched to see how often they misbehaved. Then the teacher began giving them ratings that they could trade for candy and small trinkets. Once the ratings began, the children's misbehavior dropped sharply compared with before.

p00abd1e0e.post: Four learners were taught to read sets of four sight words. In one version, a set counted as learned only when the average across all four words was perfect. In the other, each word was checked on its own, and a new word replaced it as soon as it was learned. All four learners learned the words faster with the check-each-word version.

p015019627.post: Finnish parents and teachers answered surveys about the school reforms going on at the time. Their views fell into two kinds of thinking: a selective one that treated intelligence as natural, and a comprehensive one that saw intelligence as depending on a person's social surroundings.

p0191d212b.post: People played a cooperation game and chose which of two groups to be in, one where members could punish others and one where they could not. Over time the entire population moved to the group with punishment, and the group without it emptied out.

p01c709683.post: Female college students who were very concerned about their weight and body shape were randomly split into two groups. One group had six weekly one-on-one therapy sessions focused on finding meaning in life. The other group waited seven weeks without sessions. The therapy group showed a bigger increase in meaning in life than the waiting group, right after the sessions and a month later.

p01d054681.post: Children with autism who often made repetitive, purposeless sounds worked with a teacher. Whenever a child made those sounds, the teacher gave easy spoken requests until the child followed three in a row without them. The children made substantially fewer of these sounds than in the times before the teacher did this.

p0236ddd52.post: Parents of kids aged 12 to 15 filled out an online survey about their child's exercise. They rated how they felt about their child doing aerobic exercise, which gets the heart pumping, and strength exercise, such as lifting weights. Parents had a positive attitude toward aerobic exercise but a less positive one toward strength exercise.

p02924b576.post: Pigeons pecked either of two keys to earn rewards. In one setup, the birds spent most of their time on the left key. In the other, a "stick with what pays best right now" rule predicted a move to the right key, even though that cut their rewards. All three birds eventually shifted as that rule predicted.

p0296a7645.post: Men and women were each asked to imagine their partner being unfaithful in two ways: having sex with someone else, or becoming emotionally close to someone else. They picked which would upset them more. Men and women differed a lot in which kind of unfaithfulness upset them more.

p02fa1e17d.post: After an interview about a person's problem behavior, practitioners ran test sessions that combined the likely triggers and rewards to see what kept the behavior going. A full test took about 25 minutes on average. Looking at just the first 3 to 5 minutes, the cause was identified in 80% of the 30 cases.

p030afcc04.post: Younger and older adults used a computer mouse to reach for a target on a screen. In some trials the target jumped to a new spot mid-reach, so they had to change course. Older adults took longer to correct, made more rigid corrections, and ended up less accurate than younger adults.

p032ce744b.post: Adults learned made-up names for objects, each one placed in a sentence. Some sentences strongly suggested what the thing would be, while others left it more open. Adults remembered a new word better when it went against a stronger expectation than when it went against a weaker one.

p03901e552.post: People were told they would be doing a handwriting task. They wrote either "Will I" or "I will" 20 times, plus two groups who wrote just "I" or just "Will." Then everyone tried to unscramble 10 words into new words. People who wrote "Will I" solved more of the anagrams than people in any other group.

p0434651be.post: People read 29 short scenarios, such as doing a bad job caring for your children or having poor table manners. Some rated how negatively they would view another person in each scenario. A different group rated how much shame they would feel if it were them. The more negatively a scenario was judged by others, the more shame people said they would feel.

p043ce63a0.post: College men trained for two weeks in four-person teams on a computer-simulated combat mission. Some tasks in it were done alone, and others needed the whole team. Each task was rated on new scales meant to show how team-based it is. The scales rated the team tasks differently from the individual tasks.

p049ddaa7c.post: People practiced a timing task that involved pressing keys in a set sequence. One group could ask for feedback on how they did whenever they wanted it. A second group got feedback on a schedule they had no say in. On a test given later, the group that chose when to get feedback did better than the group that did not.

p051703b7f.post: Adult wheelchair basketball players filled out questionnaires about how gritty, hardy and resilient they are, and how satisfied they are with their lives. Athletes who scored higher on hardiness and resilience reported the highest quality of life.

p05181eb67.post: Students were randomly split into two groups. One group started a two-week mindfulness program on their own online right away, and the other group was put on a waiting list. Everyone answered questions about mindfulness, stress, and anxiety or low mood before and after. Students who did the program improved on all three, while the waiting-list students did not change.

p05d479f07.post: Boys with autism were taught social skills, like facing someone and looking them in the eye, in two different ways. Each boy learned some skills with one method and some with the other, in the same number of sessions. All 18 skills taught with the teaching interaction procedure were mastered, versus only 4 of 18 taught with social stories.

p06185dc09.post: People did a reaction-time task at a fast or slow pace, then were falsely accused of hitting a wrong key that damaged the computer. Another person said she either saw them hit it or saw nothing. People in the fast task with a witness were more likely to sign a confession than those in the slow task with no witness.

p061b08ff7.post: Children in grades 1 to 7 and adults thought about traits of people, some familiar and some new to them. They reasoned about ideas like a trait being there from birth and a trait never changing. By third grade, children's ideas started to fit together, but younger children expected less of a link than older children or adults.

p0638f1e27.post: People watched and listened to a talker say sentences in a happy, sad, or neutral way. In some videos they could see only the left half or only the right half of the talker's face. Speech tended to be picked up better with a happy face than with a sad or neutral one, on both sides of the face.

p0655cf50a.post: Mothers of children five and under filled out an online survey. It asked how much shame they felt, how far they fell short of the kind of mother they wanted to be, and how much they feared being judged by others. Among mothers who greatly feared being judged, falling short of their ideal went with much more shame. Among mothers who feared it little, the two were not related.

p0677c5b89.post: Three- and four-year-olds were asked what an absent puppet or person would think about a pretend game whose make-believe setup had been changed. The children also did a standard task about what someone else wrongly believes. Even 3-year-olds judged others' thoughts about pretend happenings accurately, and did less well on the wrong-belief task.

p0677d3225.post: Young and older adults pretended to be healthcare workers. They rated how much pain patients seemed to be in and offered them help. The patients were younger and older, men and women. Older patients and male patients were offered more help and seen as in more pain than younger and female patients.

p069730776.post: Women volunteered to join a group discussion about sex. Before joining, some read very embarrassing sexual material aloud, some read only mildly embarrassing words aloud, and some read nothing. Then everyone listened to the same recorded discussion and rated the group. Women who went through the severe, embarrassing entry test rated the group as more attractive than the others did.

p069e5c000.post: People viewed upsetting and neutral pictures while thinking about their feelings, with brain activity recorded. Sometimes they used "I" to think about it, other times their own name. Using their own name gave a smaller brain signal of emotional reaction to upsetting pictures than using "I," with no rise in a signal of mental effort.

p0853ab909.post: Rats spent time getting rewards right away. A comparison group was only handled and left to grow up. Then all the rats chose between a smaller reward and a larger reward that came later. The rats that had gotten immediate rewards picked the larger, later reward less often than the comparison group.

p085addf32.post: Children and teenagers in the UK filled out a short 12-question survey about how much they are shaped by the world around them. Researchers then used a statistical method to sort the answers into groups of similar kids. The answers fell into three distinct groups: low, medium and high sensitivity to surroundings.

p08a274f76.post: Students tried two puzzles that need a creative trick to solve. Some liked exploring new approaches and others liked sticking with familiar ones, and they also differed in prior experience. Explorers mostly did better with little experience, while the familiar-approach students mostly did better with a lot.

p08b2157e1.post: Some people ranked sets of cartoons from magazines by how funny they were, and others ranked the same cartoons by how aggressive they were. The cartoons ranked as more aggressive were also ranked as funnier.

p08ec30e7a.post: Students with autism did a set of skill checks, including matching, imitating, scanning, and telling sounds apart and pictures apart. Later they trained to connect spoken sounds with pictures. For 7 of the 9 students, how they did in training was related to how they did on the skill checks.

p08f54a7b5.post: People with developmental disabilities were taught new skills, and teaching stopped once they hit an accuracy goal. The goals differed, including the common one of 80% correct in three sessions in a row. Later, researchers checked whether the skills stuck. The 80% goal was sometimes not enough for skills to last.

p0928fed12.post: Toddlers got a chance to help an adult reach his goal. To work out what he wanted, they had to notice whether he wrongly believed a toy was inside a box. The 18-month-olds took the adult's belief into account when working out how to help him.

p09b9953f4.post: College psychology students spent a semester either learning listening skills in a 10-week training, staffing a helpline after passing that training, or working at a community agency. Everyone's communication was tested at the start and end. Only the students in the listening training improved their communication skills, though all three groups grew more confident.

p09e516dcf.post: Young teens were asked about the meaning of life and what it meant in their own lives. Earlier studies had only asked college students and older adults. The share of teens who seemed to understand the question and could talk about their own meaning was just as high as in the older groups.

p09ff55d9c.post: Adults aged 80 and older answered questions about their personality, such as whether they feel anxious or are extra sensitive, about every two years. Some were later diagnosed with dementia. Looking back at their answers, those people had become more anxious and emotionally unstable in the years before their diagnosis.

p0a10b5932.post: Married couples with a young child with an intellectual disability filled out questionnaires about their mood and support, and were watched with their child. Some children had Down syndrome; others had a different disability. Parents of children with Down syndrome looked better off than the other parents, but after accounting for family income, that advantage disappeared.

p0a3c323a3.post: A national group of adults was asked to report how many lies they had told in the past 24 hours. Some people reported none, while a few reported many. Almost half of all the reported lies came from just 5% of the people.

p0a57b1a20.post: Five people with autism were taught new skills, like naming things, over many training sessions. In one version, each item was counted as learned on its own. In the other, a whole set of items had to be learned together. Counting each item on its own took fewer sessions of name training for 3 of the 5 people.

p0a59f6dc2.post: One person described their thoughts aloud in a quiet room while another, in a separate room, focused on a randomly chosen picture or video clip. Afterward the first person rated four clips, one being that clip, for how well each matched their thoughts. The right one came out on top in 32% of sessions, versus 25% expected by chance.

p0a5d88c46.post: Families with a mother, a father, a 16-month-old toddler, and an older brother or sister took part in a family cleanup session. Researchers watched how the children responded when their parents asked them to help. The older children showed more wholehearted helping and more flat-out refusing than the toddlers did.

p0aa1e528c.post: People read words out loud while doing a second task at the same time. The second task was harder for some and easier for others. Some of the words were spelled in ways that don't match how they sound. Those oddly spelled words were read 39 milliseconds faster when the second task was harder.

p0abd66bae.post: Babies watched a box open to show two objects, identical or different. Later, before the box opened, a voice named the contents with one made-up word twice or two different made-up words. Babies hearing one word twice looked longer at two different objects than two identical ones; babies hearing two words showed a different pattern.

p0b7070249.post: College students rated how much statements like "Are you easily overwhelmed by strong sensory input?" described them. Researchers had a computer sort them into groups by answer pattern, without choosing the groups in advance. Instead of the two groups many theories expect, people fell into three: low, medium and high sensitivity.

p0bf11a508.post: Men guessed heads or tails for a series of coin tosses. Some got many right early and fewer later, others did worse early and better later, and others had a random mix of hits and misses. Those who got the early guesses right rated themselves as better at predicting coin tosses than the other two groups did.

p0c36edd10.post: Teens and young adults filled out questionnaires about their self-esteem and their depression, four times over several years. Researchers then checked which one came first. People with lower self-esteem were more depressed later on, but being depressed did not predict lower self-esteem later.

p0c3bdc84b.post: People judged how big objects were while their hands were magnified or not magnified. People judged objects as smaller when their hand was magnified.

p0c6812453.post: Women with obesity were randomly put into one of two weight-loss programs. One group got a printed manual and follow-up phone calls. The other group got exercise coaching, then two months later group sessions on using the same self-control skills to eat in a controlled way. The coaching group lost about 5.7 kg (6.1% of their starting weight) by month 6 and largely kept it off.

p0c76065cb.post: Teachers in kindergarten and first-grade classrooms across Canada used a web-based reading program with their classes for a full semester, about 20 hours per child. Other classrooms did not use it. By the end, children in the program classrooms were better at blending sounds into words and at knowing which sounds go with which letters than children in the other classrooms.

p0cc1d8c95.post: People heard two minutes of religious music, regular music, or white noise through headphones. Then they did number puzzles and marked on a sheet how many they solved, with more money for more solved, so they could lie. Religious people were more affected by the religious music than non-religious people were.

p0d42ed12b.post: People filled out a survey on their attitudes toward stuttering, then filled it out again later. In between, some were given something meant to improve attitudes and others were not. In both kinds of groups, people who started with the least positive attitudes improved greatly, while those who started with the most positive worsened greatly.

p0dc20f56a.post: People saw strings of letters stacked in a column and decided whether each was a real word. In one version every letter stood upright. In the other every letter was turned on its side, as if the whole word had been rotated. People were faster to decide with the turned letters than with the upright ones.

p0dc394907.post: People sat facing a humanoid robot that looked off to one side. Sometimes it first looked right into the person's eyes before looking away, and sometimes it avoided their eyes. Attention followed the robot's gaze more strongly when it had first made eye contact than when it had avoided their eyes.

p0e013cbf2.post: Three boys with autism were each approached by an unfamiliar adult who tried to lure them away with lines like "Come with me" or "Come see the Xbox in my car." Then they were taught to say no, run to a safe place, and tell a grown-up. Afterward, all three did this when approached again, and they still did it a month or so later.

p0e0c6e008.post: People did a computer task where distracting items either agreed with the right answer, clashed with it a little, or clashed with it a lot. Stronger clashes made people slower. Having just faced a clash made the next clash easier, and that benefit did not differ in size between weak and strong clashes, in reaction times or a brain signal.

p0eec1b5ac.post: People recalled or read about an achievement they were proud of and said how intensely they would show their pride to someone else. For some the achievement was relevant to that person, and for others it was not. People said they would show less pride when the achievement was relevant to the person watching.

p0f7f57c6e.post: Parents were asked to rate how good they were at seven kinds of ability, including math, spatial skills, music, and getting along with people. Mothers and fathers each rated themselves. Fathers rated themselves higher than mothers rated themselves on math and spatial ability.

p0fd4a2355.post: Teenage girls were measured on how heavy they were, how heavy they thought they were, and whether they had ever been teased about their weight or size. They also answered questions about their body image and eating. A history of being teased was linked to how their body image and eating problems developed.

p1063c7436.post: Children gave a saliva sample for a DNA test and were assessed for signs of depression. Some had been mistreated and some had not. Children with one version of a brain-growth gene and two short copies of a serotonin gene had the highest depression scores, but only among the mistreated children.

p10bcdfa83.post: Students who rarely finished schoolwork took a test of which reward would get them working, run by a researcher and by a teacher. Then they tried plans that matched the test result and plans that did not. For two of the four students, the test agreed across both adults and the matched plan worked better.

p10dbac579.post: Babies watched short videos of a hand reaching for one of two toys, a frog or a ball. Then the toys switched places, and the hand stopped halfway between them. Other babies saw a plastic claw make the same moves. Babies who saw the hand looked first at the same toy it had grabbed before, now in a new spot.

p110cf15ca.post: People spent a short time with a humanoid robot that acted either like a person or like a machine. Then researchers checked whether people explained the robot's actions by its thoughts and intentions, as we do for people. After the human-like robot they did so more than at the start; after the machine-like one, no change.

p11546e03a.post: Children did training sessions over several weeks that taught them how things relate, such as same, opposite, more than and less than. They took an IQ test before training, after the first part, and after the second part. A matched group got no training. The trained children's IQ scores rose after the first part and rose again after the second, compared with the no-training group.

p117831118.post: Some people wrote a letter to their future self and others did not. Then they made choices that could be delinquent. People who wrote to their future self were less inclined to make delinquent choices.

p12cd107b7.post: People recalled four events from their own lives. A week later, each one described those events to another person, who was secretly working with the researchers, and heard that person's scripted "memories." The partner then slipped two new details into a summary of each person's story. Afterward, about 30% of people recalled at least one of those made-up details as part of their own memory.

p13506a216.post: People heard either a spoken word, like "dog," or a matching sound, like a bark. A second later a picture appeared, and they pressed a button to say whether it matched what they heard. Their brain activity was recorded the whole time. Within a split second of seeing the picture, an early brain response was larger after hearing a word than after hearing the matching sound.

p1373ad411.post: European Canadians and Japanese people got information about someone's behavior that could be explained by the kind of person they are or by the situation they were in. Researchers measured which explanations people formed on their own. European Canadians formed more explanations about personality than about the situation, while Japanese people formed both about equally.

p13b08190b.post: Sixteen schools were randomly split into two groups. In one group, first-grade teachers were trained to teach reading in a more explicit, step-by-step way, with ongoing coaching. Teachers in the other group did not get the training. Trained teachers gave better explicit instruction and gave students more, and more accurate, chances to practice together.

p13be02908.post: Therapists read a short description of a client who quit therapy early. Some were told it was their own client, others that it was another therapist's client. Then they rated how likely each of several reasons was to have caused the client to quit. Therapists put more of the cause on the client or outside circumstances when the client was their own.

p13c936318.post: Newlywed wives reported their marital satisfaction over time and whether they used hormonal birth control. Trained raters scored each husband's face from a photo. Wives who started the relationship on birth control and later stopped were less satisfied if their husband's face was rated less attractive, but more satisfied if it was rated more attractive.

p13d1019a9.post: College students filled out a questionnaire that scored three sides of personality: boldness (staying calm and confident), meanness, and acting without restraint. Their scores were then compared with helpful and harmful outcomes. Boldness was generally unrelated to these outcomes, and it rarely added anything beyond meanness and lack of restraint.

p1411bec10.post: Teenagers staying in a psychiatric hospital filled out a questionnaire meant to spot borderline personality disorder. Trained staff also interviewed each teen to see who had the diagnosis. The questionnaire matched the interview with high accuracy, picking out most teens who had the diagnosis and most who didn't.

p148238991.post: People who reported feeling quite depressed got feedback that went against what they had expected. The groups were led to interpret that feedback in different ways, such as explaining away evidence that contradicts what you believe. How people were led to interpret it changed how much their expectations shifted afterward.

p14a1d0586.post: Babies watched videos of a woman looking down at a table with two toys. Before she turned to look at one toy, she did something different in each video: looked right at the baby, shivered, or did nothing. The babies tended to follow her gaze to the toy after the attention-grabbing moves, but not after she did nothing.

p154f8890d.post: Men crossing a scary suspension bridge or a non-scary bridge were approached by an attractive woman interviewer. She asked them to fill out a questionnaire that included writing stories about pictures. The men on the scary bridge wrote stories with more sexual content and were more likely to try to contact her afterward.

p15a5c0d0f.post: People looked at the same hidden-image picture, made of dots, five times a day for four days. Each time, researchers timed how long it took before the 3D shape popped out. Within each day, people got faster with every repeat.

p15b7e9a5e.post: Babies watched two people each tell a short story, both in English for some babies, and one in English and one in Spanish for others. Then the two either waved and smiled at each other or turned away with arms crossed. Babies expected two people who spoke the same language to be more likely to get along than two who spoke different languages.

p15c9a7638.post: Deaf elementary school students read a short story one page at a time. After each page, they said out loud, or signed, what they were thinking as they read. They used a considerably greater variety of strategies for building meaning from the story than for checking or fixing their understanding.

p15e030e75.post: People who gamble regularly and heavily chose between hypothetical money now and a larger amount later. Each person did this twice, once inside the betting facility where they usually gamble and once in a place like a coffee shop. For most of them, the setting changed how much they valued the money they would have to wait for.

p1618a25c7.post: A boy in a remedial class at an English secondary school kept track of his own study behavior. The self-tracking was used, then taken away, to see what changed. Compared with when he was not tracking, he spent more time on task, did less off-task behavior, and felt better about schoolwork.

p161b2fe56.post: Chimpanzees were given two kinds of problems where they had to act now to get a reward later. One was a trading task. The other was a task where they had to use a tool. Every chimpanzee failed to plan ahead in the trading task, but three did plan in the tool task.

p165f0a85d.post: Mothers and their 12-month-old babies were filmed in a room with no toys, while each mother filled out a questionnaire and the baby explored. Researchers scored how well each mother responded to her baby's cues. Using only those scores, they correctly sorted 94% of the babies as securely or anxiously attached to their mothers.

p16898f3aa.post: Female first- and second-grade teachers rated how anxious math situations make them feel, such as studying for a math test. Their students were tested in math at the start and end of the school year. By year's end, girls with more math-anxious teachers did worse at math than girls with less anxious teachers.

p1720c9d42.post: Adults reported their depression and anxiety symptoms, and how much they replay sad thoughts and problems in their heads. Their symptoms were measured again later. People with more depression at the start had more anxiety later, and people with more anxiety at the start had more depression later, with replaying thoughts fully explaining both.

p17456dd56.post: Business owners in the United States and Spain were assessed for ADHD symptoms, such as being impulsive and hyperactive. They were also scored on how much their firms focus on innovation, acting early, and taking risks. Owners with more hyperactive and impulsive symptoms scored higher on that focus.

p1761cc57c.post: First-year psychology students filled out questionnaires about how anxious and tense they usually are, how much they dislike not knowing what will happen, and how much they worry. Researchers then compared the scores across the questionnaires. People who were more anxious in general and who disliked uncertainty more each tended to worry more.

p17640ce39.post: Young adults in Germany were assessed on their personality and relationships three times over eight years. Some started their first partner relationship along the way, while others stayed single. Singles who were more anxious and moody (higher neuroticism) were more likely to start one, and their neuroticism dropped once they were in a relationship.

p177f019e8.post: Doctors and scientists at one medical school who occasionally led workshops for other faculty were interviewed about why they do it. The talks were recorded and typed up, and the researchers sorted what people said into themes. Five reasons came up: wanting to learn and grow, enjoying working with others, feeling a duty to give back, wanting better teaching and patient care, and plain fun.

p17f250782.post: Some people were reminded of their own death and others were not. Then everyone read about injured people, some badly hurt and some only mildly, and rated how much each victim was to blame. People reminded of death blamed the severely injured victims more than people who were not reminded.

p188c7e4be.post: Adult twins, some identical and some fraternal, answered a phone interview about their gambling and any problems it had caused. Researchers compared how alike the twins in each pair were, for identical versus fraternal twins. About half the differences in gambling problems were due to genes, and there was no sign that growing up in the same home mattered.

p18a20364e.post: Brain scan results from nine earlier studies were pooled, each comparing people with dyslexia to people without it. Grey matter, the tissue holding nerve cells, was the focus. Across studies, dyslexic readers had less of it in the same six areas, including the cerebellum and regions toward the back and sides of the brain.

p18cbc5f52.post: Older and younger adults listened to 20-second clips of popular songs from across the 20th century. They rated how emotional each song felt, and tried to name its title, artist, and year. The older adults rated songs from their youth as the most emotional, and they remembered more about those songs too.

p190320f85.post: People looked at pairs of adult faces and rated how similar the two faces looked. Some pairs were two people of the same sex, and others were one man and one woman. Same-sex pairs were rated as looking more alike than opposite-sex pairs.

p19299fe87.post: Adults learned that one response earned a reward with items from one set, and another with items from a second set. Then they learned a new response for just one item in each set. When tested, all four adults used the new responses with the other items from the matching set, as if each set were one group.

p19789ad5a.post: People chose from a set of options that were shown either one at a time or all at once. Then they rated how satisfied they were with their choice and how committed they felt to it. People shown the options one at a time were less satisfied and less committed.

p19f2b8a62.post: Married couples were interviewed about rule-breaking as teens, antisocial behavior as adults, and heavy drinking. They also filled out a personality questionnaire and a survey on how well their marriage was going. People with more of these problems reported worse marriages, even when their personality was taken into account.

p1a1a1cdb5.post: Men applying to the Norwegian Naval Special Forces took ability tests, a personality questionnaire, and the Rorschach test, where people say what they see in inkblots. Then everyone's pass or fail result in training was recorded. Inkblot scores for things like stress tolerance and social adjustment were linked to passing, while the ability tests and personality scores were only weakly linked.

p1a432b405.post: University students from several countries filled out questionnaires about their beliefs and how lonely they felt. Some beliefs were unhelpful, like expecting the worst, and others were helpful, like accepting yourself. Unhelpful beliefs explained 36% of the differences in how lonely students felt, and helpful beliefs explained 23%.

p1a4f9a17d.post: College students read four statements and judged how believable each one was by looking at what it said, using one of three methods. Along the way, they were given outside information that made the statements seem either more or less believable. All three methods were equally easy to sway with that information.

p1a5d24872.post: Teenagers with depression and one of their parents each filled out a questionnaire, separately, about how much the two of them clash. A clinician who interviewed both then rated how hopeless the teen seemed. Teens whose parent reported less conflict than the teen did were rated as more hopeless.

p1ae3a1325.post: College students filled out questionnaires about how mindful they were, how stressed they felt, how healthy they thought they were, and how they ate, slept and exercised. Nobody was split into groups. Students who were more mindful rated their health better and reported better sleep, more exercise and less binge eating, partly because they were less stressed.

p1c13d709b.post: Young adults recalled how often parents slapped, spanked, or hit them with an object as kids. They said whether they had hit, shoved, or thrown something at a dating partner in the past year. Those punished this way were more likely to have been violent than those who weren't, even after accounting for severe child abuse.

p1c467501b.post: Children who stutter spent a week at an intensive therapy camp focused on their feelings and thoughts about stuttering. About a month later, they and their parents filled out questionnaires about talking, friendships and daily life. The children rated their attitudes toward communicating and their ability to make friends higher than before camp.

p1cc37feb5.post: People watched a video that included a salient person. Later, some described that person's face and others did not. Then everyone tried to recognize the face. People who had described the face did worse at recognizing it.

p1d75ca3cc.post: Adults from the community filled out four questionnaires about themselves. They rated how well they plan, stay motivated and understand others, and also how grateful, forgiving and satisfied with life they felt. People who rated themselves higher on motivation, empathy and planning also rated themselves as more grateful and more satisfied with life.

p1dc6e6c8e.post: People with depression were randomly given one of two talk therapies: one about relationships, one about changing unhelpful thinking. Beforehand, they rated how uncomfortable they felt getting close to others. Those who felt more uncomfortable improved more, and were likelier to recover, with the thinking therapy than the relationship one.

p1dfe854c9.post: Teens staying at a psychiatric hospital watched a 15-minute film about four people at a dinner party. The film stopped many times to ask what a character was feeling or thinking. Teens with more borderline personality traits were more likely to over-read what the characters were thinking and feeling, giving explanations that went too far.

p1e013a18e.post: Three people with severe disabilities each used a switch they could press. A computer turned each press into something to see, hear, or feel, and recorded the presses. The three people each showed a different pattern of preferences among the sight, sound, and touch events.

p1e2b8b09c.post: A man gave the same lecture on cultural influences to eight college classes, keeping his delivery natural and the same each time. What changed was his sexual orientation: gay in some classes, straight in others. Students then rated how credible he was as a teacher. They rated the gay teacher as less credible than the straight teacher.

p1e3749828.post: People decided whether a string of letters made a real German word, right after a related word flashed too quickly to notice. The flashed word was either a new word built from the target or a grammar-ending form of it. Native German speakers got a head start from both; Russian speakers who learned German got one only from the built kind.

p1e5fa657b.post: People could press a button to see a visual signal, and each press was followed by a sound. For some, pressing at their usual rate gave them less sound than they would normally choose to hear. For others, it gave them more sound than they would choose. Those who got less sound pressed more, and those who got more sound pressed less.

p1f14fdfc6.post: People in psychiatric hospital wards reported how much they rejected themselves. Wards differed in how individualized treatment was, how good the group atmosphere was, and how large they were. Larger wards had more self-rejection, a good atmosphere went with less, and individualized treatment went with less only if it didn't hurt the atmosphere.

p1f5223adb.post: Men and women tried hard math problems. Some heard it was a math test, others a problem-solving task. A third group heard it was a math test, plus that stereotypes about women and math can hurt scores. Women scored lower than men on the plain math test, but did not differ from men in the other two.

p1fa963567.post: Police officers and college students said what clues they think give away a liar, and rated 17 things a person might say. Then they watched eight video clips and judged whether each person was telling the truth. People who were more right about spoken clues were better at spotting truthful statements than people who were less right.

p203105394.post: Twice a week for up to 10 weeks, people wrote down the good and bad things that happened to them that day. They also rated their self-esteem and how much they were thinking in gloomy, self-critical ways. On days with bad events, people felt worse about themselves when no good events happened. Good events softened the hit that bad events had on their self-esteem and gloomy thinking.

p2036bdfba.post: People listened to strings of nonsense sounds and tried to spot a real word hidden inside. In some strings, the hidden word was also the start of a longer word. Spotting the word was affected both by competition from other words the sounds could fit and by the speech's rhythm pattern.

p205652dc9.post: People answered two-choice questions and were then told whether they got each one right or wrong. Because there were only two options, either message revealed the correct answer. On a later test, people had learned less from the answers they were told they got wrong than from the ones they were told they got right.

p212b52920.post: People lay in a brain scanner and came up with design ideas for a problem. They tried it with a hint close to the problem, with a hint far from the problem, and with no hint at all. With either kind of hint, people came up with more ideas than with no hint.

p214e99f9a.post: People reported on their own emotions, either over the last few hours or over the last few months. The researchers tested what people draw on to answer. For the last few hours, people drew on memories of specific moments, but for the last few months they drew on general beliefs about what they are like.

p21d024fb1.post: People did a short computer program in one of two versions. One version taught them about anxiety and had them practice bodily sensations that can feel scary. The other gave general health information. The anxiety program lowered people's fear of anxious feelings, and that in turn went with fewer insomnia symptoms a month later than the health information.

p221f89155.post: Voters filled out a survey about how rejected and low they felt, once before and once after the 2016 presidential election. Some backed Donald Trump and some backed Hillary Clinton. After the election, Clinton supporters, whose candidate lost, reported more feelings of rejection and a lower mood than Trump supporters did.

p224ecb8ba.post: Physical education students and music education students each read two passages that could be understood in two different ways. One could be a prison break or a wrestling match, the other a card game or a woodwind rehearsal. Students tended to read each passage the way their own background suggested, and their answers and recall matched that reading.

p22561c341.post: People looked at photographs of other people and rated how physically attractive each one was. The judges were photographed too, and their own looks were rated. When the people in the photos were unattractive, men who were more attractive themselves gave higher attractiveness ratings than less attractive men did.

p232aefdaf.post: People who had been diagnosed with PTSD answered a large national health interview. Researchers sorted them by which other condition they also had: panic disorder, depression, generalized anxiety, or alcohol dependence. Those who also had panic disorder were more likely to report nightmares (96%) and insomnia (100%) than the other groups.

p2332f2507.post: Rats pressed a lever to earn rewards. Sometimes they had to hold the lever down for a minimum time to get one, and later that rule was removed. Rewards came right away or 8 seconds late. Rats held the lever longer when the rule was on and shorter when it was removed, with both timings.

p23d3bb6d7.post: People with OCD and people without anxiety problems were compared on how they handle unwanted, upsetting thoughts. The ways included distracting yourself, punishing yourself, rethinking the thought, turning to other people, and worrying. People with OCD used all but distraction more often, while people without anxiety used distraction more.

p2449a2ef6.post: Teachers in some elementary classrooms taught their students to get the teacher's attention politely, follow directions, and ignore classmates who misbehave. Teams of students then earned rewards for doing these things. Other teachers carried on as usual. Students in the classrooms that used the program spent more time on task than they had before it started.

p2463e305e.post: People with social anxiety took a 12-week group course, either mindfulness training or cognitive-behavioral therapy. Questionnaires over the following year tracked their attention, awareness and mood. Mindfulness training raised the ability to watch feelings without reacting more than therapy did, and that helped explain broader awareness and, later, better skill at seeing bad situations differently.

p247fddcb5.post: Children practiced a matching task that taught them to pair faces of Black people with a positive symbol. Before and after, they rated how they felt about Black and White faces. Before training they rated Black faces more negatively, but afterward the gap was no longer clear.

p248ff2e1b.post: People looked at upsetting pictures, like spiders, snakes or mistreated animals. Sometimes they chose between two labeled kinds of picture before seeing one. Other times the same pictures were simply shown to them. When people had the choice, they reported feeling less negative than when the same pictures were imposed.

p24b47bd39.post: Students had a limited amount of time to write down adjectives that describe how materials look and feel, such as leather, metal, and wood. Most of the words people listed were about sensory qualities, like "warm" or "see-through," and most of those were about touch.

p24ec0c969.post: Some people ate a sweet food, some a food that was not sweet, and some no food. Then they rated how agreeable they were. People who had eaten the sweet food rated themselves as more agreeable and helped more.

p251aee5e2.post: Patients at 58 NHS clinics in the UK got one of three kinds of talk therapy: cognitive-behavioral, person-centered or psychodynamic. Some also got one extra approach added. Everyone filled out the same symptom questionnaire at the start and end of treatment. All the groups improved by about the same amount, so the different therapies had roughly equal results.

p25b01028d.post: Young adults read short made-up scenes in which they made another person feel angry, disgusted, or happy. They then predicted how strongly they and the other person would feel. The more social anxiety symptoms people had, the more they tended to overestimate how bad they and the other person would feel.

p26072e585.post: Mothers whose youngest child was between 6 months and 4 years old filled out an online survey. It asked about how they eat, how they feel about their bodies, their attitudes toward food, and their mood. Women whose eating style was intuitive, meaning they eat by hunger and fullness, were more satisfied with their bodies than the other women.

p2667f1480.post: Men got a nasal spray with either oxytocin, a hormone linked to social bonding, or a spray with no active ingredient. Then, in a brain scanner, they judged whether trait words like "clever" or "lazy" described themselves, their mother, a classmate, or a stranger. People who got oxytocin made these judgments faster than people who got the plain spray.

p272ce9c73.post: People watched a rapid stream of images and tried to spot a target that came right after an irrelevant picture. They did this when hungry and when full. Pictures of food made hungry people worse at spotting the target.

p272f1ec56.post: People online did a new reasoning task, then answered questions about their OCD symptoms. The task measured inverse reasoning, which means drawing conclusions about reality from imagined causes. People who agreed with this kind of reasoning more had more OCD symptoms, even when general distress and OCD-related beliefs were taken into account.

p2745f2d5f.post: Overweight people with binge eating disorder did a guided self-help program, either one about changing eating habits or one about losing weight. Some cut their binge eating by about two-thirds within four weeks. Those people were more likely to stop binge eating and improved more in eating problems and mood than people who didn't.

p27485cdac.post: People read scenarios in their native language or in a foreign language. In each, they imagined doing something under a superstitious circumstance, such as a broken mirror or a four-leaf clover, and rated how they would feel. A foreign language led to less negative feelings about bad-luck scenarios and less positive feelings about good-luck scenarios.

p2778707e5.post: Environmental activists in the US Midwest, and others tied to climate summits in Peru and Paris, answered questions about why they do their activism, drawn from two different theories. In both groups, all 11 sets of questions sorted into two kinds of motivation: reasons coming from inside the person and reasons coming from outside.

p27cb21701.post: Transgender and gender expansive teens and young adults at a university clinic answered a 22-question survey about fertility and about whether they might want to be parents someday. There was no comparison group. Over half of them lacked specific knowledge of basic fertility principles.

p2809dbc1d.post: People filled out an online survey. It asked how much they enjoy thinking, whether they get started on tasks at once or think about other things first, and how well they resist temptation. People who enjoy thinking reported more self-control, and part of that link ran through getting started at once. Some of it remained beyond that.

p2816c90aa.post: People learned to group nonsense words into two sets of three. Then they were told one word, YIM, was a good person, and later that it was a bad person. Each time, they placed tokens on the words however they liked. How the tokens were split between the sets differed markedly depending on whether YIM was called good or bad.

p2830fcfa2.post: People in 36 countries did a set of well-known psychology tasks on a computer, some in a lab and some online, with the order of tasks varied. Researchers then compared results from rich, Western-style countries with results from less Western, less rich ones. The results differed little between the two kinds of countries.

p283a1b9de.post: People read sentences while a camera tracked their eyes. Some sentences had an early word with look-alike words of a different grammar type, and a later word that fit those look-alikes well or poorly. Readers' eye movements showed they kept some doubt about words already read, and revised it based on later words.

p28a3fd7cf.post: Women browsed a fashion website that showed pictures of models. Some saw attractive models and others saw unattractive ones, and the models were either thin or obese. Afterward, women who saw attractive models reported stronger intentions, attitudes, and social pressure to lose weight than women who saw unattractive models.

p291a0971a.post: People played a money game where they could keep their possible winnings or donate them. They also reported how many sex partners they had had. People who were willing to donate reported more lifetime, casual, and past-year sex partners than people who were not.

p296e0c072.post: People chose between gambles described in terms of gains or in terms of losses. Some choices had to be made under time pressure and others not. The way a gamble was described shifted people's choices more when they had to decide fast.

p29adcba80.post: Preschool children who stuttered went through a treatment program called the Lidcombe Program, and clinicians tracked how many clinic visits each child needed before the stuttering was zero or nearly gone. Researchers then compared children who stuttered more severely at the start with those who stuttered less. Children with more severe stuttering needed longer treatment than children with less severe stuttering.

p2a6a248ac.post: Women watched pictures of their own bodies flash on a screen, each followed by a face. For some, their own body was paired with a smiling face. For others, the faces were random. Women who were very concerned about their bodies felt better about their bodies and themselves after seeing their own body paired with smiles.

p2b01bcb0a.post: German speakers answered questions, some in German and some in English. A color cue told them on each question whether to answer truthfully or lie. Lying took longer than telling the truth in both languages, but the gap in answer time was smaller in English than in German.

p2c1ca52d9.post: Children and adults in the U.S. and China heard a story based on a famous puzzle about names, where a famous deed turns out to belong to someone else. They then judged statements using the name. In both age groups, Americans were more likely than Chinese to answer as if a name sticks to the person first given it.

p2d1b55c82.post: Three preschoolers with very little speech were taught the names of everyday objects by a speech therapist. They practiced matching each object to an identical picture, and the therapist gave physical prompts to help. A month later, all three could pick out the objects on their own.

p2d204f1d0.post: College students filled out questionnaires about how grateful they are, how well they feel they are doing psychologically, and how satisfied they are with their lives. Nobody was split into groups. The students who were more grateful reported better psychological well-being and more satisfaction with life.

p2d8e62ae6.post: People decided whether a word was a brand name. Brand names were shown in their usual case, such as adidas and IKEA, or in the other case, such as ADIDAS and ikea. People identified brand names faster in their usual case.

p2dab5c1a6.post: Children, their parents, or both rated how each child notices and reacts badly to unfairness. The ratings asked about being treated unfairly, watching others be treated unfairly, and being the one who acts unfairly. In both the children's and the parents' ratings, the answers grouped into three related kinds of sensitivity to unfairness.

p2e0ce4569.post: People reported their income and how satisfied they were with their life. Researchers then checked three things: how much money each person made, where that income ranked within a comparison group, and how it compared with the group's typical income. Income rank predicted life satisfaction, while the amount earned and the comparison with the typical income did not.

p2e72637a7.post: College women answered questions about their eating habits, their body image, and their personality. Women unhappier with their bodies reported more eating disorder symptoms. That link was stronger in women who watch their looks closely, worry a lot, or have a family member and a friend with an eating disorder than in other women.

p2f51d1ca2.post: People learned a made-up language from English phrases like "purple vase" heard as "vase purple." No phrase had two describing words. At test, they picked between an order that kept English-like word order and one that followed the structure of the meaning. Learners overwhelmingly favored the meaning-based order over the English-like one.

p2f5f2c00b.post: People answered a question about one part of their life, then rated how satisfied they were with their life overall. In one version, the two questions were just placed one after the other with no link between them. When they were simply placed in sequence, people's overall rating ended up similar to their answer on the specific question.

p2fa0d1148.post: Former fighters in eastern Congo gave long one-on-one interviews at a camp for people leaving armed groups. They were asked about violence they had seen, suffered and committed, and whether fighting felt thrilling. Of everything asked, the number of violent acts a person had committed best predicted how much they found violence enjoyable.

p305f27a06.post: Adults who had never smoked, who currently smoked, or who used to smoke were checked for one particular version of a gene tied to the brain's dopamine system. They also had their personality measured. The gene version was linked to quitting, not to starting: people who carried it were more likely to have quit.

p3064e731c.post: Women gave a saliva sample every morning for one menstrual cycle. At three visits during the cycle, they looked at pairs of men's faces and picked one from each pair. The faces in a pair differed only in how masculine they looked. Among women in long-term relationships, those with higher average progesterone over the cycle chose masculine faces less often.

p310e35cdf.post: People read a long story online that gave familiar words, like "foam," a new made-up meaning, such as a safe hidden inside a piece of furniture. Each new meaning showed up two, four, six, or eight times in the story. Later, people were asked to recall the meanings. The more times a meaning appeared, the more accurately people recalled it.

p312808aa8.post: High school students either played a game in which they made a misleading news article about a politicized issue, or did not. Then they rated how reliable and persuasive fake news articles were. Students who had played the game rated fake news articles as less reliable and less persuasive.

p3151f1dd8.post: Children had to pick the shape turned a quarter turn clockwise from a shape they were shown. They were taught to label which way the first shape pointed, adjust the label for the turn, and repeat it at the choices. They did well with new shapes they already had steady labels for, and poorly with new shapes they didn't.

p318b52e11.post: People rated how happy they would be on 80 vacation destinations. Then they were told they would pick between two destinations flashed too fast to see, but only scribbles were shown. After each pick, the names were revealed. Destinations they had picked were rated higher afterward than before.

p31c852326.post: College students watched a video of a mock police interrogation that ended in a confession. For some the camera mostly showed the suspect, for others mostly the detective, and for others both equally. Those who saw mostly the suspect judged the confession as less forced than those who saw both equally, and those who saw mostly the detective judged it as the most forced.

p324a04751.post: Future teachers in a college course took weekly quizzes. In one condition, a group earned extra credit points if the group scored 80% or higher. In the other, each person earned extra credit by scoring 80% or higher on their own. Quiz scores improved in every group, and were higher overall when the extra credit depended on the group.

p326590f61.post: People heard made-up words from two voices, a "teacher" and a "student." One voice began each word with a short delay on the first sound, the other with a long delay, and for other people the two were swapped. Later they judged a new student's pronunciations. They preferred the ones matching the teacher, not the earlier student.

p328a9c433.post: A few weeks after a huge earthquake in China, adults filled out a questionnaire. Some lived far from the damage and others lived in badly hit areas. They estimated things like the chance of an epidemic and how many doctors and safety measures were needed. The more devastated people's own area was, the less concern they showed.

p32e65a336.post: Adults, none of them with any known impairment, took several reading tests that are used to estimate what a person's IQ was before an illness or injury. Each test turned the person's score into an estimate of their IQ. The estimates differed from test to test: the NART gave the highest estimate and the TOPF the lowest.

p32f15d1d7.post: People from age 7 to adulthood saw a set of shelves with objects and moved objects as a director instructed. The director could see only some of the objects, so people had to move only the ones the director could see. Teenagers aged 14 to 17 made more errors than adults.

p335d47f6a.post: Before a four-month deployment to Afghanistan, Dutch soldiers did a learning task that measured how well they could stop fearing a signal that no longer meant danger. After coming home, they reported their stress symptoms. Soldiers who had been worse at unlearning that fear had more severe posttraumatic stress symptoms later.

p33874fa31.post: Students training to become teachers were measured on how much they enjoy hard mental work. They were also measured on self-control, ways of handling feelings, and ways of coping with stress. Students who enjoyed hard thinking more also scored better on almost all of these.

p338c9f62b.post: Teenagers and young adults did pattern puzzles, picking which shape completes each one, and defined words out loud. About a year and a half later, most did both again. People who started with higher vocabulary scores gained more on the puzzles, and people who started with higher puzzle scores gained more in vocabulary.

p33b53dc86.post: While lying in a brain scanner, people held a warm pack in one round and a ball in another. Afterward they rated how connected they felt to other people. People felt more connected after holding the warm pack than after holding the ball.

p341c913a5.post: Adults with recurring depression filled out a long true-false personality questionnaire near the start and again at the end of about three months of talk therapy. Their depression was also rated at both times. Scores on both lasting traits and passing mood tracked depression level, but only changes in mood tracked changes in depression, not lasting traits.

p342cd9b07.post: Researchers followed 170 therapists as they treated thousands of patients over several years. Patients filled out the same symptom questionnaire before and after treatment, so each therapist's results could be tracked as they gained experience. On the whole, patients' improvement got slightly smaller the more experience a therapist had.

p3450c4cb8.post: Psychiatric patients took a short IQ test and a longer standard one. A formula built on one group turned short-test scores into age-adjusted estimates of the standard score. In a new group, the estimates matched real scores with correlations of .76 and .74, and ran neither too high nor too low.

p345950efa.post: Adults across the US answered a government survey about their drug use and any crimes in the past year. Some had ever used psychedelics such as magic mushrooms, and others had not. Those who had were less likely to report theft, assault, or an arrest for a property or violent crime.

p348575693.post: People read a sentence about an animal or object in a certain place, like an eagle in the sky or an eagle in a nest. Then they saw a drawing of it and said whether it had been in the sentence, or just named it. Responses were faster when the drawing's shape matched the shape the sentence implied than when it did not.

p352bc3852.post: Photos of human babies and of animals were checked for which side of the face pointed toward the camera. Portraits of adults usually show the person's left cheek. Photos of babies and of animals showed the left side of the face more often than the right.

p3546815ba.post: Couples filled out a survey that asked about the woman's hormonal birth control, both now and when the couple first got together. For some women, use now matched use back then, and for others it had changed. Matching predicted the woman's sexual satisfaction with her partner, but whether she used it now did not.

p354f46850.post: People memorized a sentence like "To make the screen blue, I have to press the left key." Then they sorted letters into vowels and consonants with the left and right keys, and the background sometimes turned blue. When the blue background appeared, people did better if the sorting key matched the one in the sentence than if it did not.

p356b7b9c8.post: People in cognitive and behavioral therapy, a kind of talk therapy, were either given homework to do between sessions or not. Pooling 27 studies, therapy with homework led to better results than therapy without it. People who did more of their homework also did better.

p357358f54.post: Students at four Scottish secondary schools filled out a questionnaire. It asked where they would rather see a counsellor: at their school, or outside it, such as at a youth centre or doctor's office. About three-quarters of the students said they would rather see a counsellor at their school.

p35b193c76.post: First-time pregnant women filled out questions about how much they worried and what they expected parenthood to be like. They also chose which information about parenthood to read, positive or negative. Women who picked more negative information were more likely to expect parenthood to go badly.

p35f5cd5c9.post: People tried to remember a list of items in order while sounds that had nothing to do with the task played. The sounds were speech or tones, played to the left ear, the right ear, or both ears. Sound in the left ear disrupted memory more than sound in the right ear or both ears.

p3615b25bf.post: Babies sat in front of an apparatus with an object in each of its four corners. Their mothers, who couldn't see where the baby looked, said a word the baby probably knew, a word the baby probably didn't know, or a nonsense word. At 13 months, babies looked longer at the object named by a known word than when the mother said a nonsense word.

p36d1033f5.post: People sat with their backs strapped with tape, so they stayed either slumped or upright. While held in that posture, they gave a stressful speech. Afterward, people who sat upright reported higher self-esteem, more arousal, better mood, and less fear than people who sat slumped.

p36f0242d4.post: People read short stories about social situations that went badly, where it was not clear whether the other person meant any harm. Some of the readers were patients being treated for severe alcohol problems, and others were healthy people matched to them. Patients with severe alcohol problems said the other person had meant harm more than the healthy people did.

p36f631ed9.post: Students aged 11 to 13 in British schools either had their usual lessons or took a 90-minute class on body image. Some classes were taught by their own teachers and others by researchers. Right after the class, girls whose teachers taught it felt better about their bodies than girls who had usual lessons.

p375982116.post: Hospital patients looked at inkblots and said what they saw. Researchers scored how the figures in those blots related to each other. They scored each patient's written life story and ratings from ward staff for the same quality. The three kinds of scores were clearly linked to each other.

p3778e9551.post: Students in grades 4 to 6 at seven schools were asked to draw a picture related to the word "radiation." Some also answered a few interview questions about their drawings. The researchers compared the drawings of younger and older students. The older the students were, the more likely they were to draw invisible sources of radiation, like nuclear power plants or mobile phones.

p37a6d4ac4.post: People looked at shapes with a made-up word inside, while flashing patterns shown to one eye kept the shape hidden. Some words fit their shape, like "kiki" in a pointy, angular one. Others did not. Shapes with a fitting word reached people's awareness faster than shapes with a mismatched word.

p37bb0b8b7.post: Students in a college psychology class took turns answering review questions in three ways: with clickers, by holding up response cards, or by raising their hands. At other times the class did none of these, as a comparison. Students scored almost 5% higher on exams after using one of the three ways than during the comparison times.

p37ebefb1d.post: People read about a person's behaviors and judged how much each behavior reflected the person's true self. People judged morally good behaviors as reflecting the true self more than morally bad ones.

p388119d4c.post: People played an online gem game, learning by trial and error which gems to collect and which to leave. Some gems paid a small reward right away, others a larger one later, matched to be equally appealing. People collected gems more often when the reward was immediate than when it was delayed.

p38ca79c06.post: New sales agents answered questions about their mindset before they started the job. Some focused more on chasing gains and opportunities, and others focused more on avoiding mistakes and losses. Then researchers counted how many sales each agent made. Agents who focused more on gains made more sales, while agents who focused more on avoiding losses made fewer.

p38d013249.post: Parents filled out questionnaires about their child's picky eating, their child's anxiety, and how sensitive their child was to things in the surroundings. More anxious children were pickier eaters, and this link was fully explained by the children's sensitivity.

p38fd2d62c.post: People practiced a computer task where their actions earned rewards. Some got a short amount of training and others got extensive training. Then the researchers checked whether people kept going for a reward that had lost its value, a sign of habit. People with extensive training did not show more habit-like behavior than people with short training.

p3952009e5.post: Sixth graders were interviewed about the people in their lives and rated how supportive each person was. They also reported their own self-esteem. Kids with above-average support from both their mother and their most supportive classmate had higher self-esteem than kids with above-average support from only one of them.

p3953060fe.post: Adults looked at Rorschach inkblots and said what they saw, while a camera tracked their eyes. The researchers counted how many times each person's gaze stopped on the blots. People whose answers were more complex, with more parts of the blot pulled together, stopped their gaze more times.

p39a41d4ea.post: College students and adults who were not students reacted to a partner's sexual unfaithfulness and to a partner's emotional unfaithfulness. Then the two kinds were compared for men and women. Among college students, men were more bothered by the sexual kind and women by the emotional kind. The nonstudent adults did not show this pattern.

p39c9e3aba.post: Skilled readers read sentences while a device tracked where their eyes landed, and then they answered questions about what they read. The sentences contained ten-letter words, some with endings that give little clue to the word, and others with informative endings. When a word got just one look, readers' eyes landed nearer the beginning of words with uninformative endings than of words with informative endings.

p39fb03742.post: Students at a Canadian university read a life-skills guide for college students that had mental health information built into it. Afterward they filled out a survey, in person or online, about what the guide had done for them. They said it improved their knowledge about mental health and mental illness and lowered their stigma toward them.

p3a105046d.post: Athletes with no track experience did sprint starts, once before and once after a first task. For some, the first task was meant to use up self-control, and for others it was not. Only those whose self-control had been used up became more likely to start before the signal.

p3a4dbeef6.post: People worldwide took an online survey early in the COVID-19 pandemic.
