They said how likely they were to follow health advice, and what they would do in dilemmas like donating face masks. They also rated how connected they feel to all humanity. That feeling predicted following health advice and helping others better than the other factors measured.

p3a82b7180.post: People rated how much uncertainty bothers them, then watched blue and yellow squares while finger sensors tracked sweat. One square was sometimes followed by a loud scream, the other never, until they swapped. After the swap, people more bothered by uncertainty sweated more to the newly scary square than the newly safe one, versus less bothered people.

p3a84a1263.post: A researcher with low-risk behavior visited 20 public health centers in Germany as a client. At each, he sat through the counseling and took an HIV test. Half the counselors told him a positive result would mean he was 100% certain to be infected, though for a man like him the chance could be as low as 50%.

p3a93b94be.post: People did a hard subtraction task while the experimenter made harsh comments about how they were doing. Afterward, about half got an apology from the experimenter and half did not. Blood pressure came back to normal faster in women who got an apology than in women who didn't, but slower in men who got one than in men who didn't.

p3aa5a0263.post: People born in one New Zealand city were interviewed five times, from age 18 to 38, about symptoms of mental disorders like depression, phobias, and drug dependence. Researchers compared two ways of grouping the symptoms. Three broad types of problems explained the pattern well, but one general dimension behind all of them explained it even better.

p3adc9de46.post: People who spoke English as a first language and people who spoke Arabic as a first language heard series of six short syllables, each a consonant plus a vowel. They wrote down what they remembered, in both English and Arabic. English speakers remembered the vowel series better than the consonant series, in both languages, but Arabic speakers did not.

p3b07afa2d.post: People with panic disorder or constant worry went to ten weekly one-on-one therapy sessions that taught them to handle anxiety. Before starting, they filled out a questionnaire on how easily they feel positive emotions. Those who more easily felt positive emotions had the biggest drop in anxiety symptoms, and had fewer symptoms at the end.

p3b767b4b6.post: People in 16 countries read 25 short situations, like being trustworthy or having many unique skills. Some rated how positively they would view another person in each situation. Others rated how much pride they would feel in it. In every country, situations that earned more positive views from others also brought more pride.

p3b7feb2be.post: People with anxiety or insomnia reported their distress and quality of life. Some were being weaned off calming pills, some still took them, and some had not started treatment. During withdrawal, people higher in neuroticism (a tendency to worry), with less schooling, or with lower quality of life felt more distress.

p3bd6c6916.post: Japanese people rated how much they liked different Japanese letters. They liked the letters included in their own name more than the other letters.

p3bd720266.post: People saw pairs of words and quickly decided whether they were real words. Some pairs came from clear, sensible metaphors, some were words people tend to link in their minds, and some were randomly matched. Responses to the metaphor pairs were no faster than responses to the random pairs.

p3c523a4d0.post: People were led to feel that their life had changed in one of three ways: a disruptive change for the worse, a non-disruptive change for the better, or no change at all. Afterward, everyone rated how nostalgic they felt. Only the people in the disruptive, negative condition felt more nostalgic than the other two groups.

p3c5a2ea78.post: People took turns giving and getting mild electric shocks with an opponent who was not real. Some had alcohol and some got a placebo, and some also had to hold four things in order in memory. People on alcohol who had the memory task were less aggressive than people on alcohol without it, even less than the placebo group.

p3d743a474.post: People studied sets of faces on a computer, then tried to recognize them. Some faces were studied while a warning said they might get an electric shock to the wrist, and others while a warning said they were safe. People remembered faces worse when they had studied them under threat of shock, whether or not they were threatened during the recall test.

p3dc668bdb.post: Caregivers filled out a behavior checklist about preschoolers. Some of the children were in foster care after being maltreated, and others lived at home with no known maltreatment. Symptoms of dissociation, such as seeming spaced out or detached, formed a separate group from other trauma symptoms, such as being on edge.

p3df9c8238.post: Women gave blood samples: some currently had anorexia, some had recovered from it, and some were healthy at a normal weight. A lab measured 92 proteins linked to inflammation in each sample. Twenty-five of the proteins were at different levels in women with anorexia than in healthy women.

p3e16b1118.post: Older adults who had lost a husband or wife in the past six months reported their symptoms of anxiety, depression, and grief, then did so again later. Researchers compared ways of sorting those symptoms into one, two, or three kinds. Treating anxiety as its own kind, apart from depression and grief, fit the answers better than using one or two kinds.

p3e3573550.post: New sorority members were randomly put into one of two short programs, each held over two sessions and led by fellow undergraduates. One program used cognitive dissonance, which works on the discomfort of acting against your own beliefs. The other used media advocacy. Both programs reduced eating disorder risk factors, but eight months later cognitive dissonance generally had done better.

p3ebd4c339.post: Trained students watched recordings of people with depression in their first therapy session. They rated how intensely each person dwelled on their problems in a repetitive, negative, passive way. People who dwelled more intensely in that first session had higher depression scores from their clinician later in treatment.

p3ef08be66.post: Students were followed from fifth to eighth grade, with their math and verbal grades, and how capable they felt in each subject, recorded three times. Doing well and feeling capable in a subject led to better grades and more confidence in that same subject later. But better grades in one subject led to less confidence in the other.

p3f1000076.post: Teen girls unhappy with their bodies were randomly put into one of four groups. Two groups got three weekly sessions: one challenged the idea that thin is ideal, the other taught healthy weight habits. The rest did writing sessions or were only assessed. By the end, the first group's eating disorder risk factors and bulimic symptoms had dropped more than in the other three.

p3f2802938.post: Infants were held and gently bounced to music while facing an experimenter, who bounced either in sync or out of sync with the infant. Then the experimenter 'accidentally' dropped objects, and researchers watched whether the infants handed them back. Infants bounced in sync with the experimenter were more likely to help.

p3f55f0446.post: Teens who had been depressed before, but were now well or nearly well, either had weekly therapy for eight weeks or only filled out questionnaires. The therapy taught them to notice when they were dwelling on bad thoughts and to switch to something else. In resting brain scans, the therapy group's middle-back and right-front brain areas worked less in sync than before.

p3f6138070.post: Young adults were randomly split into two groups. One group had three sessions of recalling positive memories and thinking about them, while the other waited its turn. Everyone rated their self-esteem, confidence in handling stress, sense of meaning in life, and optimism. Right after the sessions, the memory group scored higher than the waiting group.

p3f8fad592.post: People were asked how angry someone would get after another person harmed them. In some cases the person who did the harm gained only a small benefit from it, and in others the benefit was larger. Anger was judged to be stronger when the benefit was small.

p3fb52db05.post: People went online and watched a video of one man with a stutter in a mock job interview, then rated how well he communicated. Half saw a video of him before a course on communication skills, and half saw him after it. People who watched the after-course video rated his communication higher than people who watched the before-course video.

p404d2ec67.post: Students reported their math and German grades and how good they felt at each subject. They also rated whether being good at math goes with being weak at language. Students who believed this more strongly showed a bigger link between a higher grade in one subject and a lower self-rating in the other.

p4090feb27.post: Adults from the community filled out online surveys. One asked how much they seek out positive feelings when deciding how to organize their days. Others asked how often they felt joy, sadness and similar emotions, and how depressed they felt. People who put more priority on positivity felt more positive emotions and had fewer signs of depression.

p40b52adbe.post: People with panic disorder, people with depression, and people with neither were each given time periods as prompts. They named good and bad experiences from their past or ones they expected in the future. People with panic disorder named more bad experiences than the comparison group, but not fewer good ones.

p40d978eba.post: Adults across Canada answered an interview about how often they gambled, how much money they spent on it, and whether it had caused them problems. Researchers then compared people who gambled within certain limits with people who went past them. People who went past the limits, such as gambling more than two to three times a month, were more likely to report harm from gambling.

p40e7614b0.post: Thirty people with borderline personality disorder went to therapy twice a week for a year. Their therapists were trainees who were closely supervised. Researchers tracked things like drug use, doctor visits, self-harm, hospital stays and symptoms. Compared with when they started, the patients had improved on every measure by the end of the follow-up year.

p412956185.post: People rated how good they were, from 0 to 100, at skills like driving, shoe tying, performing magic tricks and dancing. For each skill they also said whether most people are good at it, most are bad, or whether people are mixed. People rated themselves higher on skills where they thought most others were good, and lower where they thought most others were bad.

p413b98611.post: People in a large national survey rated how attractive they were, and outside raters also scored how attractive each person looked. Each person also got one overall personality score, combining how their traits tend to go together. Higher overall personality scores went with higher attractiveness, whether self-rated or rated by others.

p4207b3aae.post: People with long-standing personality problems got one of three treatments: schema therapy, another talk therapy, or their usual care. Over three years they repeatedly filled out questionnaires on how often they felt and acted in certain ways, called modes, and on their symptoms. Four modes (Healthy Adult, Vulnerable Child, Impulsive Child, Avoidant Protector) predicted how severe their symptoms were later.

p4274e34b3.post: People did a task of spotting changes in a display while holding both hands either near the display or away from it. People were more accurate at detecting changes, and held more items in short-term memory, when their hands were near the display.

p42a0cb878.post: People looked at photos of someone about to do something, like an action just before it happens. Three days later they saw more photos and said which ones they had seen before. Some were old photos, and some were new photos showing a later moment of the same action. People falsely said they remembered the later moments.

p42eaa6e66.post: Babies watched videos of a woman who either reached for a toy or greeted them with "Hi baby!" and pointed at it. The toy was then hidden and came back unchanged, moved, or swapped for a different toy. After greetings, babies tracked what the toy was at the expense of where it was. After reaching, they tracked where it was.

p433f873d0.post: Mothers and fathers of two young children each reported whether they treated the older or younger child differently, in affection, discipline, and favoritism. Then each mother's answers were compared with the father's in the same family. The most common result was that mother and father showed the same pattern as each other.

p449e8bd22.post: People looked at photos of the faces of mixed-martial-arts fighters and rated how aggressive each fighter looked. Researchers then compared those ratings with each fighter's real record of fights won. Fighters who looked more aggressive had won a larger share of their fights, once the fighters' weight was taken into account.

p44a1b3478.post: People named pictures out loud, like a picture of a horse, while a sound played that they were told to ignore. The sound could match the picture (neighing), come from a related animal (barking), or have nothing to do with it (drumming). Compared with the unrelated drumming, the matching sound helped people name the picture, and the related animal sound slowed them down.

p44a8dad93.post: Children of different ages saw two rows of objects, one longer and one with more objects, and said which row had more. Children of about two and a half to three picked the row with more objects. Children aged about three to four and a half picked the longer row even though it had fewer. Older children again picked correctly.

p45697c724.post: Students learning English read a short story. Some read the original, and others read a version changed to fit their own culture. Within each group, some also did reading activities and some did not. Students who read the culturally adapted version understood the story better than those who read the original.

p45a3687e2.post: Toddlers at day-care centers were assessed for temperament. Based on this, the children fell into three groups: typical, easily distracted and restless, or shy in new situations. Then the researchers looked at how each group used words. The easily distracted, restless children had a more immature vocabulary, with more of the simpler, earlier kinds of words, than the other groups.

p45c8d3376.post: German and Spanish speakers learning English wrote texts at skill levels from beginner to advanced. For common sentence patterns like "agrees with her," the researchers tracked which verbs learners used and compared them with native English writing. At higher skill levels, learners' verb choices in these patterns were closer to those of native English writers.

p45dfa52e5.post: Six city classrooms tried a program that taught students polite ways to ask for attention or a short break. Students also worked in teams that shared rewards for good behavior. Whole classes were compared before the program and during it. They stayed on task more during the program than before it.

p46641d05f.post: People solved a bat-and-ball puzzle, the kind where the first answer that pops into mind is wrong. They also solved a similar puzzle built so that no tempting wrong answer comes up, and said how sure they were of each answer. People were less confident in their wrong bat-and-ball answers than in their answers to the similar puzzle.

p46bfb281d.post: Prospective teachers learned about seven teaching skills, then watched a video or animation of an expert teacher using them. Some saw it as one continuous clip. Others saw it broken into smaller chunks. The people who saw the chunked version did better on all the learning tests than those who saw the continuous clip.

p46c3ede86.post: People read about actions that happened at a nearby place or a distant one, and chose whether to identify each action by what it was for or by how it was done. People more often identified actions by what they were for when the place was distant.

p47219d70a.post: Elementary school children who had lived through frightening events joined a 10-session group program led by school clinicians, where they learned ways to cope with their feelings. Some started right away, and others waited three months first. After three months, the children who started right away had improved more in trauma symptoms and anxiety than the children still waiting.

p47286fdaa.post: People read a list of words one at a time, each shown in the top half or the bottom half of a computer screen. Some words were positive and some were negative. Afterward they tried to remember the words. People remembered more words that were in a place that clashed with their meaning (positive words low, negative words high) than words in a place that matched.

p47655fd0a.post: People rated their own personality in two ways: one general rating, and many quick ratings of how they were acting and feeling at the moment. Other people also described each person. Averaging the quick ratings did not predict what others said any better than the general rating already did.

p478a074c4.post: Six pigeons could choose between two keys. Both keys paid off equally often, but one gave longer rewards than the other. When rewards came more often overall, the pigeons split their responses and their time more evenly between the keys than when rewards came less often.

p47e8999fc.post: Children in Naples, Italy, did memory tasks that used social material rather than abstract items. Some lived in two high-stress areas, Scampia and a Roma camp, and others in a lower-stress area, Pozzuoli. Scampia children did better than Pozzuoli children on both short-term memory and working memory (holding information in mind while using it).

p485154f06.post: People went to one-on-one therapy at UK counseling services, each seeing one of 85 therapists, and filled out a questionnaire about how they felt before and after. Some quit early and some got worse. Which therapist they saw explained 12.6% of the differences in who quit and 10.1% in who got worse, after accounting for patients' own traits.

p485197652.post: People who smoked joined group programs to quit. In half the groups, members also did bonding exercises, like making agreements and practicing sharing personal things and giving feedback. Those groups tended to do better at quitting or cutting back in the short term than groups without the exercises.

p48783cd06.post: People filled out questionnaires about how they think, including how much danger they expect and how much they feel their thoughts must be controlled. They also rated their obsessive-compulsive symptoms. The thinking style that mistakes imagined danger for real danger predicted symptoms more strongly than the other styles measured.

p488154cae.post: Children with anxiety disorders filled out a questionnaire about how anxious they felt. Their mothers and fathers each filled out one about their own depression, anxiety, and stress. The more of these symptoms parents reported, the more anxious the children rated themselves.

p496134b76.post: People who had recovered from depression, but had been depressed at least three times before, filled out an online survey. It asked how much they agreed with statements like "Feeling happy is extremely important to me," and how many signs of depression they felt now. The more people valued being happy, the more depression symptoms they reported.

p4a5d331d1.post: Children and teenagers answered questions about what they do when they feel sad. Their genes were also checked. Teenagers with two copies of the Val version of the BDNF gene reported more brooding than other teenagers, but younger children showed no such difference.

p4a83d9124.post: People played a points game with another player, choosing project green to cooperate or project blue to put themselves first. The other player used either a generous strategy or a greedy extortion strategy, and showed either a cooperative or a competitive emotion. Emotion changed how much people cooperated with the generous player, but made no difference with the extortion player.

p4a9abf30c.post: People worked in a simulated control room where an automated system could handle part of the job, or they could take over by hand. They rated how much they trusted the automation. Their trust ratings were based mainly on how competent they thought it was.

p4b2dcd853.post: College students filled out one questionnaire about selfish, uncaring, and impulsive personality traits, and another about how they cope with feeling ashamed. Then the two sets of scores were compared. People who scored higher on those traits were somewhat more likely to cope with shame by turning it outward, onto others.

p4b35c8a2b.post: Parish councils in England were sent requests for information, some as formal Freedom of Information requests and others as simple informal asks. The formal requests were more effective at getting the information than the informal asks.

p4b4c3115a.post: The rights warnings that police read to suspects before questioning were collected from all over the US, 560 in all. Each was scored for how hard it is to read, using a school grade level. Depending on where it came from, a warning could be understood at grade 2.8 or needed postgraduate education.

p4b62b08fd.post: Australian students did tasks and questionnaires that measured their creativity, such as thinking up different uses for things and writing a math equation. Researchers also collected their personality scores, school grades and national college-entry exam scores. Creativity measures explained part of the exam scores (18%) beyond what grades and personality already explained.

p4bebdf2ed.post: People learned verbal material and were tested after a period of sleep or a period awake. Some were also exposed to interference before the test. Recall was better after sleep than after being awake, and the gap was even bigger when interference was added.

p4c032a435.post: People studied faces on a screen, then picked out which ones they had seen among new faces. Sometimes they were under threat of an electric shock while studying, and sometimes they were safe. They recognized fewer faces correctly when the threat came during studying than when they were safe.

p4c21ea199.post: Native English speakers listened to English spoken with a Chinese accent. Then they heard sentences from a new speaker with a Chinese accent, someone they had never heard before. When people had heard several different accented speakers during training, their adjustment to the accent carried over to the new speaker.

p4cc40336d.post: Adults filled out a questionnaire about self-defeating habits, such as acting in ways that work against their own interests. They also answered a questionnaire about how they remembered their parents raising them. Among men, the more self-defeating traits they had, the more they remembered both their mother and their father as overinvolved.

p4d166bbe0.post: People rated how grateful they felt over the past week and in general. Then their heart rate and blood pressure were tracked during a stress test. People who felt more grateful over the past week had a lower top-number blood pressure reaction to the stress than people who felt less grateful.

p4d1c58f3f.post: Supervisors at an autism clinic filled out a checklist on why therapists rarely gave children chances to practice speaking skills. Each therapist then got a fix the checklist pointed to, like a graph of her own performance. All four kinds of fixes increased those chances, compared with before.

p4d3ee20b1.post: Patients admitted to a day treatment program for mental health problems filled out questionnaires about narcissism, problems in their relationships, and general distress. Researchers sorted them into high, medium, and low narcissism groups. The more narcissistic patients reported more problems getting along with other people than the less narcissistic patients did.

p4d3f0500d.post: People in a brain scanner scanned lines on a screen from left to right, pressing a button whenever they spotted a ring with a gap. Some lines were text, others were rows of circles instead of letters. Scanning circles, compared with all the other lines, brought extra activity in the right upper-back part of the brain.

p4d698102d.post: People read about a made-up person. Some read that the person used strategies to keep themselves in check, and others read that the person just used willpower. Then everyone rated how much self-control that person had. The person using strategies was rated lower in self-control than the person using willpower.

p4e10806c6.post: College students learned to read the numbers 1 to 10 in languages they didn't know, like Mandarin and Hindi. With one teaching method, they saw one number at a time on a card. With the other, they read numbers off a worksheet as fast as they could. Every student learned faster with the cards than with the worksheet.

p4e4b98694.post: People looked at male and female faces that had been digitally altered. Some faces were made wider compared to their height, and some were made look more masculine. People judged how aggressive each face seemed. Faces altered to be wider or more masculine were seen as more aggressive than the other versions.

p4e83e346c.post: People negotiated face to face, or played a bargaining game in a lab, while changes in their testosterone and cortisol (a stress hormone) were measured. When testosterone rose, people earned more and had better relationships, but only if cortisol dropped. If cortisol rose, a testosterone rise went with lower earnings and poorer relationships.

p4eb944dbf.post: Male and female college students filled out a list of 24 traits, such as those you might want in a partner. For each kind of relationship, from a casual date to marriage to a one-night fling, they marked the lowest level they would accept. The gap between men and women was biggest for a one-night fling, where men's minimum standards were lower than women's.

p4ee9f6521.post: University students were asked to remember a favorite play experience from their childhood, draw it, and talk about it. Researchers then sorted what they described, including who they played with. Students remembered playing with friends or siblings more often than playing alone.

p4f8c26a54.post: Babies born early had their heart-based calming and sleep cycles measured at birth. They were watched for stress reactions as infants and attention as toddlers, then tested on self-control at age 5. Early body regulation predicted self-control partly through stress handling and attention, and the heart measure also linked directly to each later kind of regulation.

p4f95474f2.post: Teenagers around the world, about 400,000 of them in 57 countries, took a two-hour science test. They also answered questions about how much they enjoy science. Researchers compared students from richer and poorer countries and families. Interest in science predicted test scores more strongly in richer countries and richer families.

p4faf74fe4.post: People read about a favor done for them, either for kind reasons or for ulterior motives. Then they rated how grateful and how indebted they felt. People felt more grateful when the helper had kind intentions, but felt equally indebted either way.

p4fcb9c2b6.post: People said whether they think willpower is a limited resource that runs out or not. Then they went through an experience meant to use up their self-control, and their self-control was measured afterward. People who saw willpower as not limited did not show worse self-control afterward, unlike people who saw it as limited.

p4fd5cbb3c.post: Teenagers with disabilities tutored younger children with disabilities twice a week for 10 weeks, in reading, language arts, and math. School staff trained and supported the teen tutors. An evaluation of the program found that schoolwork improved for both the teen tutors and the children they tutored.

p50544b2d7.post: University students filled out a personality questionnaire. Some were told to answer honestly. Others were told to answer so they made an excellent impression, and were warned that the test could catch faking, so they should try not to get caught. The test's built-in checks for faking still worked fairly well.

p506e5e803.post: Students were given hypnotic suggestions to respond to. For some the suggestions went from easy to difficult, and for others from difficult to easy. The two groups' total scores did not differ.

p50bbacba9.post: Children were filmed with sound, some with severe autistic-like difficulties and others with milder reading problems. The films were then studied in tiny slices of time. Every child seemed to react to a sound twice: once when it happened, and again after a delay of up to a second.

p50d149c05.post: People were randomly given oxytocin or a placebo and were asked to trust someone with confidential information. People who got oxytocin were more trusting that their privacy would not be violated.

p5162aa5f7.post: People with different beliefs about life after death were interviewed about a person who had died. They were asked whether various things in that person's mind and body would still go on after death. Bodily and sensory states were said to stop, but feelings, wants and knowing things were said to continue.

p51abf4abd.post: Women rated how close and how full of conflict their childhood family was, and said when they got their first period. Their DNA was checked for a gene that responds to estrogen. Closer, calmer families went with a later first period in women with two copies of the rarer version of that gene, but not in other women.

p5253c5eef.post: Mothers and their 2-year-olds did tasks like free play and puzzles, while observers rated how supportive each mother was. The mothers also gave cheek swabs for a gene test. Mothers with the A-A or A-G version of an oxytocin receptor gene were rated less sensitive to their toddlers than mothers with G-G.

p528b27cb0.post: People thought of a social situation they feared and planned a small real-life test of their worst-case belief about it. Half then did an exercise where they imagined the feared moment and rewrote it in their minds. The other half just took a break. The people who rewrote the image were more willing to carry out the test.

p52a3fd8ea.post: College students answered questions about symptoms of OCD, which involves unwanted thoughts and urges, and symptoms of PTSD, which follows a traumatic event. Some scored high enough for probable OCD, some for probable PTSD, and some for both. Those who scored high on both reported more severe OCD symptoms than the other groups, but about the same level of PTSD symptoms.

p533fe38dc.post: Data science students worked alone on a data puzzle before being taught the idea behind it. Some were nudged toward good solutions with hints. Others were nudged to come up with weak solutions. After the lesson, the students nudged toward weak solutions showed higher-quality reasoning than those nudged toward good ones.

p5366fd723.post: Pigeons saw a sample that combined a color and a line tilt. After a delay, they had to match either its color or its tilt. The researchers changed how often correct answers were rewarded on color tests versus tilt tests. Accuracy on each test type shifted with its share of rewards, in a pattern a standard reward-and-choice formula described well.

p5384a792b.post: Frequent video game players filled out questionnaires about how strongly they crave gaming and how many signs of problem gaming they had. They also answered questions about acting rashly when feeling very happy. Those who tended to act rashly when happy craved gaming more, and that craving went with more signs of problem gaming.

p538788f77.post: People getting outpatient psychiatric care and a separate group of college students filled out two checklists, one about depression symptoms and one about anxiety symptoms. Answers on the two lists overlapped because of a shared feeling of general distress. Even after that shared distress was set aside, answers still showed a separate depression pattern and a separate anxiety pattern.

p53881df35.post: Young people looked at faces that had been blended step by step from clearly happy to clearly angry. For each face they had to say whether it looked happy or angry. Some of the young people had a diagnosis of severe irritability and temper outbursts, and others were healthy. Young people with the diagnosis were more likely to call in-between faces angry rather than happy.

p54333b074.post: Young French-speaking children heard sentences and had to sort them by accent. Sometimes the accents were Southern and Northern French. Other times they were the children's own accent and a strong foreign accent. The children could not reliably tell the two French accents apart, but they could tell their own accent from the foreign one.

p54396eda1.post: Content moderators, people whose job is to review and remove harmful posts uploaded to the internet, filled out an online survey. It asked how often they saw distressing content, and about their distress, trauma symptoms and well-being. The more often moderators saw distressing content, the more psychological distress and secondary trauma they reported, but their well-being did not change with it.

p546f4c12d.post: American and East Asian students looked at still photos and short animated scenes. In some, something about the main object changed, and in others something in the background changed. Participants had to spot the change. Compared with Americans, East Asians were more sensitive to changes in the background than to changes in the main object.

p546fdfc08.post: Students learned to say a different label for each of eight pictures, and to link pairs of those labels. Half learned the picture labels first, and half learned the label pairs first. Then everyone did a test with just the pictures. Those who learned the picture labels first responded faster than the others, in every part of the test.

p5494b954d.post: People wrote down a sentence saying they wished a loved one would die in a horrible car accident. Then some spent time dwelling on that thought, some dwelled on their bad mood, and some distracted themselves by thinking about everyday objects and situations. The urge to do something to undo the thought faded less in people who dwelled on the thought than in the other two groups.

p5494d1ecd.post: Mothers filled out a questionnaire about how they reacted when their children behaved well or badly. Their children had either a high or a low fear of failure. Children whose mothers were neutral after good behavior and punished bad behavior had higher fear of failure than those whose mothers rewarded good behavior and were neutral after bad.

p54c140dda.post: College students filled out a survey about the in-between stage of life after the teen years. They came from 10 schools, which the researchers ranked by what share of applicants each school turned away. Students' answers on 8 of the 14 survey measures were linked to how selective their school was.

p54e4302f3.post: Preschool children and adults did a task where they had to understand made-up figures of speech, in which a word for one thing stands in for something connected to it. Adults did better overall. Among the children, understanding seemed to drop with age, as older children more often chose the literal meaning of some of them.

p5599785e3.post: People with borderline personality disorder or depression carried a handheld computer for 28 days. It beeped six times a day, asking how hostile, sad, or afraid they felt and whether anyone had rejected or argued with them. In both groups, rejection and arguments went with more hostility, and the reverse too. The link was stronger in the borderline group.

p55ab6d71e.post: Women rated male bodies that varied in how masculine they looked. Some were tested at different points in their menstrual cycle, including the days when pregnancy is most likely. Women preferred more masculine bodies when their fertility was likely at its highest than at other times in their cycle.

p55c6c46e8.post: European Americans and Asian-born Asians rated how independent or connected to others they are, and had a dopamine-related gene tested. European Americans rated themselves more independent, Asian-born Asians more connected. That gap was bigger in people with certain gene versions than in people without them.

p563dd079d.post: Three-year-olds watched an experimenter move a toy girl's bananas from one toy fridge to another. Then each child moved the girl to where she would go for her bananas. The same children also did a standard version of the task. Most got the toy-fridge version right, but most failed the standard one.

p5681a4373.post: Treatment for a problem behavior that is rewarding in itself was sometimes handed to a new person, like a caregiver, or moved to a new place, like the home. Past records of these changes were reviewed. The problem behavior came back in 36% of the changes of person and 26% of the changes of setting.

p5743fc44f.post: College students in some classes got reading worksheets and tutorials to help them read published research articles. Students in other classes did not. Everyone took a multiple-choice test on understanding research articles, before and after. Students with the worksheets scored higher on the second test than the first, going from 73% to 79% correct.

p5789fa77b.post: Women with early stage breast cancer rated how much they valued having a good physical appearance, before their surgery. Then they reported on their mood several times over the next year. Women who valued their appearance more at the start were more distressed across the year after surgery.

p57aa8d497.post: People filled out questionnaires, some meant to measure psychopathy and others meant to measure sadism, which is enjoying hurting others. Then each questionnaire's scores were compared with 51 other characteristics. The psychopathy and sadism questionnaires showed virtually the same pattern of links to those characteristics.

p57e3836d3.post: People saw a series of dots and tried to remember the order of their positions. Sometimes they also had to tap, silently mouth words, or hear speech they were told to ignore. Memory for the dot positions was affected in ways comparable to memory on a similar task that used language instead of positions.

p582411f5d.post: Preschoolers who were at risk of struggling to read were split by chance into two groups. One group got nine weeks of small-group reading-readiness lessons in the fall, and the other got the same lessons in the spring. While getting the lessons, children's skills grew faster in knowing about print, in rhyming, and in dropping a sound from a word.

p5918af08c.post: Student teachers at a Finnish university filled out a survey. It asked how confident they felt about teaching classrooms that include all kinds of learners, and how well they cope with hard times. It also asked about their backgrounds. Of everything measured, their confidence in teaching inclusively was most closely linked to how resilient they were.

p5948df143.post: People lay in a brain scanner while faces flashed on a screen for a split second, too fast to notice, with happy and sad faces mixed together. Some people were being treated in a hospital for depression, and others were not depressed. In a part of the brain called the amygdala, people without depression reacted more to happy faces, while depressed people reacted more to sad faces.

p595421c84.post: People took an online reaction-time test meant to detect whether someone is hiding what they know, like their own country. Questions came one detail at a time. Some people also got filler words like "KNOWN" and "UNKNOWN" mixed in; others did not. Hidden knowledge was detected substantially better with the fillers than without them.

p59986fa20.post: Twins took a national scholastic aptitude test as teenagers in 1962, and their families' income and parents' education were noted. The twins were then compared across poorer and more affluent homes. In poorer homes, the environment twins share explained more of the differences in scores, while in more affluent homes genes explained more.

p59ca79f6b.post: Women who were very afraid of anxious-feeling body sensations, and women who were not, each ran for 10 minutes, 10 separate times. After each run they rated how nervous they felt and how out of control. Over the 10 runs, the fearful women's nervousness, sense of lost control, and body responses went down, but the other women's did not.

p5a0cea8bb.post: Japanese participants imagined a scenario in which they had either caused harm to someone or not. Then they decided how to share resources between themselves and the other person. People who had caused harm gave more of their resources to the other person at their own expense.

p5a2f431e6.post: People with OCD, people with social anxiety, and people without anxiety problems rated situations with a risk of harm. They said how much they wanted to fix each one, how upset they'd be leaving it, and how responsible they'd feel. People with OCD reported more of all three than the other groups in low-risk and OCD-related situations.

p5b09876b1.post: Gamers found through gaming forums on reddit filled out an online survey. It asked how much money they spend each month on loot boxes, which are in-game items bought with real money that hold random contents, and how severe their gambling problems were. The more gamers spent on loot boxes, the more severe their problem gambling.

p5b722127a.post: College students and some other adults filled out a questionnaire about whether their basic needs were being met or blocked. Some statements were worded positively and others negatively. The same people also answered other well-being questionnaires. The split between "met" and "blocked" needs probably came mostly from positive versus negative wording.

p5b8d2369b.post: Pairs of people each watched a different video of the same crime, so some details appeared in only one video. Some pairs talked about the event before being tested alone, and others were not allowed to talk. Of the witnesses who had talked, 71% mistakenly recalled details they had only heard from their partner.

p5bace8e4a.post: Students training to be teachers filled out an online survey about how they set goals, study, and look back on their learning. Researchers then used a statistical method that sorts people into groups with similar answer patterns. It found five types of learners, with labels like "process-oriented competent" and "avoiding-unreflective."

p5ce1caaf5.post: Pairs of people made a decision together in Finnish while their body movements and voices were recorded. Sometimes they could see each other, sometimes not. The talk either moved on to a next step or just kept going. Partners' body sway matched most when the talk moved on and they could see each other.

p5d3f0134f.post: Students in an online graduate course switched back and forth, week by week, between two ways of learning. In some weeks they did an activity called interteaching, and in the others they used an online discussion forum. Quiz scores were higher in the interteaching weeks than in the discussion forum weeks.

p5d6e232b7.post: Preschoolers took turns with an adult describing drawings of animals, like an elephant pulling a mouse. The adult always used the passive form ("The mouse is being pulled by the elephant") and gave stickers only for the plain active form. Five of the six children began using the passive form after hearing it, compared with before.

p5d76ae88f.post: People's scores on an adult IQ test were compared across two versions. One was the standard test. The other was a shortened one that skips the easy early questions on some sections, based on how well a person did on the general-knowledge section. Scores on the two versions lined up almost perfectly, a .999 match where 1.0 is perfect.

p5d9c08f34.post: People did a computer task while sensors tracked their sweat and heartbeat. Some were repeat entrepreneurs in the UK, others were non-entrepreneurs in the US. In both groups, the body's signals seemed to react to a future event the person couldn't know about, beyond what chance would produce.

p5e7d83b3a.post: Married people filled out a long questionnaire about their marriage. It covered things like sex, communication, parenting, and religion. The answers from husbands were compared with the answers from wives. Husbands were somewhat more satisfied with their marriages than wives were.

p5f090e054.post: Women who are twins filled out a questionnaire about hard experiences in childhood and another about mild signs of psychosis. They also gave DNA samples. Researchers compared people carrying different versions of a gene linked to how the body handles stress. The link between childhood trauma and these mild symptoms differed depending on which version of the gene a woman carried.

p5f2200c1f.post: Gifted teenagers answered open-ended questions about what being gifted means to them and how they think other people see it. They felt positive about their own giftedness but did not think others did. Their feelings were mixed: good about personal growth and schoolwork, bad about relationships with other people.

p5fa79fdb7.post: Muslim women in Britain filled out questionnaires about their bodies, beauty in the media, and how religious they were. Some never wore a hijab (a head covering); others wore one at least rarely. Allowing for how religious they were, hijab wearers had a more positive body image and cared less about appearance than women who never wore one.

p5fe7d3811.post: Children did a hands-on problem-solving task twice, once alone and once with another child. They also took a test of how well they understand emotions. Children with higher scores on the emotion test coordinated their actions better with their partner, even when age, gender and solo skill on the task were accounted for.

p60622195d.post: Children and adults were given words like happy, scared, angry and sleepy, and matched each word to photos of actors making different faces. The children were 3, 4 or 5 years old. The word-face matches could be explained by two underlying dimensions, and the same structure held for every age group.

p608a9da84.post: Men who had been charged with serious crimes were tracked after release. About half had been treated in a maximum security psychiatric hospital, and the rest were briefly assessed before prison. Researchers combined 12 pieces of information about each man into one score. The score predicted who would commit a violent offense after release in each of five subgroups of the men.

p60a654264.post: Caregivers of people with memory problems filled out a personality questionnaire about the patient twice: once for who the patient is now, and once for who they were before the memory problems. Compared with before, patients were rated as less outgoing, less organized and dependable, less open to new things, and more prone to distress.

p61c1cb717.post: Some people were exposed to the color red and others to the color blue. Then their motivation was measured: did they feel pulled to steer clear of things or to move toward them? Red mainly made people want to avoid things, while blue mainly made them want to approach things.

p61df220c2.post: College students faced made-up situations with unreasonable requests, like three people they knew only slightly asking to cut in front of them in a movie line, and responded. Afterward they rated how often they had thoughts that made refusing easier or harder. People who scored low on assertiveness reported fewer helpful thoughts and more unhelpful thoughts than people who scored high.

p61f5b065c.post: Legal professionals watched a video summing up a court case in which a man badly hurt his former boss. The man's diagnosis varied: schizophrenia, a personality disorder, or an unnamed condition. Viewers chose a sentence. Of four considerations, how much they felt the crime needed punishment was most clearly linked to their choice.

p622a9c0b7.post: Adults watched their romantic partner work on unsolvable puzzles, then tried them too. Partners were told to stay on one puzzle or to move to the next; a third group was the comparison. People who watched a partner stay switched less than both other groups; those who watched one move on switched more than the comparison.

p628f13a5b.post: U.S. Customs agents watched videos of people being questioned and judged whether each person was lying. The people in the videos had been asked one of three different sets of questions, and the sets differed in how useful they were for exposing lies. Agents were right 42% of the time with one set and 78% with another.

p62c72748d.post: People rated how intense the emotion was in instrumental music, or in the same music with lyrics. Lyrics made happy and calm music less emotional, but made sad and angry music more emotional.

p633a7ce5c.post: For 12 days, people got a prompt on their phones five times a day. Each time they rated how outgoing and how organized they had been acting, plus their mood and tiredness. When people had been acting more outgoing or organized, they felt happier and less tired right then, but more tired about three hours later.

p63698cc8e.post: People watched a film of a young woman's face saying a syllable over and over. The sound was "ba," but her lips were moving for "ga." Others heard the same sound with no video, or watched an untouched film. When sound and lips didn't match, adults reported hearing "da," but they heard the sound correctly without the video.

p63b1d8b42.post: People answered questionnaires on mobile devices about their close friends, family, and romantic relationships. They also gave a saliva sample so researchers could check small differences in their genes. People with different versions of two dopamine-related genes scored differently on the social measures.

p63d27f28c.post: People learned made-up names for 16 unusual animals, either by studying each animal and its name or by answering a question about each animal. Later, everyone was tested on real words that look like a new name, like "tomato" for "torato." Question learners were slowed on those words right after learning and the next day; study-only learners were not slowed right after.

p640506a51.post: College students filled out an online survey of 12 statements about what they expect cannabis to do to their sleep. The researchers looked at which statements people tended to answer alike. The answers split into two groups: one about good effects of cannabis on sleep, the other about bad effects.

p641808416.post: Men got a nasal spray with either oxytocin, a bonding hormone, or no active ingredient. Then they viewed pictures of people in happy or upsetting scenes, rating how much they felt for each person and guessing their feelings. Oxytocin greatly increased felt empathy, but not accuracy at guessing feelings, compared with placebo.

p646d94d57.post: Schoolchildren in Canada and Japan, from first through sixth grade, were asked to draw a landscape. A second group made landscape collages from ready-made items. Japanese children placed the horizon higher on the page than Canadian children did, and they included more pieces of information.

p6470908b5.post: Six children were taught to touch a foam cushion to get an item, attention, or a break from tasks. Then each child got two tests of why a child acts out: one checks each reason separately, the other mixes them together. The separate test found the taught reason in all six children and added no false extra reason.

p64b286316.post: People saw words on a screen and had to say "positive" or "negative" out loud, depending on whether the word was a noun or an adjective. They were told to ignore what the word meant. Responses were faster when the word's meaning matched the word they had to say than when it didn't.

p652c00375.post: Heavy-drinking students got four weekly messages about alcohol. Some got the official guidelines or how they compared with them, some how they compared with the average, and some how they ranked among others. Then they could request health information. Students told their rank were more likely to request it than the others.

p6543e01de.post: People with PTSD and a severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, took part in a 12- to 16-week talk therapy program. It taught them about trauma, had them practice calming breathing, and helped them rethink troubling thoughts. Everyone started out with a PTSD diagnosis. Afterward, 64% still had one, and three months later 50% did.

p65b16319b.post: People saw some fake-news headlines one time or four times, and other headlines not at all. Later they rated how unethical it would be to publish and share each headline. People rated the headlines they had seen before as less unethical to share, even when the headlines were clearly labeled as false.

p65b539388.post: People learned two actions that each earned a different food reward. Then they ate one of the foods until they were full of it. Before choosing again, some had a stressful cold-water test while being watched, and others had a control task. People in the control group cut back on the action that earned the food they were full of, but the stressed people did not.

p65fa74df1.post: High school juniors were assessed for symptoms of anxiety and depression, and the researchers tested how those symptoms group together. The best-fitting arrangement had three layers: one broad factor of general distress, two middle groups (anxious-misery and fears), and five narrow groups of more specific symptoms.

p65ffec5b7.post: Students looked at two pictures, recalled them, and rated how vivid each memory felt. Then one picture was recalled again, with eye movements for one group and without them for the other. Afterward, they judged whether picture fragments were ones they had seen. Only with eye movements did the re-recalled picture become less vivid, on the ratings and on the reaction-time task.

p662840bc7.post: People pressed one of four keys when a box lit up, and each key always showed a picture, like a banana. Later the picture came first: the same one, a similar new one like a pineapple, or a body part. After the same or a similar picture, people pressed the key tied to the original faster than other keys.

p66d67fe9b.post: People took an online quiz that scored seven relationship skills, including communication, stress management and knowing their partner. They also reported how well their romantic relationships were going. After communication, scores on knowing your partner and on life skills predicted good relationships best, compared with the other skills.

p6704fdc2e.post: One person with long-standing dramatic, attention-seeking and self-centered behaviors went through a fairly short course of talk therapy about how they relate to other people. There was no comparison group, only the same person tracked across sessions. Their behaviors changed over the course of the therapy, both in statistical tests and in a descriptive look at them.

p674aa1a8e.post: People with depression filled out a checklist of symptoms before starting treatment. Researchers looked at which symptoms tended to go together in one large group of patients, then checked a second, separate group. The symptoms fell into three clusters in the first group, and the same three clusters appeared in the second.

p67588427f.post: Younger, middle-aged, and older adults looked at pictures on a computer screen. After a distraction task, they tried to recall as many pictures as they could. Some pictures were positive, some negative, and some neutral. With each older age group, people recalled relatively fewer negative pictures compared with positive and neutral ones.

p681483076.post: Teachers listened to a recording about a child who was either withdrawn or aggressive. Then they heard a second recording describing several ways to help, including family therapy, time out, play therapy and medication. They rated how acceptable each one seemed. Medication was rated the least acceptable of all the options.

p688b7b1b7.post: Kids with sickle cell disease, a long-term blood illness, were compared with classmates from the same classrooms. Classmates described how sociable, accepted and aggressive each child seemed, and the kids were also measured on many signs of emotional well-being. Apart from how classmates saw them, the kids with the illness did not differ from their classmates on those emotional measures.

p68e822e8c.post: People lifted the index or middle finger when a number appeared, while watching a hand on screen lift a finger. Some were shown a real hand in a glove beforehand, others a wooden hand in a glove, though the video was identical. The watched finger affected people's own movements more when they believed the hand was human than wooden.

p694a5bdcb.post: Middle school students were randomly put into two groups. One group had a single counseling session meant to help them find their own reasons to change, and the other group waited. Students who had the session took part more in class, showed more positive academic behavior, and got higher fourth-quarter math grades than the waiting group.

p6986054b4.post: College students solved puzzles about made-up three-letter words, deciding whether two words meant the same or the opposite, or whether one meant more or less. They also took a full standard IQ test. Students who scored higher on the puzzles tended to score higher on the three main IQ scores.

p69a05550e.post: Sixth graders with learning disabilities, many still learning English, were in special education reading classes. Teachers in some schools spent about 15 minutes a day teaching four new school words a week. Another school did not get the new method. Students taught the new method scored higher on the words they had been taught.

p69a2ce862.post: People decided as fast as they could whether letter strings on a screen were real words. Just before each one, another word flashed too briefly to notice: cleaner before CLEAN, corner before CORN, or brothel before BROTH. Flashing cleaner or corner affected responses to the next word about equally, and differently from brothel.

p69ae86074.post: People watched videos of child actors telling police a made-up story of being physically abused. The child showed different emotions in different videos. Viewers rated how believable the child was and how likely the accused person was guilty. Sad children were rated most believable, and children showing positive emotion least.

p6a0efcdd4.post: Police officers read a list of 34 things that can happen on the job. They rated how hard each one would be for officers to cope with, from 0 to 4. The one rated hardest of all was making a mistake that seriously injured or killed a fellow officer.

p6a3499f19.post: Junior high students were randomly given either a hard vocabulary test they would likely fail or an easy one they would likely pass. Right afterward, all of them filled out a questionnaire measuring test anxiety. The students who got the hard test scored higher on test anxiety than the students who got the easy test.

p6a5dac4a8.post: Second-year medical students read about eight women with similar-stage breast cancer and said what treatment they would recommend for each. Some of the women were 31 or younger and others were 59 or older. For women who had already chosen to have the breast removed, the students recommended rebuilding the breast for 95% of the younger women but only 65% of the older women.

p6a61d16b5.post: Women social workers in a South Indian city filled out questionnaires about how stressed they felt, how well they bounce back from hardship, and how burned out they felt at work. Women with higher and lower resilience scores were compared. How strongly stress went with burnout depended on how resilient the women were.

p6a6fa05a0.post: People with OCD and people without it saw a series of negative, positive, and neutral words. After each word, they were told to either remember it or forget it. Then everyone was tested on all the words. People with OCD were worse at forgetting the negative words than the positive and neutral ones, while people without OCD showed no such gap.

p6af79aca9.post: Babies, 6 and 10 months old, saw individuals who acted differently toward others: one helped another, one hindered another, and one did neither. Then the babies were given two of these individuals to choose between. The babies preferred the individual who helped another over the one who hindered another.

p6b2502890.post: Two people sat down to have a face-to-face conversation. In some pairs a mobile phone was present, and in others there was no phone. Conversations with a phone present came out worse on closeness, connection, and conversation quality than conversations without one.

p6bb684f5f.post: Mothers, fathers, and two school-age children from each family were interviewed at home. Parents reported whether they showed more warmth to one child or treated them equally. In some families one parent said equal and the other said unequal. Those families, where parents disagreed about warmth, were linked to more marital distress.

p6bbb3f11e.post: People rated how sure they were that certain events happened in their childhood. Two weeks later they got a made-up "computer profile" saying a false achievement event and a false friendship event had happened to them, and they imagined and described both. People who said achievement mattered more to them were more likely to come to believe the false achievement event had happened.

p6bddd1a22.post: Students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland took their big school exams at age 16. Researchers checked how well family background, mental ability, and conscientiousness (being careful and hardworking) lined up with exam scores. Ability and conscientiousness together explained almost as much of the differences in scores as all measures combined, and far more than family background.

p6cb3f9285.post: Pigeons chose between two keys they could peck. Both keys led to a reward after the same total wait. On one key the wait was a single stretch, and on the other it was split into two stretches back to back. The pigeons mostly preferred the single unbroken wait over the split one.

p6cc8362d9.post: People saw a category name and the name of an item, and decided whether the item belonged to the category. For some, the category appeared 800 milliseconds before the item. For others, the item came first. How good an example the item was had no effect on answer speed beyond what how easily the category came to mind already explained.

p6cd5ead1f.post: University students in Norway and in the United States filled out a questionnaire about how they were working out who they are. It covered beliefs and values as well as close relationships. The Norwegian students' scores were more moderate than the American students' scores.

p6d15faa33.post: People reported sudden, intense paranormal experiences, like sensing that a friend or family member was sick or had died. For 25 published cases, researchers looked up how disturbed Earth's magnetic field was on each day. All 25 happened on days calmer than that month's average.

p6d3873671.post: Some men were put in the mindset of wanting to attract a romantic partner, and others were not. Then the men said how much they would spend on luxuries and on basic necessities. The romantic-mindset men were willing to spend more on showy luxuries than the other men, but not more on necessities.

p6dd11d5c9.post: Preschoolers repeated strings of numbers, some in the same order and some in reverse. They also did tasks about what another person wrongly believes, and similar tasks that used photographs instead of beliefs. Among children of the same age and vocabulary score, those better at repeating numbers in reverse did better on both kinds of tasks.

p6de440aa1.post: People watched a videotaped interview with a college instructor who spoke English with a European accent. It was the same man in both versions, but in one he acted warm and friendly and in the other cold and distant. People who saw the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms, and accent as appealing, while people who saw the cold version rated them as irritating.

p6e12ef14d.post: Women watched 45 short video clips while sensors tracked their body responses. Some clips were funny, like a slip of the tongue during wedding vows. Some were painful accidents, and some were in between, like a boy falling off a treadmill. Body responses to the in-between clips differed from those to the funny and painful ones, in strength and in pattern.

p6e311b83c.post: Teachers at middle and high schools across China filled out a survey about being victimized at work, how burned out they felt, and how positive their school's climate was. In schools with a more positive climate, victimization was less tied to feeling detached from others, but more tied to feeling less accomplished.

p6e3a329d1.post: People answered questions about how they go after goals and what matters most to them in life. Some were mainly focused on avoiding mistakes and losses. Those people valued following rules and feeling secure more, and valued independence and excitement less, than people who were less focused on avoiding losses.

p6e3da285a.post: People decided as fast as they could whether strings of letters were real words. Some words were more iconic, meaning their sound resembles their meaning. People responded faster and more accurately to the more iconic words.

p6e620864f.post: Three heavy coffee drinkers tracked and charted every cup they drank. Each got a daily limit that slowly got lower. They won money for staying under the limit and lost part of a deposit they had put down when they went over. Their coffee dropped from almost nine cups a day to under three, a 69% cut.

p6ec0fb80c.post: Children and adults watched a flashing explosion-shaped figure while hearing a beep. They judged whether the flash and the beep happened at exactly the same time, when the beep came anywhere from no delay to half a second off. Children who once had a language disorder were much worse at telling the two apart than children with typical language development.

p6edfdcc35.post: Teenagers were randomly assigned to one of two programs. One was a program built to get them thinking about their ethnic and racial background. The other was a comparison program that gave them attention but wasn't about identity. Teens in the identity program explored their background more than the comparison group, and then felt more settled about what it means to them.

p6eecbc579.post: People with borderline personality disorder and people without it each did an interview, and their answers were scored two ways. A rating scale judged how well they understood their own and others' thoughts and feelings. A computer program scored the same answers by counting 54 word patterns. In both groups, higher rating-scale scores went with higher computer scores.

p6f42e7aab.post: Some people were reminded of money, and others were not. Then everyone answered questions about whether society and the world are fair, and said how high up they felt they stood compared with other people. Money reminders made people more or less accepting of the system depending on how high up they felt.

p6f50545a4.post: Undergraduates read a persuasive message that argued against what they already believed. Some read strong arguments and some weak ones, and the message came from a source that was either an expert or not. For some students the issue mattered a lot to them personally, and for others it hardly did. When the issue mattered to them, students were swayed mostly by how strong the arguments were, and when it did not, they were swayed mostly by how expert the source seemed.

p70135390f.post: Two large sets of data held people's achievement test scores, their school grades, and measures of their personality. The researchers checked how much of the differences between people in scores and grades lined up with differences in personality. Personality explained a substantial part of the differences in test scores and grades.

p70218946d.post: University students were randomly assigned to study groups. Students became more conscientious when assigned to conscientious peers, more open-minded when assigned to open-minded peers, and more competitive when assigned to competitive peers.

p7051d2b1f.post: Some people held a hand in ice water for three minutes while a stranger watched; others used warm water, unwatched. Then everyone learned which screen symbols won chocolate milk or orange juice, and later ate one of those foods until full. Stressed people's choices did not shift away from the food they were full of, compared with the warm-water group.

p711a5ed1b.post: College students answered questions about what they knew and how they felt about mental illness. Then some attended a presentation from the In Our Own Voice program, and others attended a talk about careers in psychology. Everyone answered the same questions again. Students who attended the In Our Own Voice presentation improved more in knowledge and attitudes than the career talk group, on all three measures.

p712c7581f.post: Community college students in a math course got a message before a class exam. Some were taught that a racing heart and other signs of stress can help them perform. Others were told to ignore their stress. The students taught that stress can help reported less math anxiety and did better on the exam than the students told to ignore it.

p717184656.post: People were asked about events from their lives, some involving alcohol and some not, and about how much they drank in a typical week. Past unpleasant feelings usually fade faster than pleasant ones. Among light drinkers, that extra fading of bad feelings was larger for ordinary events than for alcohol events.

p71a5e34d6.post: Four clinic supervisors role-played giving feedback to a pretend therapist. At different times, each one then watched a video showing how to give good feedback, with a voice explaining each step. Their feedback was scored on eight skills before and after the video. After the video, all four supervisors mastered the skills.

p720bc0344.post: Marines who had fought in Afghanistan answered questions one month after coming home. They reported times they were in danger, times they broke their own moral values, and times trusted others let them down. Eight months later they reported their anger and PTSD symptoms. Marines who felt betrayed had more PTSD symptoms, and the link ran through anger.

p724b11e30.post: People judged items in a series on a physical scale. For some, the items were split into classes that followed the scale, with smaller ones in one class and larger ones in another. For others, the series had no classes. Items from different classes were judged as farther apart than in the series with no classes.

p725af0ba8.post: People watched videos of a face saying a syllable while hearing a different syllable, then wrote down what they heard. Half were trained conservatory musicians and half had no music training. Musicians were not fooled by the mismatch on any syllable, while the others were fooled on several.

p725afa587.post: Adults with social anxiety did a computer attention task for 15 minutes, twice a week, for four weeks. Some got a standard version and others a modified version meant to shift attention. Some did it in a lab and others at home. Symptoms dropped in every group, with no clear difference between the standard and modified versions.

p72be9ed2f.post: Bilingual Chinese people and European Americans organized objects, and the Chinese bilinguals did it in either English or Chinese. The Chinese bilinguals grouped objects more by how they relate to each other, and less by category, than European Americans did, in both languages.

p72d246c93.post: People with binge eating disorder were asked about their eating habits in two ways: a face-to-face interview and a written questionnaire. Both asked how many times they had binged. People who reported more binge episodes in the interview also reported more on the questionnaire.

p732466290.post: People played a slot machine game where they won money only if two icons matched. On some rounds they picked their own icon, and on others the computer picked it. Rounds that ended in a near-miss were rated less pleasant than clear misses, but people said they wanted to keep playing more.

p735e9d867.post: People saw statements about attitudes, some they strongly agreed with and some they strongly disagreed with. For some statements they pressed the button for their true answer. For others they were told to press the opposite button, as a lie. Lying responses were slower than truthful ones, and brain recordings also showed more mental effort for lying.

p736247111.post: People kept watch for rare but important events over a long stretch of time. The researchers tracked how willing people were to say they had spotted one. They found that a shift over time in this willingness can look like people getting worse at telling real events from background noise.

p736e7028f.post: People in China who had offended were assessed four times over one year. The assessments covered how well they handle their sense of self and relationships, their everyday personality traits, and their problematic traits. Problematic traits were partly predicted by the other two measures combined.

p73ad44fb3.post: College students each shared 10 memories that helped define who they were. Each memory was scored for the kinds of events in it and the emotion people felt when recalling it. The students also filled out a questionnaire that measured how distressed they felt. The events in their memories and their feelings while recalling them predicted how distressed they said they were.

p73d1f48dd.post: People looked at grids of faces, eight disgusted and eight neutral, for six seconds each while their eye movements were tracked. Some had social anxiety disorder, some were very socially anxious students, and some were students who were not anxious. Both anxious groups spent longer looking at the disgusted faces than the not-anxious students did.

p73f991936.post: College women in the UK filled out questionnaires. They covered media beauty ideals, how often they watched how their body looked, how ashamed they felt of it, and how satisfied they were with sex. Women who watched their looks more and felt more body shame reported less sexual satisfaction.

p740db5049.post: Children and adults learned about two made-up groups, Hibbles and Glerks, that typically ate different kinds of berries. They then judged individuals who ate the berries typical of their own group or of the other group. Children judged the individuals who ate the other group's berries negatively, less so as they got older.

p7421d30e9.post: People in romantic relationships were nudged to feel nostalgic about times with their partner. In one experiment they did a writing task, and in another they listened to music. Others were not given that nudge. People nudged to feel romantic nostalgia reported stronger benefits for their relationship than the others.

p7488648e2.post: Patients being treated for pain filled out questionnaires about their moods, their pain, and traits of borderline personality disorder. People with more of those traits reported more pain. But that link disappeared once their depression, anxiety and hostility were taken into account, and depression explained most of it.

p74ddb6db2.post: Adults rated how physically easy it is to say different consonant sounds at the start of a word. Those ratings were then compared with earlier data on how well three-year-olds had mastered the same sounds. Sounds that adults rated as easier to say were the ones three-year-olds had mastered better.

p74f4c64ce.post: People traded in experimental markets where they could know about upcoming dividends. In some markets everyone knew, in some no one knew, and in some only some traders knew. Bubbles were smaller in the markets where only some traders knew more than the others.

p75055e1e1.post: People with a strong fear of enclosed spaces went through treatment that meant facing those spaces. Some had safety aids available, some actually used them, and some had none. Others got a placebo treatment or waited. Knowing safety aids were available hurt fear reduction about as much as using them, compared with having none.

p75a560fab.post: Pigeons pecked a key either once or 20 times, then saw a pair of colors, one that led to food and one that did not. Each effort level had its own colors. Later they chose between colors from the two levels. They preferred colors that followed 20 pecks over matching colors that followed one peck.

p75cbb5db1.post: Third and fourth graders practiced reading words from drill sheets that looked like a car racetrack, with timing and a correction whenever they missed a word. Each child's reading was measured before the sheets started and again during. Every child more than doubled their rate of correctly read words compared with before.

p765be5284.post: Teachers in one preschool class taught all 16 children skills like following instructions, waiting, and making friends. They taught during normal activities like circle time and meals, using role play, modeling, and feedback. Children showed more than four times as many of these skills as they did before the teaching.

p7678b5ae2.post: Gamblers with moderate to high gambling problems and gamblers without problems did an online task, pressing keys to pull pictures toward them or push them away. Some pictures were about gambling, matched to each person's usual games. Others were neutral. Compared with the other gamblers, those with problems had a stronger tendency to pull gambling pictures than neutral ones.

p76aaebe4c.post: Men in a Chicago-area jail were interviewed about their lives, and the answers were used to score four parts of psychopathy. Another interview covered their use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids. Once the other three parts were taken into account, only the interpersonal part was linked to cocaine dependence.

p76ccaaf70.post: A patient with a reading disorder was taught which sound goes with each letter. The patient still could not blend separate sounds into a whole word, but could say a word's first sound, and that worked as a hint for reading it. Spoken naming also improved after the therapy, because the written word could give the same kind of sound hint.
