p7724688cb.post: College students filled out a questionnaire about why bad things happen to them, plus a depression questionnaire. A month later they filled out both again. Students who blamed bad events on causes that last and that affect everything in life were more depressed a month later.

p777411842.post: People read explanations for why a person behaved a certain way. Some explanations appealed to a named tendency or condition, and others gave the same explanation without the name. People found the explanations with the name more satisfying.

p779576483.post: People with agoraphobia, a strong fear of leaving safe places, and people without it tried to recall five passages. Three contained information related to that fear and two were neutral. Those with agoraphobia recalled more of the pieces of information from the fear-related passages than the others did.

p781347a7a.post: Nurses, medical staff and emergency responders used a phone app once a day for a week. Each session had some writing, an exercise for handling feelings, and either one or two activities meant to bring on good feelings. Their daily boost in positive emotion was bigger for those given two such activities than for those given one.

p7870d99e5.post: Hospital patients being treated for cancer filled out two questionnaires. One measured how well they cope with hardship, called resilience. The other measured anxiety and depression. Patients who scored higher on resilience had lower emotional distress, even after accounting for other differences between patients.

p78aa2a67f.post: Black clinicians read the same made-up case about a man with sexual problems. Some were told he was black and others were told he was white. They also filled out a questionnaire about traditional social beliefs. Clinicians with less traditional beliefs rated the patient more favorably when he was labeled black than when he was labeled white.

p791ae57f7.post: People went through the items on a common anxiety questionnaire, such as feeling tense or worried. For each item they answered three questions: how much of the time they felt it, how likely they were to feel it when stressed, and how long it lasted once it started. Both how likely and how long each predicted people's usual anxiety scores, and each added something the other did not.

p79ee02de4.post: Future teachers said what they believed about making struggling students repeat a school year. Then they read scientific evidence that either backed up their belief or went against it. Those who read evidence that went against their belief rated educational research as less able to answer this question, and trusted its sources less, than those who read evidence that agreed.

p7a043f482.post: People did a memory task that secretly contained hidden patterns. Later they rated how much they liked items, some of which fit those patterns. People also differed in how mindful they were, meaning how little they react on autopilot. More mindful people liked the pattern-fitting items less than less mindful people did.

p7a6dbf0f8.post: People who were high or low in social anxiety gave an impromptu speech. Researchers measured how anxious they felt and acted, how aroused they thought their bodies were, and how aroused their bodies actually were. High-anxiety people felt and acted more anxious and thought they were more aroused, but their actual physiological activation did not differ.

p7a8fa7e08.post: Typists of different ages and skill levels did simple tasks, like hitting one key when a letter appeared or two keys in a row. Older typists with low skill did worse than younger ones at both choosing the right key and moving the finger. Older typists with high skill did worse only at choosing the right key.

p7a9ee8dfb.post: People learned a movement skill and then a list of words, or the words first and then the skill. For some, the first memory was made stable, so nothing could disrupt it. Learning one kind of task helped with the other kind, except when the first memory had been made stable.

p7b1a02605.post: Preschool children heard sentences with the word "or," some of them also containing "every." The researchers checked how the children understood each sentence. Often, the children treated an "or" sentence as if it said "and," so both things had to be true.

p7b706fe4f.post: Teenagers in China filled out questionnaires about how well off their family was growing up and how greedy they tend to be. Some were only children and others had siblings. Teens who grew up better off were greedier, and this held for only children but not for teens with siblings.

p7b820792f.post: Students who get special education help with reading had their reading progress checked with short reading measures. Researchers compared checking every week with five schedules that checked less often. Decisions based on the less frequent checks were as accurate as decisions based on weekly checks.

p7b88dedbf.post: Infants aged 6 and 12 months saw novel actions demonstrated. Some then took a nap of at least 30 minutes and others did not. Later they were tested on whether they remembered the actions. Only infants who had napped remembered the actions.

p7b8c1bd21.post: People stared at a dot while a tilted oval flashed off to the side, between two other ovals. They turned a bar to match the middle oval's tilt, while the outer ovals' tilt changed from trial to trial. When the outer ovals pulled answers toward their tilt, answers were more precise, with less error overall, than with no outer ovals.

p7bcb6b79b.post: Young children did two kinds of tasks about a person who believes something that isn't true. In some tasks the children were asked outright about that belief, and in others they weren't. Both 3-year-olds and 4-year-olds passed the tasks without direct questions, but only the 4-year-olds passed the ones with them.

p7c18dc39a.post: Students filled out a questionnaire about seven unpleasant thoughts that had popped into their heads uninvited. For each one, they said how they dealt with it and how they judged it. Within the same person, thoughts they tried to escape or avoid were judged more disapprovingly than thoughts they tried to think through.

p7cb125292.post: Some people were given reminders that atheists are common, and others were not. Then they rated how much they distrust atheists. People reminded of how common atheists are distrusted them less.

p7cb6525a1.post: Teenagers from a clinic and matched teenagers not from a clinic filled out two questionnaires. One asked about closeness, parenting style and conflict in their family. The other asked how they saw themselves. The two groups described their families in much the same way, but how teens described their family was strongly linked to how they saw themselves.

p7cd1acb8d.post: Working-class and middle-class Americans decided which products to buy after learning what other people had chosen. Working-class Americans were more influenced by others' choices than middle-class Americans.

p7cf2e81a9.post: Preschoolers heard a made-up verb in a sentence while watching events, such as 'the girl is fezzing' or 'the tall girl is fezzing'. Then they pointed to the event they thought the verb meant. Children picked the right event for 'the girl is fezzing' but not for 'the tall girl is fezzing'.

p7d18e3c62.post: Students at a large city community college took a psychology course with a lot of reading and writing. School records showed the highest English class each had finished: regular college English, or a catch-up class for weaker skills. Students who had completed college English were more likely to pass than students still at the catch-up level.

p7d51b3d13.post: People saw a face flash for a split second, then get covered by a neutral face. After each, they said whether the flashed face looked fearful. Some people could reliably spot the fear and others could not. Those who spotted it better also scored higher on a general anxiety questionnaire.

p7d5a6d92a.post: English speakers learned a made-up language from cartoon pictures, like a red ball. Each person learned two kinds of describing words, then picked between two word orders for a phrase they were never taught, like "two red balls." They preferred adjectives closest to the noun, then numbers, then this/that, most strongly for adjectives versus this/that.

p7d9846410.post: Community college students who felt very anxious about tests joined a nine-session program. They learned to relax their muscles, then worked through a list of 25 test-related situations that made them nervous. Other anxious students got no program. Students in the program raised their grade point average from 1.73 to 2.39, while the others' grades did not change much.

p7da9e7cdb.post: Women and men chose how much money to put into a shared group pot. Each player had one of two versions of the MAOA gene, called L or H. Women with L were less likely than women with H to be weak free-riders, who give little to the pot.

p7dc522e06.post: Preschool boys with autism or a similar diagnosis did 100 extra rounds of naming practice each day. Researchers counted how often each boy named something or asked for something on his own, during short checks at free play, lunch, and in the hallway. After the extra practice, the boys named and asked for things more often than before.

p7df457eb6.post: Young women in the US were followed for years and asked every so often whether they took diet pills or laxatives to control their weight. Researchers then checked who later got a first eating disorder diagnosis. Women who used diet pills or laxatives were more likely to be diagnosed within the next 1 to 3 years than women who did not.

p7ee960c95.post: People listened to a nonstop stream of made-up speech with no pauses between words. The only clue to where the words began and ended was which vowel sounds tended to follow one another. People did not use that vowel pattern to pick out the words.

p7f012e090.post: People from a gambling support forum read a message about a gambling game and rated their chances of winning on a 7-point scale. Half read "This game has an average percentage payout of 90%." The other half read "This game keeps 10% of all money bet on average." People who read the "keeps 10%" version rated their chances of winning lower.

p7f237e83b.post: Toddlers from Greek-speaking families, from about a year and a half to almost three, had their vocabulary checked with a Greek version of a US word survey. Their results were compared with those of US toddlers on the original survey. Greek toddlers seemed to get off to a slower start in learning early words than US toddlers.

p7f2f71c6e.post: Workers in five kinds of jobs, such as police, managers and salespeople, had their personality measured and their job performance checked. The results of many earlier studies were pooled together. Being outgoing predicted job performance for managers and salespeople, jobs with a lot of dealing with people.

p7f4fc7744.post: Students solved three statistics problems on a computer, using textbook slides. Half also saw a worked-out solution for each problem, and half had only the textbook. All had earlier done a task measuring how easily they switch between mental tasks. Worked examples were especially helpful for people who were worse at switching, compared with solving problems alone.

p7f7739ea9.post: Intro psychology students filled out two questionnaires about meaning and purpose in life, one called the PIL and one called the SONG. Researchers then checked how the answers grouped into themes. The PIL gave six themes and the SONG added four more, about how strongly people want to find meaning, so the SONG complemented the PIL.

p803e5e9ed.post: Young children wrote their own names, going from right to left instead of the usual left to right. Children who write left to right tend to flip letters that face left, like J. Most of these children flipped mainly letters that face right, like B, D and E, the opposite of the usual pattern.

p80482d50e.post: People filled out a 70-question personality questionnaire about being outgoing, being anxious, and whether they were being honest about themselves. Researchers checked which answers tended to go together, then repeated this in a second, similar group of the same size. Liking company and acting on impulse showed up as two separate traits, only partly related, in both groups.

p805549f33.post: High school students wrote down their usual school-night bedtime and wake-up time. They also said how often in the past two weeks they felt sad, hopeless or tense, and whether they used things like alcohol, tobacco or drugs. Students who slept more hours reported fewer of these problems and behaviors than students who slept less.

p8064f8e3b.post: People judged whether two stacked words were related. Sometimes the layout matched real life, like ATTIC above BASEMENT, and sometimes it was flipped. The words were flashed to only the left or only the right half of the brain. A flipped layout made a reliable difference for the right half, but not for the left.

p807a90de8.post: People imagined giving money to a made-up charity. Some saw just one charity, while others saw two side by side. One charity spent little on administration, and the other saved more than twice as many lives per dollar. People who saw one charity gave more to the low-administration one, but people who saw both gave more to the one that saved more lives.

p81889a24a.post: People clicked on two planets on a screen to earn points. Later, clicking one planet sometimes brought up a spaceship, followed by an attack that took away some of their points. Most people learned to avoid that planet, but not everyone. Some learned right away, some only after being told the rule, and some kept clicking it even after being told.

p819ad7c86.post: People in Poland answered questions about their personality, their beliefs about the coronavirus, and what they did during the pandemic. People with more "dark" traits, like being manipulative or callous, took fewer precautions and hoarded more. Beliefs about the virus fully explained why dark traits went with fewer precautions, and partly explained why they went with more hoarding.

p81c38d5e1.post: Children and adults were asked how they felt about math, once when thinking about whole numbers and once when thinking about fractions. Their math skill levels were also taken into account. The vast majority of both children and adults felt negative about fractions, even though they felt positive about whole numbers.

p827eb2da7.post: People studied golf-putting instructions and practiced putting. Some expected to teach another person how to putt afterward, and others expected to be tested on their own putting. A day later, everyone was tested on their putting. People who expected to teach putted better than people who expected a test.

p82be004cc.post: Researchers collected the lineups of keynote and invited speakers at state behavior analyst conferences over three years. For each talk, they searched Google Scholar for the speaker's published research papers on that talk's topic. Nearly a third of the speakers had no published papers on the topic they presented.

p833b32986.post: Parents of preschool twins took part in a 'don't touch' task, where they had to get each child to stay away from attractive toys. Some parents then got five sessions of coaching with video feedback on how they interacted with their kids, and others got none. The coached parents were better at setting limits in a positive way than the parents who got no coaching.

p83565d446.post: Male veterans staying in a hospital took a standard personality test called the MMPI. Some had been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, and others with different personality disorders. The borderline group scored higher on six of the test's 13 standard scales.

p83675b956.post: Healthy adults filled out a questionnaire about how often they handle feelings by rethinking the situation. They also had their brains scanned while resting, to see which areas rose and fell in activity together. The more people said they rethink situations, the less in sync parts of the amygdala, an emotion area, were with two other brain areas.

p84159028b.post: Undergraduates filled in two questionnaires: one on how they treat themselves when things go wrong, and one on their health habits. Researchers looked at which parts of self-compassion went with a healthier lifestyle. Students who were kind to themselves, saw their struggles as part of being human, and were mindful lived healthier lives.

p8451aae45.post: People who had taken psilocybin on their own in the past year filled out an online survey. They looked back on their state of mind at the start and on what the experience was like. Surrender at the start best explained mystical experiences, and preoccupation best explained challenging, dread-filled ones.

p846fd2bd7.post: People sang two popular songs from memory, and their pitch was compared with the pitch of the original recordings. Many people sang at least one song at the right pitch.

p84f015d9c.post: People read sentences while a tracker followed their eyes. One word was swapped for another just as their eyes reached it, and the first word either made sense in the sentence or didn't. Early on, people read faster after a sensible first word than after a nonsensical one, but later, a sensible unrelated word gave no benefit.

p84fb4ac3e.post: Adult twins in the UK, some identical and some fraternal, filled out a questionnaire at home about their sense of humor. It asked how much they agreed with statements like "I laugh and joke a lot with my friends." For all four humor styles, differences between people were explained by genes and by experiences that twins don't share, not by the home they grew up in together.

p853fe9156.post: Students with developmental disabilities learned to read new words one-on-one with a teacher. When a student made a mistake on some words, the teacher said the word and the student repeated it. On other words, the teacher said the word while the student just looked at the card. Students read more words correctly when they had repeated the word out loud, including later tests and words read in sentences.

p855645b23.post: College students in a subject pool could sign up to take part in a study whenever they liked during the semester. Some signed up early, in Weeks 3 and 4, and others waited until Weeks 15 or 16. Everyone filled out a personality questionnaire, among other measures. The early signers scored higher on neuroticism, a trait that covers things like anxiety and moodiness, than the late signers.

p85b6ab3b5.post: Five students with or at risk for emotional disturbance did their schoolwork in a regular classroom. Some of the time they were given a choice about which assignment to do, and other times they were not. The students paid more attention to their work and did better on it when they had a choice than when they did not.

p85e6c6809.post: Soldiers who had been through trauma answered questions on a laptop. They reported how many likely head injuries they'd had, how much they fear that trouble focusing means going crazy, and their stress symptoms. For soldiers with high fear, more head injuries went with more stress symptoms; for those with low fear, the link was weaker.

p864e97b84.post: People tried a new kind of task and were told, falsely, that they had done well or badly. Other people watched and listened in. Then everyone was told the scores were made up and random. Afterward, both the people who did the task and the watchers still judged the performers' abilities in line with the fake feedback.

p8662c097e.post: Clients at a counseling center rated their most recent therapy session. They said how strong their bond with the therapist felt, and how much the therapist used feelings-and-relationships techniques and thought-and-behavior techniques. When the bond was strong, more feelings-and-relationships techniques went with better change after the session. More thought-and-behavior techniques without them did not.

p868bcdcc2.post: Women who had been abused by a partner and had PTSD were randomly put into two groups. Some started a course of trauma therapy right away, and others were put on a waiting list to start later. Among the women who finished the therapy, PTSD went away in 87% of them, and their depression and guilt dropped a lot.

p86c26ef17.post: Parents filled out a questionnaire about how close and flexible their family was. Their young teens named their friends, rated their best friendship, and rated how well they were doing. Family scores were more strongly linked to teens' self-ratings for those without a close friend than for those with one.

p8749b2175.post: People listened to sentences about hand actions, foot actions, or abstract ideas. Meanwhile a magnetic pulse over the brain made their hand or foot muscles twitch. Twitches were smaller when the sentence was about an action with that same body part than when it was abstract.

p879eee914.post: People with panic disorder and people without it did two word memory tasks. One was a fast recognition task, the other was recalling words freely. The words were threatening, positive, or neutral. People with panic disorder remembered the threatening words better than the positive and neutral ones, and the other group did not.

p8846597af.post: At-risk kindergartners went through an early program called First Step to Success. This was a repeat run with a new group of children, and the results were compared with those from the original test of the program. The new group's outcomes were nearly identical to the original group's.

p887f3f577.post: Women saw photographs of men who were more or less attractive, each with a description of how he behaved in different situations, altruistically or not. They rated how desirable each man was. Women preferred the altruistic men, especially for long-term relationships.

p891faf307.post: Children who had trouble with movement and coordination were randomly split into three groups. One group practiced imagining movements with an interactive CD-ROM, one did traditional movement training, and one was put on a waiting list. The imagery practice helped the children's motor skills about as much as the traditional training did.

p89629c88f.post: People did eye-movement tasks. Some had OCD, some were healthy close relatives of people with OCD, and some had no family history of it. In some tasks they chose for themselves where to look; in another, what they saw guided their eyes. The OCD group and the relatives were both slower than the third group at choosing where to look.

p8a29d6deb.post: Five elementary school students with learning disabilities practiced spelling by listening to a tape that read out a word list, then writing each word. For half the words, they checked and fixed their spelling after each word. For the other half, they waited until they had tried all 10 words. On the end-of-week tests, every student learned more new words when they had corrected after each word.

p8a51bb608.post: People with alcohol dependence and people without it did a word task on a screen. A threatening word, like one about being hurt or put down, came first, and then a word about alcohol or a neutral word. The threatening words sped up responses to alcohol words only for alcohol-dependent people who had been emotionally abused as children.

p8a5b9154d.post: Adults who often binge ate were randomly split into two groups. One group got eight short sessions over 12 weeks with a therapist who walked them through a self-help program. The other group got the usual care their health plan offered. A year later, more people in the therapist-guided group had stopped binge eating: 64% versus 45%.

p8a855dbb7.post: People did two vision tasks: noticing a short gap in time, and noticing a small gap in space. Sometimes what they looked at was near their hands, and sometimes it was far from their hands. People did better on the timing task and worse on the space task when it was near their hands than when it was far.

p8ac5cd6c5.post: People played an on-screen ball-tossing game with two other players, with brain activity recorded. Some first played a version in which they lost control. Then everyone started getting the ball less often. Those who had lost control first showed a smaller brain response to being left out, and said they felt less excluded, than the others.

p8afdc482e.post: Elementary school teachers got regular emails with visual feedback on how often they used specific praise, which means praise that names what a student did well. Their rate of specific praise went up compared with before the feedback, and it was still higher 3 months after the emails ended.

p8b1fd80fa.post: People walked on a treadmill without a motor, at whatever pace they liked, while music played. In some parts of the session the music played no matter how fast they walked. In others it played only while they sped up, or only while they slowed down. People walked faster when music depended on speeding up, and slower when it depended on slowing down.

p8b217dda5.post: Students in many countries rated how good they felt they were at math and science, and those ratings were compared with their achievement. This was checked two ways: student by student, and country by country using averages. Students with higher achievement rated themselves higher, but countries with higher average achievement had lower average self-ratings.

p8bad614da.post: People looked at black-and-white photos of faces with hair and ears cropped out. They rated how much each person looked like a leader during a war, or during a time of peace, and how masculine or feminine each face looked. Faces that looked more masculine were picked as better war leaders, and faces that looked more feminine were picked as better peace leaders.

p8c53db6a6.post: Bonobos and chimpanzees were each given food in a setting where they could eat together with other apes. Researchers watched how well each species put up with sharing space around food. Bonobos were more tolerant of eating together than chimpanzees were.

p8c58a4889.post: College students kept a diary for a week. They wrote down their social conversations and every time they lied in them, whether face to face, on the phone, by instant message, or by email. The students lied most on the phone and least in email.

p8cef47fe9.post: Therapy clients and some students filled out a personality questionnaire called the 16 PF. Researchers used the answers to predict each person's scores on personality disorder scales, then checked them against a different personality disorder test the same people took. Ten of 11 predicted scores were related to the other test's scores by more than chance.

p8d09c3b4a.post: People solved math problems that have an intuitively tempting wrong answer, and also reported how strongly they believe in God. People who gave more of the tempting intuitive answers reported stronger belief in God.

p8d4fd8ab7.post: People took part in experiments on nostalgia, the sentimental longing for your own past. Nostalgia boosted people's sense of belonging and acceptance by others. That stronger sense of connection helped them feel that their past self and present self are linked.

p8dc046cec.post: People with obsessive-compulsive disorder said whether a common serotonin-targeting medication had helped them. Most said it did, and some said it did not. Researchers then compared DNA across the whole genome between the two groups. The strongest difference was at one spot in the DNA, near a gene called DISP1.

p8e0222481.post: People listened to information spoken by native and nonnative speakers and judged how believable it was. Some first got a short exposure to foreign-accented speech, and others did not. Those with the exposure showed less of the usual bias against believing accented speakers.

p8e78f3b38.post: People were asked to think about one of three things: death, a death that someone chooses for themselves, or dental pain. Then researchers measured how strongly they defended their own culture and its norms. People defended their culture more after thinking about death than after thinking about dental pain or a self-chosen death.

p8e7d8034e.post: Mothers were videotaped giving their sons a short lesson; all the boys had a learning disability. Researchers scored how each mother guided her son, then tested the boys' resilience and how much they improved with help. How mothers guided, the home environment, and family income all helped predict the boys' resilience and improvement.

p8e8482ae3.post: Employees sat through spoken feedback sessions while researchers watched how they received it. Everyone was observed first without training, then got training on how to receive feedback, starting at a different time for each person. After training, people showed appropriate feedback-receiving behavior and kept it up, compared with before training.

p8f3074663.post: Young adults in dating relationships were randomly put into three groups. One group did a computer program about their relationship, one did a computer program about handling depression and anxiety, and one was a control group. Eight weeks later, both program groups had less depression and anxiety and better relationships than the control group.

p8f6ceea35.post: People used a phone app that asked them 10 times a day for one week how much they had tried to look at their situation in a calmer, more positive way. It also asked how much control they felt they had over what was happening. People with higher well-being used this more when they felt little control, and less when they felt more control.

p8ff1d021b.post: Children with and without dyslexia heard the syllable "ba" repeated at a steady beat, twice a second, while their brain activity was recorded. They pressed a button whenever the beat was delayed. The slow brain waves of children with dyslexia lined up with a different point in the beat than those of the other children.

p9013bd75f.post: Women with anorexia nervosa who had recently regained a healthy weight had their body fat, body mass index and stress and appetite hormones measured. Researchers then followed them through a trial meant to prevent relapse and rated how each woman did at the end. Women with lower percent body fat were more likely to have a poor long-term outcome.

p9029f7700.post: People's pupils were measured while they read single words that conveyed brightness, such as day, darkness, such as night, or neither, such as house. Pupils were largest for the dark words, in between for neutral words, and smallest for the bright words.

p90a3c1c54.post: Primary school students in Hong Kong studied 20 English adjectives in two sessions. For some words the two sessions were one day apart, and for other words they were eight days apart. Four weeks later, they took a multiple-choice test. They did better on the words studied one day apart than on the words studied eight days apart.

p9151a0434.post: People filled out a long online survey of statements about how they handle their thoughts, feelings and daily life. The statements were pulled together from many existing questionnaires. Then the researchers checked whether the answers grouped into 12 separate themes. A statistical test found strong support for the 12-theme grouping.

p918145186.post: Young children watched two identical videos of a woman talking, side by side, while one soundtrack played. In one video the sound matched her mouth. In the other, her mouth ran 0.3, 0.6, or 1 second ahead of the sound. Children without autism, matched to the autistic children on language level, looked more at the matching video when the delay was 0.6 or 1 second.

p9184a27b1.post: People held either expansive, open poses or contracted, closed poses. Then they prepared and gave a speech to two evaluators in a mock job interview. People who had held the expansive poses performed better and were more likely to be chosen for hire.

p919a45315.post: People saw a list of seven letters on a screen, then wrote them down in order after a pause, while ignoring a looping sound of three spoken syllables in headphones. For some, all syllables came from one spot. For others, each syllable came from the left, middle, or right. Spreading the sounds out disrupted memory less than playing them all from one spot.

p91bd33e44.post: People tried to keep track of several moving objects on a screen at once. In some cases all the objects they had to follow were on one side of the screen. In others the objects were split between the left and right sides. People could successfully track twice as many objects when they were split across both sides as when they were all on one side.

p925cbfbd2.post: Women and men were randomly assigned to be primed to think about having either low or high social support. Then they looked at faces and chose which ones they preferred. People primed with low support preferred more feminine-looking faces, of both sexes, than people primed with high support.

p9264dda97.post: People read statements and looked at graphs about climate change, such as rising temperatures and sea levels. Some read a range of how bad things could be by a fixed date. Others read a range of when a fixed level of harm would arrive. People who read the arrival-time ranges saw the threat as more serious and were more likely to urge action than people who read the outcome ranges.

p92deb4f42.post: Before each game at a major European soccer tournament, the players sang their national anthems. Researchers compared how much passion each team showed while singing across the tournament's 51 games. Teams that sang with more passion went on to concede fewer goals than teams that sang with less.

p936a82ed1.post: People guessed the populations of many countries. Some were then shown the true populations for a set of countries, and later everyone tried to recall their own first guesses. Learning true numbers for some countries pushed people's memory of their guesses toward the truth, even for countries whose numbers they were not shown.

p93affe6e6.post: Professionals who evaluate people for legal cases filled out a survey about their own work. It asked how often they use practices meant to respect the cultural background of the people they evaluate. What they reported doing varied from one evaluator to the next, which suggests they do not always follow the official practice guidelines.

p93c723e2d.post: Women rated how attractive male figures were, one at a time, from 1 to 7. The figures were computer-made men of the same height, but with legs that ranged from shorter to longer. Some were plain silhouettes and others were detailed figures. For the detailed figures, the most attractive leg length was a bit longer than average, about half a standard deviation above it.

p94176c315.post: People who were in a better or worse temporary mood rated how satisfied they were with their life overall. They also rated how satisfied they were with specific parts of their life. Mood strongly shaped their ratings of life overall, but had only a weak effect on their ratings of specific parts of life.

p942d9db33.post: Children learned to press a button for two jars with equal water, and not press for unequal. Then one jar was poured into a differently shaped jar, and children signaled without words whether the amounts were still equal. Young children who failed the spoken version were more likely to show they understood pouring doesn't change the amount, using buttons.

p943d99cff.post: Adults with anorexia began a course of talking therapy. At the start, they answered questions about their eating attitudes, like restricting food and worrying about body shape, and their weight was tracked over 10 sessions. In sessions 6 to 10, those with more unhealthy eating attitudes gained weight more slowly than those with less unhealthy ones.

p943ead727.post: People tried to influence a machine that spits out random numbers, just by intending a result. Researchers pooled 380 such studies, checking whether the machine's output lined up with what people intended. Overall it did, but the effect was very small.

p94659b29b.post: People pressed one of four buttons, and each press made a tone play. Sometimes the tone was the one linked to that hand, and sometimes it was a different one. Brain responses to the tone were weaker when it matched what that hand predicted than when it did not.

p94af2ad10.post: People who reported high or low social anxiety were randomly put into a social threat condition or a non-threat condition. Then they made choices between rewards now and rewards later. In the non-threat condition, highly socially anxious people discounted later rewards more than people with low social anxiety, meaning they valued them less.

p94cae7e25.post: Some men and women were put in the mindset of wanting to attract a romantic partner, and others were not. Then everyone said how willing they would be to take risks in several different areas of life. Men in the romantic mindset reported being more willing to take risks than men who were not.

p94f6b10d6.post: Nine preschoolers in public pre-K classrooms sat in small groups with headphones and listened to recorded stories. Vocabulary and comprehension lessons were built into the stories. The researchers checked each child's learning on the lesson targets. Children showed modest improvements in vocabulary and comprehension, and this repeated within and across children.

p9526588ab.post: Married Jewish women, religious and secular, answered an online survey about how satisfied they were with their sex lives and with their marriages. The researchers compared women in shorter marriages with women in longer ones. Sexual satisfaction and marital satisfaction were more closely linked in longer marriages than in shorter ones.

p95498aeb7.post: People told the truth about a route they had taken, and also lied about it, describing it either in normal order or in reverse order. Other people then read the transcripts and judged which accounts were lies. Observers detected lies better when the route was described in reverse order.

p95f565a02.post: Preschoolers did play activities in a lab, like racing toy cars and blowing bubbles, plus newer, scarier ones, like a stranger walking up. Researchers rated each child's joy and how wary they were of new things. In the familiar play, children who showed less joy approached less, but wariness was not related to approach.

p95f91137c.post: Birth dates and places were pulled from the biographies of famous French scientists, athletes, and actors. For each person, the sky positions of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn at birth were worked out, and their personality descriptions were rated. Introverts were more often born just after Saturn rose or peaked in the sky, and extraverts just after Mars and Jupiter did.

p966768c70.post: People read poems and rated the mood of each one. Some poems had a lot of burst sounds like P and T, made by briefly stopping the air. Others had a lot of nasal sounds like M and N. Poems with more burst sounds were rated pleasant and lively, and poems with more nasal sounds were rated unpleasant and low-energy.

p968d3ab16.post: People rated 10 stigmatized conditions. For each, they judged whether the person caused it, how they felt toward the person, and whether to help. Some conditions were physical and others were mental or behavioral. Mental or behavioral ones were seen as more the person's own doing, and drew less pity, more anger, and less willingness to help than physical ones.

p96bcc3573.post: People with moderate depression were randomly given 12 weeks of either cognitive therapy, a kind of talk therapy, or an antidepressant drug. Before starting, they filled out a questionnaire on self-control skills. In cognitive therapy, people with high self-control scores did better than people with low scores.

p96de709cf.post: Students in Belgium, Britain and Slovakia estimated their own IQ scores. They also estimated the IQ of their parents and their brothers and sisters. Men rated their own overall IQ higher than women rated theirs, but the two groups did not differ in how they rated their parents or siblings.

p972b0c117.post: Children watched short video clips of objects appearing in different ways. Each clip was described with a made-up verb inside a made-up sentence pattern. Afterward, they heard new descriptions in that same pattern and picked the new scenes that matched. The children could match the new descriptions to the right new scenes of something appearing.

p973753552.post: U.S. college women rated how much they see their own body as an object to be looked at. They also rated their support for the current gender system and their involvement in gender activism. Women who saw themselves more as objects backed the current gender system more and were less involved in gender activism.

p97391c0a4.post: English speakers and Thai speakers learned a made-up language in which describing words came before or after the noun, unlike in their own language. They only practiced phrases with one describing word, then had to guess how to say phrases with several. Both groups put adjectives closest to the noun, then numbers, then demonstratives like "this" or "that."

p9739ae4ce.post: Widowed people were interviewed about six months after their spouse went into the hospital. They answered questions about grief, depression, and anxiety symptoms. A statistical method then sorted the symptoms into clusters that go together. Grief symptoms formed their own cluster and barely overlapped with depression or anxiety symptoms.

p97bcb718e.post: People viewed a few organic foods, comfort foods, or control foods. Then they were asked to volunteer time to help a needy stranger. People who had seen organic foods volunteered less time.

p97d15f5e1.post: People judged how well coordinated two people were with each other. Some pairs had similar skin tones and others had different skin tones, but the actual amount of coordination was the same. Pairs with different skin tones were judged less coordinated than pairs with similar skin tones.

p982906c65.post: People saw pictures and named each one out loud, in either Mandarin Chinese or English. The names were words built from two smaller words. Some whole words were common while their parts were rare, and others were the reverse. Naming was driven by how common the whole word was, not by how common its parts were.

p9836afc12.post: Young adult gamers who did not gamble reported how much money they spent on loot boxes, the video game prizes you pay for without knowing what you'll get. Six months later, they said whether they had started gambling. Those who had spent more on loot boxes were more likely to have started gambling, and to spend more on it.

p9843f1b69.post: Some people were reminded of their own death and others were not. Then they answered questions about a group they belonged to. People reminded of death identified more strongly with their group and showed more bias in favor of it.

p98607ed47.post: People looked at upsetting pictures and, for each one, chose how to feel less bad about it. They could think about something unrelated, or rethink the picture to make it seem less negative. Some people were led to form a long-term goal. They chose to rethink the picture more often than people without one.

p9861e9966.post: People saw a word like WALKER and decided whether it was a real word. Just before it, a brief flash showed the ending alone ("er"), a whole word with that ending ("baker"), or an unrelated prime. Compared with primes that only shared letters, a shared ending gave the word a boost, whether it came alone or inside a whole word.

p98e572e46.post: People watched yellow squares of four sizes while finger sensors tracked their sweat response. Either the biggest or the smallest square sometimes came with a loud scream in headphones; the other squares never did. While learning, people more bothered by uncertainty reacted to the safe squares too; less bothered people told the scream square apart better.

p98fa43947.post: University students drank a beverage. Some were told it would make them anxious, and others were told it would have no side effects. Then everyone did a task where they pressed a key or held back, while a cap recorded their brain's response to mistakes. Students told the drink would make them anxious showed a smaller brain response to errors than students given no such explanation.

p991b4eacd.post: Students thought about their country and rated how much they agreed with statements like "My group is extraordinary." Their answers were compared with how they felt about their group. People who scored higher felt better about their group privately but thought others saw it less well. They also had lower automatic, gut-level good feelings toward it.

p99afd39af.post: Students filled out an online survey the summer before college. They rated how important reasons like moral values or not feeling ready were in deciding whether to have sex, and said whether they had ever had sex. Those who rated values and not feeling ready as more important had less sexual experience.

p99e214664.post: Depressed patients got one of two talk therapies: one worked on thinking habits, the other on relationships. Patients also differed in how avoidant or how obsessive their personalities were. The thinking therapy worked better than the relationship therapy for more avoidant patients, and the relationship therapy worked better for more obsessive ones.

p9aab41f17.post: Preschool boys with autism learned to touch the picture that matched a spoken word. Some words were taught at a table with picture cards and treats. Others were taught inside a game, like a jumping game or a toy train. Teaching at the table and inside the game were equally effective and efficient.

p9add81229.post: College students said whether they smoked, drank alcohol, or believed in God, and reported their SAT scores. Then they rated how much they agreed with a statement tied to each habit, such as "Secondhand smoke is a health hazard for nonsmokers." Students with higher SAT scores were not clearly less biased toward their own side than students with lower scores.

p9afa3f78e.post: Students filled out a survey that scores how hard-driving, rushed, and competitive a person is, a style called Type A. Their scores were then compared with their grades. Students who scored more Type A had higher grade point averages than students who scored less Type A.

p9b4450d97.post: People with schizophrenia, living in the community and stable on medication, were measured on symptoms, thinking skills, daily-life skills, and how they managed real life. Researchers mapped which measures were linked to which. Skills for handling everyday tasks were the most connected to all the others.

p9ba3b95b4.post: Infants raised with one language or two learned to look at one side of a screen ahead of time because a cue predicted a reward there. Then the cue began to predict the reward on the opposite side. Only the bilingual infants managed to switch their looks to the new side.

p9ba666b51.post: Rats pressed a lever in one setting where it paid off, and in another where it did not. Some got all of the first setting, then all of the second. Others switched between the two every day. Back in the first setting, lever pressing returned more in the switching rats than in the others.

p9bfcd4c0b.post: Five speakers were recorded reading aloud 16 words that can be either a noun or a verb, such as answer or design. Each word was read once as a noun and once as a verb. There were slight but consistent differences in how the words sounded when read as a noun versus as a verb.

p9c074d116.post: Physically active people walked briskly on a treadmill four times: with music, with a music video, with a music video hiding cues too quick to notice, and with nothing. The hidden-cue walks felt better, were remembered and expected to be more pleasant, and felt less hard than the other three.

p9ca90ee07.post: Interviewers asked parents, children, or both about kids' past trauma and current symptoms. Each child was screened for developmental trauma disorder (a proposed label for lasting harm from childhood abuse or neglect), PTSD, and other disorders. The other problems that came with developmental trauma disorder overlapped with those of PTSD but also included panic, separation anxiety, and disruptive behavior disorders.

p9cc532bf1.post: Toddlers played with puppets that made happy "yum" noises when they got a treat. Sometimes the toddlers were asked to give treats to the puppets, and at other times they got treats themselves. Their happiness was rated each time. Toddlers were happier giving treats to the puppets than receiving treats themselves.

p9d0effa6b.post: People answered questions about how common certain things are in real life, and the computer timed how fast they answered. They also said how much television they watch. People who watched more TV guessed that those things were more common, and they answered faster than people who watched less.

p9d3ea37cb.post: Preschool children with developmental delays were taught to name letters or letter sounds. Some items were taught with examples shown one after another, and others with examples shown together. On average, the children reached the learning goal in fewer sessions with examples shown together than with examples shown one after another.

p9d528fc73.post: Some people first had the chance to disagree with blatantly sexist statements, and others did not. Later they chose whether to favor a man or a woman for a stereotypically male job. People who had first disagreed with the sexist statements were more willing to favor the man.

p9e83032e0.post: College students took tests of reasoning, knowledge, math, visual skills and memory, plus tests of noticing, understanding and handling emotions. The researchers tried several ways of organizing the scores. One setup that fit acceptably put emotional ability as a branch under general intelligence, alongside skills like reasoning and visual processing.

p9ed3e3a6e.post: People played jurors watching a filmed mock murder trial. For half, the defendant was described as having a "severe personality disorder, borderline pattern"; for the rest, "complex mental health problems." The two groups did not differ in how often they chose the lesser verdict of diminished responsibility, which treats mental illness as partly excusing a killing.

p9ef269669.post: Rats learned to press a lever for food. Then some only got food after a pause with no pressing. Others got food at the same moments no matter what they did. Lever pressing dropped faster and more sharply in the rats rewarded for not pressing than in the rats fed regardless.

p9f41d416e.post: People heard either a word such as 'cat' or a sound such as a cat meowing, and then saw a picture and said whether it matched. People verified the picture faster and more accurately after the word than after the sound.

p9f613d27b.post: Care staff were asked what they would do, right away and in the long run, about a made-up young man's hard-to-handle behavior. Their long-term plans fit the aims of psychological treatment. Their right-away responses instead resembled the counter-habilitative ones (those that work against a person's growth) found in earlier research on staff.

p9f73971b3.post: People tried to think up unusual uses for objects. Then they had a break with a hard task, an easy task that lets the mind wander, plain rest, or no break, before going back to the same problems. People given the easy task did better on those problems than the other three groups.

p9fa2007d3.post: People in counseling, mostly at college centers, filled out a well-being questionnaire before every session, for 5 to 25 sessions. Researchers sorted them into three groups by how their scores moved over time. One group, who started with moderate distress, improved early, leveled off, then improved again later.

p9fe16101a.post: People read a report about a college quarterback who wanted to play more consistently. In one version he worked on it with his coaches, and in the other he worked on it with a sport psychologist. Then people said how strongly they would recommend drafting him. They recommended the quarterback who saw a sport psychologist less strongly than the one who worked with his coaches.

pa028ff2ea.post: Students in an introductory college chemistry course filled out a questionnaire about how they felt toward chemistry, and their answers were tracked as the course went on. There were no separate groups. The results fit a "low-involvement" pattern, where thinking about a subject and acting on it come before feelings about it.

pa0a292be2.post: University students solved logic problems presented in text, in formulas, or in combinations such as text with formulas or text with graphics. Students given a combination of representations outperformed students given just one.

pa0c77aaa9.post: During a COVID-19 lockdown, people filled out an online survey about how their eating had changed and about their eating habits, including how well they could resist cravings. Of the habits measured, being worse at controlling cravings was the strongest sign of eating more high-calorie sweet and savory foods.

pa0f67143b.post: College students filled out a questionnaire on how much they study by choice, did a word task meant to detect that motivation without asking, and took memory tests. Grades were collected at semester's end. Students who said they study by choice got better grades only if the word task also showed it and their working memory was average or high.

pa1ba0dfd5.post: People picked the more attractive face from pairs, such as a more masculine and a more feminine version of one face. Then some watched pictures hinting at germs, while others saw pictures with no such cues, and everyone picked again. After the germ pictures, people's picks changed mainly for opposite-sex faces, not same-sex faces.

pa1f40f24b.post: People with social anxiety had their brains scanned while resting, then took a course of cognitive behavioral therapy, a type of talk therapy. Their improvement was predicted either from the brain scans or from how severe their anxiety was at the start. Each kind of brain measure predicted improvement better than starting severity did.

pa1f699895.post: People read statements that describe playful adults, which the researchers built from an analysis of everyday language. They also filled out two existing playfulness questionnaires. The answers sorted into seven kinds of playfulness, such as cheerful, whimsical and impulsive, and the two questionnaires left some of them out.

pa25bd18bd.post: People who had lived through a traumatic event and were very afraid of feeling anxious were split into two groups. One group got a program meant to lower that fear. The other got a comparison program. A month later, the first group had fewer trauma symptoms than the second, counting where each person started.

pa2b4a91c7.post: People learned that some symbols meant an upsetting picture might appear, and others meant it was safe. Then, when a symbol signaled a threat, they could take an action to stop the picture from showing. After each time the picture was successfully stopped, they rated how pleasant the relief felt. People who usually get less enjoyment from things rated that relief as less pleasant.

pa2ce74b69.post: Some high school classes had regular gym lessons for 7 weeks. Other classes got a short skills program built into gym, with four 20-minute lessons and two times to reflect. Students reported how much they exercised and played sports. Students in the skills program reported more exercise and sport than those in regular gym.

pa36f9e739.post: Twelve military veterans who had been diagnosed with PTSD went through a 3-week training program built around a psychiatric service dog. They filled out questionnaires a month before the training, when they arrived, and six months later. There was no comparison group. Their PTSD and depression symptoms were lower after the training than before, and still lower at six months.

pa3c66dde0.post: College students read the first sentences of a passage aloud into a microphone, and each had a front-facing photo taken with a neutral expression. Strangers of the opposite sex rated how attractive each voice was. The more lopsided a person's face was, the less attractive their voice was rated, in both men and women.

pa46e9344f.post: Babies stayed in a lab while their mothers left and came back, and were rated on how secure they seemed. Years later they were interviewed about their parents and partners, and gave cheek cell samples. Early security predicted adult security only in people with the G/G version of an oxytocin receptor gene, not those with other versions.

pa475c204e.post: People who had recently had their first episode of psychosis filled out a 21-item questionnaire about their lives. It asked how much they felt in control of their choices, capable, and connected to others. People without psychosis of the same age also answered it. The group with psychosis reported less satisfaction of these basic needs.

pa502ade57.post: College students ticked off the unwanted thoughts and urges that had popped into their heads on a checklist. They also filled out questionnaires on how depressed, anxious, and guilty they felt. Guilt was the best predictor of these thoughts and urges, while depression and anxiety were not strong predictors.

pa506d096d.post: Children with dyslexia did 8 weeks of training on reading words by sounding them out, and 8 weeks of training on learning tricky words as whole shapes. Some did sounding out first, some did whole words first, and some did both together. Both kinds of training led to gains in how fluently the children read words.

pa51060072.post: A team went through articles on child abuse and neglect from three journals, published between 1977 and 1998. They checked whether each article reported participants' ethnicity and whether it used ethnicity in its analysis or design. Ethnicity was used more over time, but in 1995 to 1998 three quarters of articles still left it out.

pa545ea0c4.post: Young men came to a lab twice, at least a week apart. One time they took a stress hormone (cortisol) or a male sex hormone (testosterone), and the other time a dummy treatment, without knowing which. Then they played a trading game with investments. With either hormone, they moved their money toward riskier investments than they did with the dummy.

pa579d35c7.post: People took a personality test, then got magnetic pulses to the head that made a muscle twitch. Sometimes a weak pulse came just before a strong one. The higher people scored on neuroticism, a lasting tendency toward anxiety and negative feelings, the bigger their twitch to the pair compared with the strong pulse alone.

pa58af61d4.post: People saw one item flash up, then a second item that they had to name out loud. The first item felt either pleasant or unpleasant. In some versions the items were shown again and again, and in others no item was ever repeated. The first item's good or bad feeling still affected how people named the second one, even without repetition.

pa59fa649c.post: Some people went through an unrelated situation meant to make them sad, and others did not. Then everyone put a price on an object, either what they would sell it for or what they would pay to get it, with real money at stake. Sad people asked less to sell it but offered more to get it.

pa5a2720e7.post: Patients hoping to get on a heart transplant list took a personality questionnaire about their emotional distress, plus a set of thinking tests. Some answered the questionnaire in a guarded way, trying to look good, and others did not. Among the open patients, more distress went with worse thinking scores. Among the guarded patients, the two were unrelated.

pa5bd01a96.post: Children aged 6 to 11 were told about the carrots other children had eaten: a large amount, none, or no information. Then they got carrots to eat. Children who thought other children had eaten a large amount of carrots ate more carrots than all the others.

pa5d0fe452.post: People looked at pictures that were positive, negative or neutral. Then they said which pictures they had seen before, mixed in with new ones. Another person, who was working with the researchers, gave wrong answers, correct answers or none. People's answers shifted toward what the other person said more for neutral pictures than for emotional ones.

pa5d30116a.post: Beginner French students at a state school spent two lessons doing tasks that got them to notice how French shows plurals, and the teacher never explained the rule. A comparison class only took the tests. The students who did the tasks understood more of the new words and plural forms than the class that only took the tests.

pa5fd08df3.post: People had a chance to cheat by overreporting how well they did on a task. Then they did tasks that measure creativity. People who cheated were more creative afterward than people who did not.

pa657232e0.post: People did visual tasks in which something in a scene changes, which people often fail to notice. The researchers modified these tasks. Even when people did not notice a change, they still showed sensitivity to it.

pa6576ed03.post: People guessed their own chances of going through 70 bad life events, like a robbery or Alzheimer's disease. After each guess they were shown the average person's real chances, then guessed again. Some were people with depression and some were not. People without depression changed their guesses more when the news was better than expected than when it was worse, but people with depression did not show this pattern.

pa67f4f4c0.post: Salespeople from many kinds of companies filled out a questionnaire they got in the mail about how they listen to customers. Each person's answers were turned into a listening score. Those scores were linked to both how well the salespeople performed and how much sales experience they had.

pa69956311.post: Adults looked at photographs of trees shown in patterns based on the seasons, or in random order, and rated how meaningful their lives felt. People who saw the patterned photographs reported more meaning in life.

pa6b20ea61.post: Students in 64 countries were tested in reading and math and asked if they planned to study or work in math-heavy fields. Girls were stronger in reading compared with math than boys were. Once that gap was accounted for, the girl-boy difference in plans for math fields shrank by around 75%.

pa6bf8a4e6.post: Married people read short stories about couples having pleasant or unpleasant moments. In some stories the couple talked about their relationship, and in others they did not. After each story, readers rated how content the characters felt. Readers rated the couples as feeling better when they had talked about their relationship.

pa77619f85.post: Young people at high risk were asked about abuse and neglect in their past, and about their mental health: emotional troubles, behavior problems, and trauma symptoms. Some had lived through several kinds of mistreatment, others fewer. Emotional abuse was the main predictor of having more symptoms, over and above the other kinds of abuse and neglect.

pa79fd9704.post: People listened to tones, including target tones they had to react to, while their brain activity was recorded. Some had OCD and took no medication. Others were healthy and matched for age and sex. People with OCD had a larger attention-related brain signal, which came sooner on the right side, and reacted faster to target tones.

pa7fc68680.post: A fourth-grade class was split into two teams to play a game. Each time a child left their seat or talked out of turn, a mark went on the chalkboard, and everyone on that team could lose privileges like extra recess. The game cut down the out-of-seat and talking-out behavior, first in math period and then in reading period.

pa8bb9afe3.post: Older people whose husband or wife had died a few months earlier answered questions about how they were feeling. Researchers then checked which symptoms tended to show up together. The symptoms split into two separate sets: one for grief, such as yearning and disbelief about the death, and one for depression.

pa8c1f52c4.post: People made choices where they could leave another person with more options or fewer options. They also filled out questionnaires about their personality, their empathy, and how much they care about good outcomes for others. People who left others more choice scored higher on honesty, agreeableness, empathy, and caring about others' outcomes.

pa8da2ad41.post: A mother gave her 3-year-old daughter set commands, like "Put the book on the table," while an observer scored how each of them acted. The girl had a diagnosis for defiant behavior, and the mother was in parent training. Over the training, the scores changed for both the mother's behavior and the girl's.

pa93f1c889.post: College students in the US, Britain, Germany and Japan did tasks meant to show how much people see themselves as separate from others. One measure looked for a puffed-up sense of self. This was strongest in Americans, in the middle for the British and Germans, and absent in Japanese students.

pa964d9bdb.post: People played an online dice game in which they placed columns of dice into slots to win or lose money, and the game tracked how fast they played. Players were sorted into high-involvement and low-involvement groups by the game company. Both groups started the next round faster after a loss than after a win.

pa976ea523.post: People watched a ring flash on a screen while a short beep played through headphones. Sometimes the beep came just before the ring, sometimes just after, and sometimes together. After each one they said whether the two happened at the same time. A single brief mismatch on one trial was enough to shift what people judged as simultaneous on the next trial.

pa99e450e1.post: Some people were made to feel grateful to another person, and others were made to feel good in general. Then everyone could help that person, even though helping was unpleasant. People who felt grateful put in more effort to help than people who did not feel grateful.

pa9ebb1439.post: Students who said they were trying to eat healthily answered questions about self-control and how automatically they ate unhealthy snacks. Then they kept a diary of their snacks for a week. Students with more self-control had weaker unhealthy-snacking habits, and those weaker habits accounted for why they ate fewer unhealthy snacks.

paa0fa7857.post: Six people with developmental disabilities were shown snack items two at a time and picked the one they wanted. The snacks came from four kinds: chocolate, salty and crunchy, gummy, and fruit and vegetable. Snacks from the kind each person liked best, including ones not in the choosing game, worked as rewards for them.

paa2dd8e1b.post: University students filled out surveys on how well their basic needs were met, why they exercise or diet, what they planned to do, and what they did. The surveys covered two areas: exercise and dieting. In both, the answers fit the chain the researchers expected: needs met, then self-driven motivation, then plans, then behavior.

paa9ff16f0.post: Practicing counselors reported how often they ran into ethical dilemmas at work, how often they reflected on them, and how burned out and stressed they felt. Counselors who ran into more ethical dilemmas reported more burnout and stress.

paac27842a.post: Six adults with developmental disabilities learned to set a table and put away groceries by watching videos. For some tasks, they watched 10 short clips, each showing one step, and then tried the task. For others, they watched one long video showing all 10 steps. The step-by-step clips helped almost everyone learn quickly, but the single long video mostly did not help.

pab1fb164e.post: College students filled out questionnaires about how nervous they feel when talking with others and how shy or sociable they are. They also watched a set of short videotaped scenes of people interacting and answered questions about what was going on between them. Students who felt more nervous talking with others scored lower on the video task.

pab759937a.post: People wrote statements about an event, some as mock criminals who were lying and some as innocent people telling the truth. Half of each group were told beforehand that their statements would be checked for details that could be verified. Being told made truth tellers, but not liars, give more details that could be checked.

pab99e57e1.post: Ninety-seven top young football players answered questions about what drives them: why they play, what goals they set, and how much they want to achieve. A year later, the researchers checked which players had made the under-15 national team. The players whose drive came most from inside themselves were more likely to make the national team than the other players.

pabecce004.post: Some people were first led to think about the ways they differ from other people. Then they were tested on whether they would take another person's visual point of view without being asked. People primed to focus on differences were more likely to do so than people who were not.

pacb8a6f9d.post: College students wrote about their own death. Some had first received magnetic pulses to a spot in the front of the brain, and others got a fake version. Then everyone rated statements like "There exists an all-powerful, all-knowing, loving God." The students who got the real pulses reported about 33% less belief in positive religious ideas, such as God, angels and Heaven, than the fake-pulse group.

paceb30928.post: Students learning French practiced a French past tense by choosing what sentences meant. Some also got a short lesson and practice on the matching English grammar, while others got only the French practice. Those who also got the English lesson later understood French sentences more accurately and read them faster than those with only French practice.

pad0ff58dc.post: Women and men across the US filled out a personality questionnaire covering 15 traits, such as warmth, dominance and tension. The researchers combined the differences on all 15 traits into one overall score. Men's and women's personality profiles overlapped by only about 10%, a very large overall difference.

pad72b2dad.post: Junior and senior psychology majors saw a list of 42 famous names in psychology, half men and half women, including several people of color. For each name, they rated how well they knew the person, from never heard of them to could describe most of their work. Students recognized the women and the people of color less than the White men.

padd5e3725.post: Depressed patients, anxious patients and people with neither problem saw a word, then a second word printed in color, and named the color. Some words were adjectives they had rated as describing themselves. Among depressed patients, naming the color took longer when both words described them than when only the second one did.

padfb38c29.post: College students wrote short stories about a man or a woman. Some saw a picture or a written description of an overweight character, and others saw a normal-weight character. Students who wrote about overweight characters wrote sadder, more negative stories and made the characters more unpleasant than students who wrote about normal-weight characters.

pae21cdd49.post: College students in China and in the US each wrote down two memories that said the most about who they are. Researchers sorted the memories into types, such as achievement or guilt and shame. Memories about academic stress were far more common among the Chinese students (28 of 120) than the American students (4 of 120).

paf7de9c2b.post: Married couples each filled out a questionnaire about how emotionally mature they were and another about how well their marriage was working. Each spouse also rated the other's maturity in private. Husbands who rated themselves as more emotionally mature tended to score higher on how well their marriage was working.

pafde36699.post: People in a brain scanner judged whether faces looked happy or fearful, with the word "HAPPY" or "FEAR" written across each face, sometimes clashing. Some people had generalized anxiety disorder; others did not. Healthy people adapted to clashes from one trial to the next, but people with the disorder were completely unable to.

pb00f0916d.post: People read short descriptions of psychological findings, each followed by an explanation of why it happens. Some explanations were good and some just restated the finding. Half the people saw explanations with an added, irrelevant line about brain scans, and half saw none. People without neuroscience training rated explanations as more satisfying when they included the brain information.

pb02e47638.post: Younger and older adults took tests of spotting awkward remarks and reading other people's emotions. Some were made to feel close to the experimenter or the person in the task, and others were not. Older adults did worse than younger adults without the closeness, but with it they did about as well as younger adults.

pb07685506.post: People played a gambling game where each round offered a choice. They could take a small prize right away that was unlikely to pay off, or wait a bit for a bigger prize that was more likely to pay off. They also rated how much they dislike not knowing what will happen. People who disliked uncertainty more tended to pick the quick, smaller, less likely prize.

pb0aa2ab91.post: College students went into a professor's office and either stole an exam or put back an exam that had been stolen earlier. A week later, each was interviewed. Half told the truth and half lied to avoid blame. The honest students gave longer, more detailed answers and admitted more possible mistakes than the liars.

pb1202b3b5.post: People got bursts of mildly painful heat and rated them. Some heard a recording guiding them to pay attention to their breathing and body sensations, and others heard fairy tales. Among people who tend to think the worst about pain, the guided group felt less pain than the story group. Among people who don't, it was the reverse.

pb1b416f54.post: First graders who were struggling to read got extra small-group help every day, in schools assigned by chance to one of two plans. In some schools, regular class reading lessons were improved and the extra help matched them. Others used the standard district lessons and help. Children in the matched-plan schools improved more on sounding out words and reading aloud smoothly.

pb23974844.post: Babies went through a mildly stressful lab visit where they were briefly separated from their caregiver, and researchers watched how they acted. Their DNA was checked for two variations in one gene. Babies with both risk variations had about ten times the odds of disorganized attachment, meaning confused, mixed-up behavior toward the caregiver.

pb241c1063.post: Older adults went through a session that quietly brought to mind either positive or negative ideas about aging, without them realizing it. Then their memory was tested. Those given positive ideas tended to do better on memory, while those given negative ideas tended to do worse.

pb28f0d287.post: Adults filled out an online questionnaire about the languages they speak, how well they know each one, and how much they use it. They also rated statements like "I can adapt quite easily to changes in a situation." The more multilingual people were, the more easily they said they adjusted their goals.

pb293fc5d1.post: Women who were lesbian and women who were straight, none of them in clinical care, filled out a questionnaire about their relationships with their parents. The study suggested that how the women reacted to their parents' behavior may matter more than the parents' behavior alone.

pb29f01275.post: In New Haven, registered voters were randomly assigned to receive a get-out-the-vote message just before an election, from a canvasser in person, by mail, or by telephone. Then researchers checked who voted. Voter turnout rose substantially with canvassing, slightly with mail, and not at all with phone calls.

pb3026f7ee.post: College students were taught to name a set of visual items, then taught to answer one spoken word with a related word. Afterward they matched the items to each other and answered spoken tests, including with new sets. In a second experiment, some of the matching tests were left out. Thirteen of 17 students passed every matching and spoken test.

pb309f14b4.post: Six children with autism watched two models act out a play scene together, then stepped into one model's role while the same scene was repeated. For some training rounds, the children also had to describe the scene out loud before they joined in. The children did not learn to play cooperatively until the out-loud description was added to the training.

pb3543b1a6.post: Students were measured on how mindful they naturally are, meaning how well they stay in the present moment. They were also measured on how much they replay worries in their heads and how out of control that replaying felt. Among students who replayed worries a lot, the more mindful ones were less likely to feel they couldn't stop.

pb41b6fdef.post: Men got a nasal spray with oxytocin, a hormone linked to bonding, on one visit and a spray with no active ingredient on another. Afterward they rated themselves on traits like "independent" and "self-confident." Men who tend to worry about being close to others rated themselves as less independent and self-confident after oxytocin than after the placebo, while the average man showed no change.

pb47a18a39.post: Students filled out questionnaires about things like how they relate to others and how they see life. Two months later they did it again. Some had a traumatic event in between and also rated how much they had grown from it. Their own ratings of growth were generally unrelated to how much their answers actually changed.

pb47bebeaf.post: Mothers rated their 3-year-olds on defiance, tantrums and showing little guilt. The children also took part in a lab session with their mother that measured their bond, and teachers rated their aggression each year through sixth grade. Among kids with a disorganized bond to their mother, those high on both defiance and little guilt were likelier to stay highly aggressive: 38% versus 7% overall.

pb4b4a73fc.post: Women with binge eating problems joined group sessions for 8 weeks. Some had a therapist lead everything, some watched a taped lesson and then talked with a therapist, and some watched the tape and led their own talk. Others were put on a waiting list. All three groups binged less over time, with no difference among them, and all did better than the waiting list.

pb54ec7496.post: People listened to a steady stream of random syllables played at a fixed pace, while whispering syllables of their own at the same time. Researchers measured how closely each person's whispering lined up with the beat they heard. The scores did not spread evenly.
