They fell into two clusters: people who matched the rhythm and people who did not.

pb5526de4a.post: Obese women answered a structured interview about their eating before starting a weight-loss program. Based on it, they were sorted into four groups: no overeating, overeating without feeling out of control, overeating with loss of control, and full binge eating disorder. The more binge eating problems a group had, the more dieting, impulsivity, and perfectionism they showed, and the lower their self-esteem.

pb577c74d1.post: College students got pairs of signals and said whether the two were the same or different. A pair could be two sounds, two visual signals, or one of each in either order. Women gave more correct answers than men.

pb5aa4c4f5.post: Women with symptoms of anorexia and women without them estimated body size and were tested on noticing changes in it. Women without symptoms who were lighter overestimated their size, and heavier ones underestimated it. Women with anorexia symptoms responded very differently: at low weight they were very accurate, but as weight rose they overestimated more and more.

pb5cd4b4b7.post: Women were photographed at two points in their menstrual cycle: during the days when they could most easily get pregnant, and during a later phase of the cycle. Men and women then looked at the photos and rated how attractive each face was. Both men and women rated the photos taken in the fertile window as more attractive than the photos taken in the later phase.

pb5f52d610.post: Full-time workers filled out an online survey about how often they chewed gum, how stressed they felt at work and in life, and their health. About six in ten were gum chewers. The people who chewed gum reported feeling less stressed, both at work and in life in general, than the people who didn't.

pb61518d6f.post: After John McCain lost the 2008 U.S. presidential election, conservative voters rated how much they saw him as part of themselves. They also rated how much they felt they belonged, felt good about themselves, felt in control, and felt life had meaning. Conservatives who saw McCain as more a part of themselves felt those needs were met less than conservatives who saw him as less a part of themselves.

pb64a8731b.post: People answered questions about how much uncertainty bothers them. Then they did a computer task that makes mistakes likely, while their brain activity was recorded. Those more distressed by uncertainty had a bigger brain response to mistakes. Those who tend to hold back when things are uncertain had a smaller one.

pb66f6f4bc.post: Some people were first asked how much they would donate to help one needy person, and then how much to donate to help a whole group of needy people. Others were asked only about the group. People who were asked about one person first gave more to the group.

pb6a03b3f7.post: People thought about their own death or about dental pain. Then they chose between $50 now and increasingly attractive rewards in three months. People who had thought about death accepted a smaller later reward in place of the $50 than people who had thought about dental pain.

pb726a7974.post: Women being treated for depression were shown messages flashed too fast to notice consciously. One message read "Mommy and I are one." Other messages, like "Succeed for myself," were tested too. After the "Mommy and I are one" message, the women gave fewer depression-related responses.

pb72f6a516.post: College students filled out a questionnaire about how well they control their impulses and emotions. They also answered questions about their gambling, such as whether they had bet more than they could afford to lose. Students whose gambling put them at higher risk scored lower on self-control than students at lower risk.

pb775f25ca.post: Researchers went back through the clinic files of 111 women who had come for treatment of bulimia, an eating disorder. They checked which women had quit therapy early and what had happened to them in childhood. The more childhood trauma a woman had been through, the more likely she was to drop out of treatment.

pb78c07199.post: A patient who reads one letter at a time named written words out loud. Some words had many look-alikes that differ by one letter, others few, and some had easily confused letters. Words with many look-alikes were named faster than words with few, but not when their letters were easily confused.

pb80f0374e.post: Teachers of children with attention or behavior problems used a daily report card, a regular rating of how the child did on set behavior goals. Each teacher got coaching from a clinician, counselor, or social worker. Behavior was tracked month by month. Most children improved by a large amount in the first month, and kept improving through month four.

pb81ec5e95.post: Elementary school students were randomly put into two groups. One group heard a positive label, like "clever," tied to a specific reading habit, such as answering questions. They were also challenged to do better than before and better than another student. The reading fluency and comprehension of students with reading disabilities improved more with this than without it.

pb82124009.post: People going door to door sold packs of note cards to raise money for a local charity. Some sellers gave the price in dollars. Others said it in pennies, "300 pennies," and then right away added "It's a bargain." Households that heard the pennies price plus the bargain line were more likely to buy than households that got the usual dollar price.

pb85cba73c.post: People listened to short clips of spontaneous English speech from Mandarin speakers and two native English speakers. They typed what they heard and rated how foreign each accent sounded and how easy it was to understand. Even clips rated as heavily accented were mostly understood, so a strong accent did not necessarily make speech harder to understand.

pb872f1ab2.post: People saw face portraits from university yearbooks on a computer screen and rated how attractive each face was, from 0 to 100. Some portraits were tilted toward the viewer, like a greeting bow. Others tilted backward or stayed still. The bowing portraits got higher attractiveness ratings than the other two kinds.

pb89f51c24.post: Native English speakers heard odd sentences, like 'the mother gave the candle the daughter', and said what they thought was meant. Some were spoken with a foreign accent and others with a native accent. People were more likely to take the odd sentence as the sensible one when the speaker had a foreign accent.

pb8a0c40c8.post: People and three AI chatbots were each given four everyday objects, such as a rope or a candle. Everyone was asked for creative, unusual uses for each one, in 1 to 3 words. The AI answers were rated as more creative on average than the answers from the people.

pb8ba8ddcb.post: Children and adults learned names for new kinds of objects. In one version, a knowledgeable teacher chose which objects got named. In the other, the learners chose them. Both groups applied the name more narrowly, only to objects most like the named ones, when the teacher chose than when they chose themselves.

pb928dcf81.post: People were timed naming the ink colors of words like "hot" and "cold" printed on cards. On some cards, the feel of the word matched the feel of the color. On others, it clashed. People were slower to name the color when the word clashed with it than when it matched.

pb93d3f042.post: Married couples were followed from the third month of pregnancy to two months after the birth. Wives and husbands each reported how much space they felt their own bodies took up. Wives' sense of body space changed over that time, but husbands' did not, so spouses' patterns did not match.

pb9478336e.post: Patients went through psychotherapy while their progress was tracked. For some patients, their therapists were given feedback on how the patient was doing. For others, therapists got no feedback. Among patients expected to do badly in treatment, those whose therapists got feedback had better outcomes than those whose therapists did not.

pb992fd1ff.post: Psychiatric patients in a veterans hospital took a short test and a long standard IQ test. Researchers built a formula that turns short-test scores into an estimated IQ, using 100 patients, then tried it on 50 new patients. The estimates tracked the long test's scores closely (correlations of .87 and .85) and did not run too high.

pb9ba564a1.post: Students first did a brief task that made them anxious. Then some colored a mandala, some colored a plaid pattern, and some colored on a blank piece of paper. Anxiety went down about equally for the mandala and plaid colorers, and more than for the blank-paper colorers.

pb9be44827.post: People seeking treatment for a gambling problem filled out a questionnaire about their gambling history and answered a doctor's interview. Some had mainly played gambling machines, and others had mainly played older kinds of gambling. The machine players went from regular gambling to a gambling problem in about 1 year, compared with about 3.6 years for the others.

pb9dde425a.post: College students who scored low on a self-esteem test were split into three groups. Two groups watched a video with a message against their low opinion of themselves, one told as coming from a highly credible source and one from a less credible source. The third group watched nothing. Students who saw the high-credibility video came away with higher self-esteem than the others.

pb9e1f1111.post: People with chronic heart failure and people without it did a lab task that imitates remembering to do things later in a normal day. Some tasks were cued by an event, some by a time, and some repeated. People with heart failure were worse at remembering than the comparison group, across these task types.

pb9e414274.post: Boys being held while they waited for court hearings looked at inkblots and described what they saw. Their answers were scored, then compared with scores from teenage boys who were not delinquent. The held boys generally scored lower, and the authors concluded the non-delinquent scores were not a fair yardstick for them.

pba52c6eb2.post: Native English speakers and people who speak English very well as a second language were tested on how well they understood the Miranda rights, the warnings read to suspects in the US. Most of the second-language speakers did not understand their rights. They also did worse than native speakers at basic processing of the wording.

pbaabe24f1.post: People saw faces of other people described as students at their own university or at a different one. Later they tried to recognize the faces. People recognized faces of their own university's students better.

pbb37c963c.post: People who said a psychedelic drug experience had changed their beliefs filled out an online survey. They rated whether animals, insects, plants, fungi and even objects can have conscious experience, as they felt before the experience and after it. After the experience, more people said these things can be conscious.

pbba258e36.post: People had a chance to claim money they were not entitled to. Some were told 'Please don't be a cheater' and others 'Please don't cheat'. People told 'Please don't cheat' claimed more money than people told 'Please don't be a cheater'.

pbba789cda.post: Toddlers learned a new word for an object from a speaker who had been either accurate or inaccurate before. Then they were tested on what the word meant. Toddlers responded less systematically when the speaker had been inaccurate.

pbbb8c675e.post: Working professionals reported on the technology they use at work and the kinds of job stress they feel. The stresses were too much work, unclear expectations, loss of privacy, work crowding out home life, and fear of losing the job. Of those five, too much work and unclear expectations were the two most dominant.

pbbfbd3c4c.post: People with dyslexia and people who read typically took three vision tests: detecting a visual illusion, detecting motion, and reading small details to check eyesight sharpness. People with dyslexia did worse on the illusion and motion tests than the other group, but both groups did about the same on eyesight sharpness.

pbc2b4b2f1.post: Chimpanzees watched short video clips of one object being held up by another. In some clips the support was enough, and in others it was not. Researchers timed how long the chimps looked at each kind. The chimps looked longer at the impossible clips than at the possible ones.

pbc3c4ed7a.post: People video-chatted with a robot named Pepper twice a week for five weeks. It asked them questions about everyday topics like work and health, framed around the Covid-19 pandemic for half the people and not for the other half. Over the ten chats, people shared more about themselves with the robot and rated it as more social and competent.

pbd372ecff.post: People with PTSD described the images from their trauma that kept flashing into their minds. In therapy, they also relived the memory and reported what they felt and thought at its worst moments, called hotspots. The intrusive images often matched those hotspots.

pbd46a5192.post: People did a task where they had to tell two things apart, and correct answers earned a reward. One of the two correct answers paid off more often than the other. People also filled out a depression questionnaire. Most people leaned toward the answer that paid off more, but people with high depression scores did not.

pbd4fb9ca5.post: Children spent a week at a summer camp, where counselors rated their behavior and feelings. Researchers sorted the children using child protection records of the kinds of maltreatment each had faced and in how many stages of childhood. The sorting found four groups: three with distinct maltreatment patterns, based on type and how long it went on, and one with no maltreatment.

pbe41ce4ee.post: Government records followed Queensland, Australia children known to child protective services, from birth until age 17. For some, maltreatment happened only in early childhood. For others, it started or continued into the teen years. Children maltreated in their teens were more likely to offend as juveniles than those whose maltreatment ended before adolescence.

pbea37cee3.post: Young children with autism or developmental delays were shown cards with pictures, words, or numbers and asked to name them. The teacher waited a bit longer over time before giving the answer to copy. Some cards were taught with extra information added after the answer, others without. The extra information can make teaching more efficient.

pbecc04662.post: Adults did a creativity test in which they came up with uses for everyday objects, once while sitting and once while walking on a treadmill. Most people scored higher on creativity while walking than while sitting.

pbf398b70f.post: People played a money-splitting game as the one making the offer, with a robot as the supposed partner. A drawn mouth on the robot's screen either stayed flat or turned up and down as they moved a slider. Offers were 13% higher when the mouth changed.

pbf3b572a2.post: German twins rated themselves on the 240 statements of a personality questionnaire, and people who knew them rated them on the same statements. Researchers removed from each statement whatever its broader trait already explained, leaving a narrow leftover. Most leftovers showed reliable agreement between self and others, and kept people's relative ranking over time.

pbffd1b573.post: People repeatedly saw the word "I" paired with positive traits, flashed too fast to notice. In control conditions, "I" was not paired with positive traits. Afterward, researchers measured implicit self-esteem, meaning automatic gut feelings about yourself. People who saw the pairings scored higher than the control groups.

pc0ade8d90.post: Silver and bronze medalists at the 1992 Summer Olympics were observed right after their events and on the medal stand, and their emotional reactions were analyzed. Bronze medalists tended to be happier than silver medalists.

pc19669eb8.post: People watched campaign advertisements that were the same in every way except for their tone, negative or not. Then they said how likely they were to vote. People who saw the negative ads reported lower intentions to vote.

pc1bb14b9e.post: Schools were randomly split in two. Some ran an antibullying program for 9 months, and others carried on as usual. Students filled out surveys about bullying, and classmates also reported on each other. Students in the program schools reported less bullying and being bullied than students in the other schools.

pc1c55d8e4.post: People practiced a timing task made of a series of movements, and they could choose which trials they got feedback on. One group decided after each trial whether they wanted feedback on it. The other group had to decide before each trial. On a later test with new timing demands, the group that decided after each trial did better.

pc21d2179f.post: Researchers noted what color shirt each woman was wearing. They also worked out whether each woman was at a high or low chance of becoming pregnant that day, based on where she was in her monthly cycle. Women at high chance of conceiving were more than 3 times as likely to be wearing a red or pink shirt as women at low chance.

pc28ea6705.post: Women were led to value happiness, or were given no such prompt. Then some did something designed to make them feel happy and others something to make them feel sad, and they reported how they felt. Women led to value happiness reacted less positively to the happy activity, but not to the sad one.

pc2bfff1fd.post: People took a questionnaire about how well they notice, understand and manage emotions. Then some were asked to give a public speech, which was meant to be stressful, while others did a neutral task. People who scored higher on the questionnaire had less bad mood and less of the stress hormone cortisol in their saliva after the stressful task.

pc2ee1d4bd.post: People learned to sort 'aliens' into ones to approach and ones to avoid. After each answer they got feedback, and then a nonsense label was either shown or not. People who saw the labels learned the categories better, even though the labels added no new information.

pc3456a47a.post: Students heard a news story about a burglary, then had sensors on their fingers while they went through items, some from the story. Half imagined being the burglar hiding it. Half imagined being a witness who wanted to be detected. In both groups, story items raised the skin's sweat response by a similar amount compared with other items.

pc38b1398f.post: Women with bulimia were measured on how much they dieted and how depressed they felt. Researchers then sorted them into groups based on those two scores. Most of the women (62%) fit a group defined by dieting alone, and the rest (38%) fit a group that combined dieting with depressed feelings.

pc38eaad5d.post: Younger and older adults read Chinese sentences while a camera tracked where their eyes landed and how long they stayed on each word. Some words were easy to guess from the sentence so far, and others were hard to guess. For older adults, the time spent on a word changed more with how guessable it was than it did for younger adults.

pc42fe285f.post: Preschoolers did a set of tasks that test whether they understand that people act on what they think and want. Each child's version of a gene for a brain chemical called dopamine was also checked, some shorter and some longer. Children with the shorter version did better on the tasks than children with one or more longer versions.

pc4e756266.post: Young children with autism each worked on two or three skills, like tasks from a teaching curriculum. For each skill, they were tried with two kinds of help: one built around rewards, the other around prompts, which are nudges that show what to do. The quick testing method was useful for matching each skill to the kind of help that worked.

pc50ad504d.post: In April 2021, people filled out an online questionnaire about how much they followed COVID-19 precautions, such as social distancing and wearing masks. They also answered questions about personality traits, including being cold and manipulative, thinking very highly of oneself, and having unstable moods and relationships. People who scored higher on these traits reported following fewer precautions.

pc57d487b7.post: Kindergarten children who showed early signs of trouble, like aggression, severe tantrums and picking on others, were picked out by screening. Half were randomly chosen to start a program at once, involving their teacher, classmates and parents. The rest waited. Children in the program showed measurable gains compared with those waiting, and the gains lasted into the early grades.

pc5b21bd19.post: People briefly saw several things on a screen, then a signal told them which one to report. The signal came after a short or a long delay, and the things were either threatening or neutral. Memory of the flash faded more slowly for threatening things than for neutral ones.

pc5e224040.post: Professional fighters had their faces measured for how wide they were compared with how tall. Researchers then checked those measurements against how good each fighter really was in combat. A face's width relative to its height predicted actual fighting ability.

pc60bd2095.post: Male students were measured on how much they gambled, how much antisocial behavior they showed (acts that break rules or hurt others), and their personality. Some were not problem gamblers, and some were pathological gamblers. For every kind of gambling and antisocial behavior, the two went together: students who gambled more also showed more antisocial behavior.

pc6343117b.post: People with panic disorder, most of whom had not improved with earlier treatment, all went through the same four-day treatment program. An independent assessor then interviewed them by phone about their panic symptoms right after, and again three months later. About 72% counted as in remission, both right after treatment and at three months.

pc64ec6bfc.post: Scottish people who had taken an intelligence test at age 11 took ten different mental tests again around age 70. They also said how many years they had spent in school. More schooling went with better scores on specific skills, not through a boost to general intelligence.

pc671dfc10.post: People learning a second language studied new words in two ways. Some saw each word with its translation, and others had to figure it out from a sentence in the new language. Afterward everyone was tested on recall. Learning with translations helped people remember more words, but weaker learners could not use those words in new sentences.

pc6781f286.post: Pairs of children, and pairs of college students, each solved a visual puzzle on a computer and could see how their partner was doing. They could place pieces in the partner's puzzle, or keep working only on their own. The conditions ranged from competing to helping to being forced to cooperate. Most people chose to solve their own puzzle alone.

pc6b657c9a.post: Two children with autism were taught to name sounds they heard. Sometimes the sound played by itself, and sometimes it came with something to look at. The children learned better when the sound came with something to look at than when it played alone, but this got in the way of naming objects they already knew.

pc77935d09.post: Japanese university students learning English kept a diary for one week about confidence-building activities they did. Researchers read the diaries to see what feelings came up, with no comparison group. The diaries showed mostly positive feelings, sometimes mixed with negative ones, and supported basic psychological needs such as feeling capable.

pc79dfe21f.post: Patients arrived at a mental health clinic 20 minutes early to fill out a short questionnaire. Then an interviewer who hadn't seen their answers did a full diagnostic interview. Compared with the interview, the questionnaire caught 80% of people with a disorder while correctly clearing 78% of those without one. Set to catch 90%, it cleared only 66%.

pc7d28af00.post: Deaf adults who mainly use sign language judged whether two English words were related in meaning. For some pairs, the signs for the words looked alike in American Sign Language, though no signs were shown. These pairs were judged faster when related and slower when unrelated, compared with pairs whose signs looked different.

pc810308cc.post: People saw slides of a car hitting a pedestrian. Afterward some got information consistent with what they saw, some got misleading information, and some got irrelevant information. Then they took a recognition test. People who got misleading information were less accurate.

pc855bad66.post: Children from middle-class and working-class families were asked to guess how much money people in different jobs earn. They were also asked whether the differences in pay were fair. The middle-class children guessed higher pay for every job than the working-class children did, and they saw bigger gaps between jobs and a clearer split between manual and non-manual work.

pc873eecee.post: People filled out a questionnaire that measures how manipulative and cynical they are. They also answered questions about whether they use deceptive tactics to attract dates, and how close they felt in their relationships. People who scored higher on manipulativeness were more likely to use deceptive tactics and reported less closeness in their relationships.

pc88cdf5ac.post: People looked at face photos of strangers and judged whether each pair was related. Some of the people were firstborn children and some were later-born children. The later-born people were better than the firstborns at spotting which strangers were related.

pc93c1ce3f.post: Students in China answered a big survey about learning English, including how they used mental pictures. Researchers compared men with women, and students who had used mental pictures before with those who had not. The ability to form mental pictures was part of what drove students' motivation to learn English.

pc9af89349.post: Students in adult psychology classes filled out a personality questionnaire about how outgoing they are. Right after, they rated themselves on a scale from shy and reserved to outgoing. Students who rated themselves as outgoing or as reserved also tended to land in matching groups on the questionnaire, so its scores fit how people saw themselves.

pca2418b6d.post: People read some texts, then listed keywords for them and rated how well they understood what they read. Some listed the keywords right after reading and others after a wait, and the other time gaps were varied separately. Only the wait between reading and listing keywords made people's ratings match their real understanding better.

pca2e91c21.post: Children who had been tested on reading in first grade were tracked down ten years later, as 11th graders. They were tested on how much they read, how well they understood what they read, their vocabulary, and their general knowledge. The better a child read in first grade, the better they did on all four.

pca58ff6c6.post: People played money games with partners, where they could trust the other person with their money or hold back. Some played while exposed to a fishy smell, and others were not. People exposed to the fishy smell became more suspicious and cooperated less than people who weren't.

pca77a6451.post: Men filled out questionnaires about how well adjusted they felt in different parts of life. Some were gay and some were straight, and none were recruited through clinics. Gay men rated themselves as less well adjusted than straight men on four scales, better adjusted on three, and no different on six.

pcacbb3d19.post: People read about a local recycling program and the officials running it. Some saw more female first names among the officials, and others saw fewer. Then they rated how willing they were to recycle and compost. Women were more willing to cooperate when more of the officials had female names.

pcaeb18ade.post: Trainee therapists at a mental health center each worked with clients while one of 23 supervisors oversaw them. Using five years of records, the study compared clients' progress in therapy across the different supervisors. Who the supervisor was explained less than 1% of the differences in how clients did.

pcb3207826.post: People reported on temptations they ran into over time, whether they resisted or gave in, and whether they felt guilty or proud afterward. Then the researchers checked what happened the next time the same kind of temptation came up. After people felt guilty about giving in, resisting that temptation became more important to them.

pcc0be0981.post: Nine deaf children who also had trouble with language were taught social skills: waiting their turn, starting interactions, and playing with others. Teachers and residential staff also supervised them, gave feedback, and set goals with them. For all nine children, the share of appropriate social behavior went up after the training began, compared with before it.

pcc57a09af.post: Two people with autism were taught to ask for what they wanted instead of acting out. In one condition, any request worked. In the other, a request worked only if it differed from the last one. Both people varied their requests more when they had to differ than when any request worked.

pcc7976107.post: Younger and older adults held a handle on a robot arm and moved it between two targets while the robot pushed their hand sideways. Both groups learned to make up for the push about equally well. Compared with younger adults, older adults kept less of what their slow learning process had picked up from one movement to the next.

pccabc9e3f.post: People from age 8 to 36 lay in a brain scanner and looked at faces that were blends of happy and angry, some clearly one or the other and some in between. For each face they labeled the emotion. Older people were better at telling the emotions apart than younger people.

pccb1b920a.post: People pressed a left or right key to sort shapes and colors flashing on a screen. In some rounds, one key was for blue or circle and the other for yellow or triangle. In other rounds the pairings were flipped. There was no speed advantage for the pairings an artist had predicted would feel natural, such as blue with circle and yellow with triangle.

pccd080bde.post: People read about someone whose action brought a personal benefit and also helped charity, or about a similar action that brought only the personal benefit. Then they evaluated the behavior. People judged the action that also helped charity as worse.

pccf366b6b.post: People watched a distressing film. Then some thought about it on purpose, some did a demanding task knowing the film would matter later, and some did it believing the study was over. Those who did the task knowing the film would matter had fewer unwanted memories of the film than the others.

pcd3735d69.post: People learned computer skills in one of two ways. One group was guided to avoid errors. The other group was given problems too hard to solve without making errors. The group that practiced with errors scored higher on tests that were not timed.

pcd5825cd1.post: Students in grades 7 to 9 took reading comprehension tests with multiple-choice answers. Some got the full test. Others got it with the text removed, the questions removed, or both. Even when there was no text to read, students got more answers right than random guessing would give.

pcd64e06f3.post: Some people walked around however they liked, some walked in a rectangle, and some sat. Everyone also did creative thinking tasks. People who walked freely scored higher for how original their ideas were than people who walked in a rectangle or sat.

pcda9efb45.post: Children who stutter were assessed for temperament, how chaotic their home was, and major life events. Mothers and clinicians each rated how severe the stuttering was. Both sets of ratings were linked to scores on effortful control, the skill of focusing attention and holding back impulses.

pcdee22107.post: People pressed buttons to earn M&M's and Fritos to eat later. Some trained for one day, others got six times as much practice. Then everyone ate one food until it stopped being pleasant and pressed again. Extensive training made pressing less sensitive to a food losing its value than light training did.

pcefdb7cf3.post: Young adults said which personality traits they wanted to change and whether they had plans for doing it. Twelve months later, their personality was checked again to see how it had actually changed. Goals and plans to become more organized and dependable, or less anxious and moody, predicted change in the opposite direction from the goal.

pcf2052337.post: Children with autism were taught new skills, like touching the picture the instructor named. For half the skills the instructor recorded every answer, and for the other half only the first answer. When the two differed, skills were usually learned faster with first-answer recording and remembered better with every-answer recording.

pcf5a05dd1.post: Ninth graders and their teachers each answered questions about themselves. Some teachers were told five things they had in common with certain students, and some students were told the same about their teachers. Five weeks later, teachers who got this feedback about specific students said they had better relationships with those students.

pcfa15c092.post: People who slept badly were split into four groups. Three groups learned to control a body signal using biofeedback, a device that shows you your own body activity as it happens. The fourth group got no treatment. People who got the type of biofeedback that seemed to fit their own specific problem slept better afterward, while people who got a type that did not fit did not.

pcfde8400c.post: Children who could not yet read worked through a program with 51 words. They matched printed words to words they heard, and they copied words using movable letters, then said them aloud. Afterward, five of the seven children could also read words that were not in the program, and their spelling improved.

pcff656aef.post: College students looked at photos of three people of the opposite sex. Each photo was paired with a job and income, either low, middle or high. Students said how willing they would be to have relationships of different kinds with each person, from sexual relationships to marriage. Women placed more weight than men on a partner's job and income in relationships involving affection and marriage.

pd0efb7e40.post: Adults were asked to describe what changing means to them and what coping means to them. They also described what pushed them to change and what stressful life events pushed them to cope. What pushed people to change was not linked to what pushed them to cope.

pd1259b9ae.post: Adults across the US went online every day for 10 days early in the pandemic. Each day they reported how they felt, how worried they were about COVID-19, and whether they had done things like social distancing and hand washing. Fear and worry about COVID-19 each pushed the other up, and together they went along with doing more of these protective behaviors.

pd176b6aff.post: Students played a trust game in which one player could send some of their money to an unknown partner. Days later, they gave a blood sample so researchers could measure oxytocin, a hormone. Students with very low or very high oxytocin sent more money than students with middle levels.

pd25a91711.post: Teachers in elementary and middle schools rated each student's social, academic, and emotional behavior on a checklist. They also nominated students. Researchers combined the nominations and the checklist into a two-step screening process. The combined process was acceptably good at both spotting students at risk and not wrongly flagging the rest.

pd27671c51.post: People first did a task meant to use up their self-control, or a control task. Then they worked on matchstick arithmetic puzzles, which are solved by suddenly seeing the problem in a new way. People whose self-control had been used up solved more of them correctly.

pd29389b46.post: People thought about purchases that were either experiences, like a trip to Rome, or material things, like a flat-screen TV. For some, the chance to talk about the purchase was taken away. Losing that chance reduced the enjoyment of experiences compared with being able to talk, but not the enjoyment of material things.

pd2ecf5d78.post: Children were asked to pretend to use eight objects that weren't there. Some got help in words, some got practice, some were shown how, and some got an imaginary setting. Children who were shown how made more realistic hand positions, as if holding the object, than children in the other three groups.

pd2f90adc2.post: Patients in a hospital day program for mental health problems answered a 28-question survey about dissociation, such as feeling cut off from your surroundings, memories, or sense of self. Researchers looked at which questions tended to go together in people's answers. After dropping questions that would not stay in one group, the remaining 16 questions formed three clusters.

pd330c3c8b.post: First-grade classrooms were randomly assigned to one of two kinds of lessons. Some teachers taught a 10-day unit on how Arctic animals survive, built around science reading. Others kept teaching their normal reading program. Students in the Arctic unit knew more science word meanings in depth than students in normal instruction.

pd336188c9.post: Fourth graders in the U.S. and China took a reading test. They also filled out questionnaires about why they read and how much they read. Kids who read because they enjoy it scored higher on the test, in both countries. Kids who read mainly for outside rewards scored lower, unless they also enjoyed reading.

pd3469b077.post: People learned that made-up words matched either a happy or an angry emoji. Then they saw a word with an emoji and pressed "true" or "false" for whether the two went together. When an angry-linked word appeared with a happy emoji, people were faster to press "true" than "false," even though they had learned the two did not match.

pd3c14780d.post: People answered questions about how assertive and how aggressive they are. They also said how likely they would be to talk about a bad service experience with different people, from family to acquaintances. More assertive people were more likely than less assertive people to say they would discuss it with acquaintances and others.

pd402ec786.post: College students clicked a mouse to choose between two options, and clicks on either one paid out money at unpredictable times. In some conditions, clicks also cost them money at unpredictable times. Losing money worked as an effective punishment, meaning it reduced the clicking it was tied to.

pd446a26b8.post: Twenty-three healthy people filled out personality scales, including one that measures how much they present themselves in a socially approved way. Each person also had a brain scan that measured how many of one kind of dopamine receptor they had in a deep brain area called the limbic striatum. People with more of these receptors there scored higher on the social desirability scale.

pd46ffaa55.post: People took part in a mock crime, stealing either a ring or a watch. Then, lying in a brain scanner, they denied taking either object, so some answers were true and some were lies. Using the scans, researchers correctly told which object each person stole for 93% of people in one group and 90% in a second, separate group.

pd489907a4.post: People were measured on social anxiety, on depression, and on how much they fear being judged, both badly and well. Researchers compared how these measures fit together. Fear of being judged well was the feature that set social anxiety apart from depression.

pd4dac7ad4.post: A teacher laid out three picture cards and asked a child, "Where is the problem?" One card showed a problem, like a toy with no batteries. While teaching the child to pick it, the teacher also added extra information about why it was a problem. All three children with autism picked up at least some of those explanations without being directly taught them.

pd55f8c3e4.post: Beginning algebra students solved simple problems presented either as story problems or as equations that mean the same thing. Students were more successful at solving the story problems than the equations.

pd5c5a7f70.post: Toddlers watched a woman communicate with them. In one version she held a false belief, meaning she was wrong about something. In the other she did not. The toddlers understood the same message differently when she had a false belief than when she did not.

pd62ccdd71.post: People read about how Japan treated prisoners of war from their own group in World War II. Some were first reminded that apologies are common these days, and others were not. Everyone then read an actual apology. Those reminded of the trend rated the apology as less sincere and were less willing to forgive than the others.

pd66d76044.post: Male prison inmates were interviewed about their lives, and their prison files were reviewed to rate how psychopathic each one was. The same men also filled out questionnaires about distress, fear and anger. Men high on the cold, charming, manipulative side of psychopathy reported less negative emotion. Men high on the rule-breaking, impulsive side reported more.

pd6e9f1831.post: People drank fructose, glucose, or a placebo drink. Ten minutes later, they tried to solve word anagrams. People who drank fructose or glucose solved more anagrams than people who drank the placebo.

pd7998d757.post: People read three stories: washing, checking, and one unrelated to OCD. Each switched between what could be sensed and what might possibly be true, while doubt was measured. People with more OCD symptoms or stronger fears about who they might be felt more doubt than others, and more swings in it, mostly in the washing and checking stories.

pd7ade5d83.post: Animals could work at either of two options to earn rewards. Pressing one option moved only that option closer to paying off. Pressing the other moved both options closer. The animals favored the option that moved both, which is the choice that earns the most rewards overall.

pd7f3e3ea0.post: Men who are attracted to men did an online program. Some got one meant to reduce negative feelings about their own sexuality, and others got a similar program about managing stress. Afterward, the two groups differed in their overall scores on those negative feelings, and on two of the three more specific parts.

pd89748fb3.post: College students filled out a survey rating how friendly and how careful they are, and how much that changes from one situation to another. Then they were watched in a group discussion and a waiting room, and their parents and a roommate rated them too. Some students acted alike across situations and others did not, and the researchers could tell in advance which was which.

pd8c0e2a41.post: People sat with electrodes on their scalp while their brain activity was recorded. They alternated between keeping their eyes open and closed, for up to 8 minutes. Everyone also filled out a personality questionnaire. A computer could predict how agreeable a person was from their brain activity, in each of the four recordings.

pd8cb18576.post: Girls of similar intellect filled out a questionnaire about their attitudes toward math in ninth grade, and again in twelfth grade. In between, some took one year of college-prep math and others took up to four. The girls who went on to take more math had rated math as more useful and felt more confident learning it.

pd8ee825f2.post: Children aged 6 and 10 listened to stories in which a character hides how they feel. They were asked how the character would look and how the character would really feel. Both age groups could tell the difference quite accurately.

pd91b977ab.post: People answered 22 standard questions that test cognitive biases, such as overconfidence and anchoring. Some were first told to notice three new things, which was meant to make them mindful. Mindful people were less likely to show the bias on most of the questions.

pd95601d20.post: Women gave short unplanned talks at two points in their monthly cycle, once around ovulation and once just before their period. This was repeated over two cycles. They tripped over their words, such as starting a phrase and then changing it, more often just before their period than around ovulation.

pd9741b925.post: Young men who played action video games most days and young men who rarely played did a screen task with distracting items next to a target. When the target task was hard, the gamers were influenced more by the distractors than the non-gamers were.

pd9e2aaf63.post: College athletes answered questions about whether they think of themselves as spiritual, religious, both, or neither. They also filled out a questionnaire on how grateful they usually feel in life. Athletes who called themselves both spiritual and religious scored higher on gratitude than athletes who called themselves spiritual only or neither.

pd9f3759ac.post: People did a Stroop task, where you name the ink color of a word instead of reading the word itself. It is meant to wear out self-control. Then they did a second task. People who had done the draining first task did worse on the later task than people who had not.

pda30f06ca.post: Two boys were each given a bedtime pass that could be traded for one trip out of the bedroom after bedtime. The pass was in use during some stretches and not during others, while crying and leaving the room were counted. With the pass, crying and coming out of the bedroom after bedtime fell to zero in both boys.

pda46001d8.post: People read a sentence that implied an object's color, then saw a picture of the object in a color that either matched or mismatched, and said whether the object had been mentioned. They responded faster when the colors mismatched than when they matched.

pda7d62f5c.post: Students saw still animations of four made-up characters: a fellow student, an elderly person, a successful businessperson, and an alcoholic. For each one, they guessed how likely it was that good and bad events would happen to them. For the alcoholic character, students expected more bad events than good ones.

pdb59460c9.post: Students in Berlin, from fifth through tenth grade, were assessed on aggressive behavior with a new system. It tried to separate what aggression looks like, openly hurting someone or damaging their relationships, from why it happens, to get something or to react to being provoked. The results split into four separate kinds: two forms and two reasons.

pdc34d0ec1.post: People who were feeling mildly to moderately down, and people who were not, spent 8 minutes thinking about one of two things. Some focused on their current feelings and personal traits. Others read descriptions of places and objects. Among the down people, those who focused on their feelings felt worse afterward, while those who thought about places and objects felt better.

pdc848472b.post: People were assigned to a high-power role or a low-power role. Then they chose between smaller immediate rewards and larger future rewards. People in high-power roles were less likely to prefer the smaller immediate reward.

pdcb0a1b1a.post: Men made risky choices on their own, where a bad outcome could mean real physical pain and losing money. Then they met in groups and talked until they agreed on one choice. The group's choice was riskier than the average of what its members had chosen alone.

pdd1bb1024.post: North American adults filled out a survey about how hard they try to look after their health. It also asked how much risk they felt of dying from things outside their control, and how they rank in society. People who felt more of that outside-their-control risk said they put less effort into looking after their health.

pde031f368.post: Female college students took part in an intensive program about eating and body image, while a matched group of students did not. Everyone filled out surveys at the start and again four months later. The program group had lower scores on dieting, body dissatisfaction, eating disorder symptoms and weight, while the comparison group showed no such changes.

pde08d547e.post: Couples filled out a questionnaire about their relationship, covering eight different parts of life together. Then the researchers grouped couples whose answers looked alike. The couples' answers sorted into distinct types of relationships, rather than forming one blur.

pde145e238.post: People in many earlier studies were measured for math anxiety, the tense, uneasy feeling some get when facing math. The results were pooled and compared across groups, such as different school grades and college majors. People still training to become arithmetic teachers were especially prone to math anxiety, compared with other groups.

pde1fbc569.post: People from East Asia and from Western countries rated themselves in many different ways, across published studies that were pooled together. Some tasks asked them to compare themselves to the average person. East Asians saw themselves in a flattering light when comparing to average, but were self-critical in the other kinds of tasks.

pdebe2ad95.post: People who often chewed or sucked on their own hands were given a toy to use instead. They could touch the toy with their hands or with their mouths, and researchers tracked which they did. For all of them, the feeling in the hand, not the mouth, was the main thing that kept the habit going.

pdee803466.post: Overactive preschool boys were given a training package meant to teach them to instruct themselves, starting at a different time for each boy. Observers tracked how often each boy stayed on task in the classroom. On-task behavior increased dramatically once the training began, compared with before it.

pdf9b36e9a.post: People learned that colored shapes were linked to different amounts of money. Then they did a quick button-press task, where a beep sometimes told them to stop their response. Half the shapes came with beeps and half never did. Afterward, people bid less money for the shapes that came with stop beeps than for the shapes that did not.

pdfa531cc8.post: People were handed a pen and asked to fill in the missing letters of word beginnings. Some used a red pen and others used a black pen. People with red pens made more words about errors and poor performance than people with black pens.

pdfc8e06b8.post: Students living in one college dorm filled out a survey about using computers and any aches they felt. It asked about the past two weeks. In that time, 42% said their arms or hands hurt or felt uncomfortable when they used a computer.

pe09e4977d.post: Preschool children played a game where they earned points by responding slowly, under two different versions of the rule. In some sessions a signal showed when a response would earn a point and when it would not. In others, only the "no point" signal appeared. Having both signals helped children keep responding in both versions, compared with the "no point" signal alone.

pe0d7b180f.post: Some people were led to think about having power and others were not. Then they played a golf putting game. People who had been led to think about power putted better.

pe1378cd9a.post: Men sniffed a nasal spray on two occasions. One time it contained oxytocin, a hormone linked to social bonding, and the other time it was a spray with nothing active in it. Then they looked at photos of eyes and chose which feeling each person was showing. They did better at this after the oxytocin spray than after the empty spray.

pe169a08bd.post: Bosses and workers each rated how willing the workers would be to do the tasks bosses assign. They rated how enjoyable, how undesirable, how far beyond the call of duty, and how likely to be resisted the tasks were. Bosses rated the tasks as less enjoyable, more undesirable, more beyond the call of duty and more likely to be resisted than workers did.

pe19d738c4.post: Eighth graders wrote poems, stories, math equations, and math word problems, and experts rated how creative each one was. The researchers then set aside differences in IQ, reading skill, and math skill. After that, a student's creativity score on one task did not go with their scores on the other tasks.

pe226f1e58.post: Children learned English words in two ways: picking the picture that matched a spoken word, or saying the word when shown a picture. Later they were asked to translate between English and Portuguese, which they had not been taught directly. Words learned by saying them were translated correctly more often than words learned by picking pictures.

pe23f1cdb4.post: Teenage boys were grouped by their overall pattern of personality traits, so that boys with similar patterns landed together. Then the same grouping was checked separately for African American boys and white boys. Three personality types showed up, and the same three appeared in both groups of boys.

pe2aa557ab.post: Spanish speakers practiced telling apart two similar sounds from Basque, a language they knew little about. Some only listened. Others also said the sounds out loud after each trial, either right away or after a wait. Waiting longer before speaking reduced, and even eliminated, the harm that speaking did to learning.

pe2c85a598.post: Smokers saw cigarette package warnings with pictures that were more or less graphic, or with no picture. Then they reported how much they intended to quit smoking. More graphic pictures strengthened smokers' intentions to quit.

pe2d521eca.post: Older married couples each rated themselves on adjectives like organized, hardworking and careless. They also rated their own health and said which everyday activities, such as climbing stairs, were hard for them. Husbands who rated themselves as more conscientious had wives with better health, even after accounting for the wives' own personality.

pe3a6c3ee5.post: Students did a computer task where a word like beer or vodka appeared on screen, and pressing the space bar brought up a picture. For some students, alcohol words were paired with unpleasant pictures. For others, they were paired with neutral pictures. The students who saw alcohol paired with unpleasant pictures came to feel more negatively toward alcohol without realizing it, and they drank less than the others.

pe41d4f603.post: In March 2020, people online read messages urging them to take steps against the coronavirus. Some messages said prevention protects you, and others said it protects the public. Then people said how likely they were to take those steps. Messages about protecting the public worked better than messages about protecting yourself.

pe4355fe08.post: Male college students tried to learn an underhand basketball free throw from a student acting as their coach. Some got negative feedback from the coach and some got none. Some also watched for and recorded their own successes, and some did not. Those who recorded their successes shot worse than those who did not.

pe4400ba34.post: People saw other people show angry or afraid expressions. Some of these people belonged to the viewer's own group, and others belonged to a different group. Researchers measured how much the viewers' own faces copied the expressions. Viewers copied angry and afraid expressions more when they came from their own group than from the other group.

pe45d559d4.post: College students read a short story about a woman who was offered help she didn't need. The woman was either young or old, and she either accepted the help or turned it down. Students thought the help was fine more often when the woman was old, and they rated her as warmer and less capable. When the older woman turned the help down, their view of her competence improved.

pe48fb5dbd.post: Asian American participants were prompted to think about their American self, their Asian self, or things in nature. Then they recalled important events from their lives. Those prompted to think about their American self recalled more self-focused and less socially oriented memories than those prompted to think about their Asian self.

pe4f8e6190.post: People repeatedly chose between a sure amount of money and a gamble with two equally likely outcomes. Every few choices, they rated how happy they felt at that moment. Their happiness was explained by what they had expected to win and by how much each result beat or missed that expectation, not by how much money they had so far.

pe50892472.post: In the Netherlands, Muslims and non-Muslims rated how much they believed conspiracy theories, some about Muslims or Jewish people and some unrelated, such as that the moon landings were fake. Muslims believed both kinds more strongly than non-Muslims did.

pe5230b495.post: Mothers wore sensors on their fingers and chest while doing tasks with their 6-month-old babies that were meant to upset the baby. Afterward they watched the video and described what they thought and felt. Among mothers whose bodies calmed themselves well, more physical arousal went with more empathic, baby-focused thoughts about the crying.

pe57b6b57c.post: People first did a task that used up their self-control, or a control task. Then they reported how well they had done on another task, with money at stake. People whose self-control had been used up overstated their performance more.

pe58c10218.post: Female secondary school students did three thinking tests. Some did them in silence, some with UK garage music playing, and some with background noise. Introverts did worse than extraverts with music or noise on all three tests, but in silence the two groups did about the same.

pe60a9be44.post: Adults with disabilities were split into two teams during activity sessions. In some sessions nothing special happened. In others, the team with the most steps at the end got into a prize drawing. All 10 people took more steps per minute during the team game than during the plain sessions.

pe6216c16c.post: Caretakers filled out a checklist about the child they looked after, covering signs of dissociation, such as seeming spaced out or disconnected. The children were in one of three groups: children with documented abuse, children with ADHD, and children with no abuse or psychiatric record. Children with abuse histories scored higher on dissociation than children in the other two groups.

pe62d2c6f2.post: Parents and children who had come to a clinic for the child's anxiety filled out checklists about behavior problems, such as arguing, disobeying and trouble finishing things. Researchers then looked for groups of children with similar patterns. The children fell into three groups: high, moderate and low on these behavior problems.

pe64af564f.post: Children watched a doll act out a story about two bags in two places. In one version the doll was wrong about which bag was where, then asked for the bag in place 1. In the other the doll was right. Children did better at saying which bag the mistaken doll wanted than on a separate task about a person's mistaken belief.

pe6b553725.post: Veterans of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars gave blood, reported how much combat they had seen, and were interviewed for PTSD. Their blood was checked for a gene version called ε4. Among non-Hispanic Black veterans, ε4 made no difference after little combat, but after heavy combat, those with two copies had the highest PTSD rates.

pe72a5064c.post: People looked at fearful faces while their brains were scanned. Some faces were shown plainly, and others were flashed and covered so fast that people did not know they saw them. Scores on an anxiety questionnaire predicted how one part of the amygdala, a fear-related brain area, responded to the hidden faces, and also people's reaction times.

pe77949923.post: Adults learned about the structure and function of the human heart from paper materials. Some were told to gesture, such as pointing and tracing, as they learned, and others were not. Then they took a knowledge test. People instructed to gesture performed better.

pe7999af45.post: High school students filled out a health survey that asked about eating carrots, height, dentist visits, and sexual identity. Researchers flagged students whose answers looked like jokes, then compared health gaps between LGBQ and straight students with and without them. Removing suspected jokers shrank the average gap by up to 46% for boys and 23% for girls.

pe819ac7e6.post: Toddlers in Italy and the United States were checked with the same word survey to see which words they used. Italian late talkers, who were slower to build a vocabulary, were compared with younger Italian children who had about the same number of words. The late talkers used similar kinds of words to the younger children.

pe83fa6eb6.post: People chose two candy bars. For some, the choice was framed as picking two single candy bars, and for others as picking one bundle of two. People picked more variety when they chose single candy bars than when they chose a bundle.

pe857168d1.post: Adults of many ages rated how much they make room for things that feel good, and how often they feel positive and negative emotions. Results were split by age. Making room for positivity went with more positive emotions in older adults but not younger ones, and it was linked more to fewer negative emotions in younger adults than in older ones.

pe88b9eb0b.post: School counselors in one large Southeastern school district filled out a questionnaire about how students get assigned to them. Some worked in middle schools and others in high schools. Middle schools mostly assigned students to counselors by grade level, while high schools mostly assigned them by the alphabet.

pe8c4e3f86.post: University students filled out a questionnaire meant to pick up traits linked to schizophrenia risk. Researchers ran a statistical test on the answers to see whether people spread along a smooth scale or fell into two kinds. The answers pointed to a distinct type of person, rather than a smooth range, and about 1 in 10 people belonged to it.

pe92fe29f3.post: People tasted small samples of bitter, sweet, sour, salty and savory solutions, plus flavors like coffee and vanilla. After each one, they picked the musical note that best matched the taste, from low notes to high notes. Bitter and savory (umami) tastes were matched to lower notes.

pe95fc253e.post: People looked at emotional pictures and chose how to deal with their feelings about them. Some pictures were easier than others to see in a new light, such as imagining a different explanation for what was happening. How easy a picture was to rethink changed which strategy people chose, even after accounting for how intense the emotion was.

pe968867b1.post: People learned about someone who either cared a lot or cared little about a hot-button social issue. Then they judged how much they could trust that person. Some of the people they judged shared the observer's view, and some strongly disagreed. People trusted those who cared more than those who cared little, even when they disagreed with their view.

pe97a581b6.post: Staff trainees watched videos of someone teaching a child step by step, and rated how accurately each step was done. Then they practiced the teaching method themselves with a person playing the child. Their own teaching got better, and the improvement carried over to skills they had not watched or rated.

peac917cad.post: Children who had been referred to a clinic were tested on intellectual ability and school achievement. Some had an anxiety disorder, some had other mental health disorders, and some had no major problems. Children with anxiety disorders scored lower than the referred children with no major problems.

peb1925ef0.post: People who were in a relationship were asked to reflect on nostalgic memories of an ex-partner. A control group did not do this. Then they rated how good their current relationship was. People who reflected on the nostalgic memories rated their current relationship as better than the control group did.

peb65fee81.post: People saw faces of famous athletes, some footballers and some tennis players, and had to say who each one was. They answered with either a foot or a hand. Foot answers were slower for footballers' faces, and hand answers were slower for tennis players' faces, than for the other kind of athlete.

pebc79fdae.post: People watched a hand reach across a touch screen for an object. Sometimes a second object blocked the way, and the hand either went over it or took a path that ignored it. The hand vanished mid-reach, and people touched where they last saw it. When the hand moved in a way that didn't fit the obstacle, people's touches were pulled toward the efficient path.

pec0fb4280.post: People were asked to imagine one day each year when all crime was legal, like in the movie The Purge. They said how likely they would be to commit crimes that day. They were also measured on self-control and on psychopathy, a set of traits like coldness and little remorse. People with lower self-control, and people with more psychopathic traits, said they were more likely to commit crimes.

pec29322d1.post: Korean university students in an English class played a murder mystery video game called Her Story, which tells its story in fragments. Then each student wrote their own version of what happened. Their writing was scored for originality, flexibility and elaboration, and it showed considerable creativity on all three.

pec602469b.post: People read about a deceased person and several candidates who might be that person's reincarnation, each matching the deceased in one feature. They chose the candidate most likely to be the reincarnation. Candidates sharing a physical mark, such as a mole, or a specific autobiographical memory were chosen more often than candidates sharing other features.

peca1dc719.post: Two boys who sucked their thumbs at night wore a boxing glove to bed for about a week. Then they wore cotton over the thumb for 11 nights, and then a small bandage on the fingertip for 10 to 11 nights. Their nighttime thumbsucking stopped completely, compared with before the treatment.

pecb9ca4d3.post: Students went through 120 personality statements and marked which ones fit them. The same men and some other women then rated how socially desirable each statement was, meaning how good it looks to say it fits you. Women's answers matched those ratings more closely than men's did.

pecee3d41f.post: University students, split into three groups, gave short speeches on a topic that was new to them. They were taught to notice their verbal stumbles and to pause silently instead. Their speech stumbles dropped compared with before the training.

pee16b97fc.post: Norwegian children did a story task that scored how disorganized their bond with a caregiver was. Each child's version of one gene was also checked, and their behavior was followed from age 4 to 6. Highly disorganized children with two copies of the valine version showed bigger increases in aggression than highly disorganized children carrying the methionine version.

pee2d20adb.post: People about to sing karaoke, give a speech, or do math either tried to calm down or told themselves they were excited, for example by saying 'I am excited' out loud. People who told themselves they were excited felt more excited and performed better than people who tried to calm down.

pee7b5535f.post: People played rock-paper-scissors, trying to win as many rounds as they could. In some pairs both players were blindfolded. In other pairs one player was blindfolded and the other could see. When both were blindfolded, draws happened about as often as chance predicts, but when one player could see, draws happened more often than chance.

peea6074b0.post: People listened to recorded speech. Some were told they would hear two different talkers, whose voices differed only slightly in pitch. Others were told it was one talker, or were given no special instructions. The people expecting two talkers showed the performance costs people typically show when adjusting to a new voice.

peeac5aaa1.post: About a thousand students in Grades 6 to 8 answered 16 questions about how they feel at school. The questions covered feeling connected to school, feeling able to do the work, enjoying learning, and seeing a purpose in education. Their answers grouped into those four distinct areas.

peeeb06d99.post: Older adults took a set of memory and thinking tests, then did a word search while trying to remember timed tasks, like telling the tester when 15 minutes had passed. How much a person's scores varied from test to test was linked to how well they remembered the timed tasks.

pef0dd96bf.post: People working in their second language did a quick task, deciding whether strings of letters were real words. Some word pairs sounded natural in their first language but not in the second, and these were compared with pairs that sounded natural only in the second. The results showed no sign that the first-language word pairs switched on while people worked only in their second language.

pef1254bd7.post: People recalled a series of related events from their lives, either in reverse order ending with a target event, or in chronological order starting with it. Then they rated how far away the target event felt. The event felt closer when people recalled the series backward.

pef354ddae.post: Teenagers rated their parents on how accepting and involved they were, and on how strict and watchful they were. Those ratings sorted families into four types. Teens who described their parents as both warm and strict scored highest on competence and lowest on emotional and behavior problems. Teens who described neglectful parents showed the reverse.

pef860b2f5.post: People described an intention in an interview, some telling the truth about what they planned to do and some lying about it. Researchers counted how many details about places and times each person gave. People telling the truth gave more spatial and temporal details.

pefd7dba80.post: People thought about different situations that might or might not be called a lie. The situations varied in how well they fit the word, with some fitting better than others. Of everything that makes something a lie, knowing that what you say is false mattered most.

pf001587df.post: People saw two digits and then a symbol, and said as fast as they could whether the symbol was a number. Before it, a word flashed too briefly to see: either 'add' or a control word. When the symbol was the sum of the two digits and the hidden word was 'add', people identified it faster.

pf045b33ac.post: Older adults with dementia sat with an experimenter who offered two items at a time, some foods and some leisure items, and said "pick one." All of them picked leisure items more often than food.

pf05cccc8f.post: People rated 464 metaphors, some taken from poems and some made up by the researchers, on ten qualities, such as how easy each was to understand and how familiar it felt. The average ratings were reliable, with a consistency score of 0.88, where 1 would be perfect.

pf05fc8cff.post: People did a task while trying to remember to respond to a cue that rarely appeared. Half spoke Turkish and English, and half spoke only Turkish. In one version the task made the cue easier to notice, and in the other it got in the way. The two-language group showed no clear advantage over the Turkish-only group at remembering.

pf1677ff81.post: College students with mild to moderate depression were split into two groups. One group did four attention training sessions over two weeks, and the other did no training. Students who did the training had a bigger drop in depressive symptoms than students who did none.

pf1f126322.post: People took tasks that measure how well you read other people's feelings and social cues. Some were told the tasks were a test of social skills, and others were told the same tasks tested academic skills. Lonely people did worse than non-lonely people when it was called a social test, but just as well or better when it was called an academic test.

pf232b0d8f.post: Parents of preschoolers spent 20 minutes a day at home for 30 weeks doing a program with their child. Some parents did a program to build talking skills. Others did a program aimed at movement skills. Right after the program, children in the talking group had gained more in language and storytelling than children in the movement group.

pf23993bc3.post: College students filled out questionnaires about hope and optimism. Their answers went through a statistical test that can tell whether people fall into two separate types or spread out along a smooth scale. The answers fit a smooth scale of optimism, not two types, optimists and pessimists.

pf2627dff8.post: Staff at a national education service in New Zealand were trained to assess children's behavior and write support plans. Some were trained by outside experts, and others by the service's own newly trained team. Their work was checked against 140 set criteria. The in-house team trained staff to meet the same standards as the outside experts.

pf28ea3262.post: White and Black people acted as eyewitnesses to a man who either held a weapon or did not. For some people the man was White, and for others he was Black. Later their memory of him was tested. The weapon's effect on memory was weaker when the man was Black than when he was White.

pf29c14a01.post: Teachers who had never run a preference test practiced offering snacks to a pretend client to see which one the client picked. They first used written instructions alone, then a version with less jargon plus pictures, diagrams, and step-by-step examples. Accuracy was low with the first, but the teachers carried out the tests accurately with the improved instructions.

pf2b3c5bd8.post: People saw three color words stacked on a screen and pressed a left or right key for the middle word, ignoring the other two. Each key stood for two of the four words. Responses were affected both by whether the ignored words matched the middle word and by whether they shared its key, a link made only by the instructions.

pf2b90bbed.post: Women wore a cap recording brain activity while pressing keys for the middle letter in a row of letters, then rated their worry. Some used hormonal birth control and some did not. For users, more worry went with a bigger brain response to mistakes; for nonusers the link was smaller and unclear.

pf2c28c96d.post: College students rated imaginary people on a set of opposite-word scales, such as good versus bad. Some rated 25-year-olds, some 50-year-olds, and some 75-year-olds, and the people being rated were either men or women. The older the person being rated, the more negative the ratings were.

pf2c38096f.post: Men were given either a single dose of testosterone or a placebo. Then they answered brain teasers where the first answer that comes to mind is wrong and you have to stop and think. The men who got testosterone scored lower than the men who got the placebo.

pf2e79f717.post: People did mental tasks while sounds they were told to ignore played in their left ear or their right ear. In some versions the ignored sound changed more, in others less. Sound in the left ear disrupted people more than sound in the right, but only when the ignored sound changed in an ordered way and the task meant keeping things in order.

pf312f285f.post: People lay in a brain scanner and played a money game with a partner they never met. They saw how much money each of two options (Blue or Red) would pay, then told the partner which option was better for the partner. They could lie or tell the truth. When people lied, four brain areas were more active than when they told the truth.

pf329b669f.post: One woman who had lived with chronic pain for 11 years went through a treatment that taught her to relax, scheduled activities she valued, and showed her graphs of her progress. Her worries about pain were measured before and after. Her anxious thoughts about pain declined, even though the treatment never targeted them directly.

pf34f7f5f5.post: People used or saw words that were either adjectives, which are abstract, or verbs, which are more concrete. Then they did tasks that showed whether they focused on the big picture or on the details. People who got adjectives focused more on the big picture, while people who got verbs focused more on the details.

pf3a414dc0.post: Some men and women were put in a mindset about finding a romantic partner, and others in a mindset about protecting themselves from danger. Then they made choices involving possible gains and losses. Men in the romantic mindset no longer weighed losses more heavily than gains, which people usually do.

pf4587336f.post: People in a clinic were treated for destructive behavior by getting what they wanted when they asked in a better way. Step by step, that payoff was made available for less of each session. After bigger drops in how much of the session it was available, the destructive behavior came back more than after smaller drops.

pf458a88cf.post: In some cases, people called themselves by a slur that others use against their group, such as "queer" or "bitch." In other cases, they used a plain label like "woman." People who used the slur for themselves felt more powerful, and observers saw them and their group as more powerful.

pf50402ad5.post: People answered yes/no questions in two ways: by saying the answer out loud, and by resting their hands on a Ouija board and letting it move. When they felt they were only guessing, their spoken answers were right half the time, which is chance. Their Ouija board answers were right about 65% of the time.

pf5397cc44.post: Patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder or panic disorder with agoraphobia rated how much criticism they felt from family members, and their anxiety symptoms were measured. Then they went through behavioral treatment, and symptoms were measured again. Patients who felt more criticized before treatment had more severe anxiety after treatment, beyond what their symptoms before treatment would predict.

pf5512ff15.post: People saw two strings of letters, one after the other, and pressed a button to say whether each was a real word. Some pairs rhymed and looked alike (BRIBE-TRIBE), some rhymed but were spelled differently (EIGHT-MATE), and some were unrelated. Rhyming pairs got quicker answers than unrelated pairs, and the speedup was equal whether or not the spellings matched.

pf5c83fb41.post: Adults filled out a questionnaire measuring neuroticism, the tendency to feel negative emotions. Their DNA was checked at one spot in a gene called MAMDC1, where people carry zero, one, or two copies of a less common version. Neuroticism scores were not reliably linked to the number of copies, though they tended to rise with more copies.
