pf5ed58a76.post: People sniffed a nasal spray with oxytocin, a hormone, on one occasion and a spray with no drug on another. Each time they did a task testing how accurately they read other people's feelings, and they also filled out a questionnaire on social skills. Oxytocin improved accuracy only for the less socially skilled people.

pf62cf67d9.post: Six graduate students training to be special education teachers practiced in a simulated classroom while a coach worked with them one-on-one. They were learning a method for teaching students with autism: give the smallest hint first, and add more help only if needed. Coaching increased how closely they followed the method's steps.

pf638bd591.post: People watched two colored disks disappear and reappear on a screen, with a phrase like "the purple and the green" or "the purple or the green" above them. The disks either vanished together or took turns. People judged whether the phrase matched. They linked "and" with disks that changed together, and "or" with disks that took turns.

pf65bd4aca.post: People turned a crank either clockwise or counterclockwise. Then they chose between familiar things and new ones. People who turned the crank counterclockwise preferred the familiar, while people who turned it clockwise preferred the new.

pf66e52be8.post: Adults filled out a new questionnaire about how emotions work. Some items were about whether changing how you think can change how you feel. Others were about whether feelings just happen automatically after an event. The answers fell into two related groups, one for each kind of belief.

pf68bfda18.post: Incoming college STEM students took part in a one-week program just before their first semester. It included small-group activities, mentoring, and career planning. Students filled out surveys before and after the week. Their science identity and their sense of belonging to STEM and to the university went up.

pf69e96e7d.post: Patients took two personality tests: one asking what they see in inkblots, the other a questionnaire about themselves. Researchers also looked at each patient's general style of answering on each test. Patients with a similar style on both tests had distress scores that lined up strongly across the tests. When style was ignored, the scores did not line up.

pf71c72d72.post: People pressed a button whenever a dot appeared in one of two squares on a screen. In some rounds they held one hand against the screen next to a square; in others neither hand was near it. Dots next to the held-up hand were detected better than dots away from it.

pf76460000.post: Teachers attended a four-day training series spread over a year, with coaching and practice between sessions. It taught them how to figure out why a student misbehaves and build a plan around it. They answered the same questions about 15 ideas and strategies before and after. Their scores were higher after the training on every one.

pf7b9000c1.post: College students filled out questions about how religious they were. They also said how much they supported killing animals in different areas of life. People who were moderately religious supported killing animals less than people who were not religious at all or very religious.

pf7bb88ff5.post: Care staff were asked about a made-up young man whose behavior was hard to handle. They described what they would do right away and what they would do over the longer term. Their long-term plans matched what psychologists aim for, but their immediate responses resembled the unhelpful reactions seen in earlier studies of staff.

pf7c8f385c.post: People negotiated on a computer and were told whether their opponent was angry, happy, or neither. People gave in more to an angry opponent than to a happy one.

pf85070837.post: People chose between a basic option and a premium option, such as direct flights. For some, the premium price was shown as the extra cost, 'for $20 more'. For others it was shown as the total, 'for $60 total'. More people chose the premium option when its price was shown as the extra cost.

pf94f09dc5.post: Young children with autism learned to point to the picture that matched a spoken word. Each child learned one set of pictures by practicing the pieces separately first, and another set by practicing the full word-to-picture matching from the start. Starting with the full task was more reliable and efficient.

pf961c0c06.post: People in an online survey rated their own health as excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor. For some, the choices were listed starting with "excellent." For others, the list started with "poor." People rated their health as better, and fewer said "fair" or "poor," when the list started with "excellent."

pf9f1d422f.post: People looked at slides of eight kinds of animals, shown in the wild, in a natural-looking zoo, or in a caged zoo. Others saw no slides. Everyone rated the animals on word scales. Zoo animals were rated as restricted, tame, and passive, while wild animals were rated as free, wild, and active.

pfa769feac.post: Couples kept a daily diary for 12 days, noting whether they felt less close to their partner than they wanted, or more close than they wanted. Researchers tracked how those feelings changed from day to day. Feeling too close faded faster than feeling not close enough, and it depended less on how much contact the partners had that day.

pfa82b51b5.post: People in 55 countries filled out a personality questionnaire that covered traits like extraversion and agreeableness. Researchers compared women's and men's answers across countries. The gap between women and men was larger in countries with longer healthy lives, more education and more wealth than in countries with less.

pfb552fe3f.post: Three-year-olds watched a box that seemed to play music when certain pairs of painted blocks were placed on top. One block showed up in both pairs that worked. Then each child picked between two pairs: two matching blocks, or the two different blocks that had worked. Children in the US mostly picked the matching block, while children in China mostly picked the pair that fit the "different" pattern.

pfbaf6e6f7.post: People reported on their current and past romantic relationships, saying who confessed love first and how they felt when a partner said 'I love you'. People thought women confess love first and feel happier when they hear it, but in real relationships men confessed first and felt happier hearing it.

pfbb4d5d44.post: People wrote about either a nostalgic event from their past or an ordinary one. Then they played a computer game with 30 virtual balloons. For each balloon they chose how many times to pump it, earning money per pump but losing it all if the balloon popped. People who wrote about a nostalgic event chose more pumps than people who wrote about an ordinary event.

pfbd15ae21.post: Preschoolers each spent time with their mother, were separated from her, and then were reunited. Half had been referred to a child psychiatry clinic for serious behavior problems, and half were children without behavior problems. Most of the clinic children, 84%, showed an insecure bond with their mother, compared with 28% of the other children.

pfc060f363.post: People filled out a personality questionnaire that scores two close traits separately: Intellect, a taste for ideas and abstract thinking, and Openness, a taste for art and beauty. They also had their intelligence measured. Intellect was linked to overall, verbal, and nonverbal intelligence about equally, but Openness was linked only to verbal intelligence.

pfc1c510f0.post: College students judged how well different ways of attracting a partner would work. The ways were judged for men and for women, and for someone after a short-term fling versus a long-term partner. Showing you are sexually available was judged most effective when women used it to find a short-term partner.

pfcb38528a.post: American and Chinese college students answered a survey about dating attitudes and behaviors. American students had more liberal views, started dating younger, dated more often, and were more likely to have sex with their dates than Chinese students.

pfcc7f2492.post: Patients leaving the hospital after treatment for schizophrenia or for depression each had a close relative who was assessed for how much emotion they expressed about the patient. Nine months later, researchers checked who had relapsed. In both groups, the relative's expressed emotion was linked to relapse, even after accounting for the other social and clinical factors measured.

pfcfaf7274.post: Mothers were watched at home with their 6-month-old babies during feeding and play. Later, at 12 and 18 months, each baby was put through mild separations from the mother in a lab, and the babies' DNA was tested years afterward. Babies with the short version of a serotonin-related gene were more likely to show attachment patterns with more distress than babies with the long version.

pfd1be9e46.post: People studied prose passages. Then some repeatedly restudied the material and others repeatedly took tests on it. One week later everyone took a final test with new questions that required drawing inferences. People who had repeatedly taken tests did better than people who had repeatedly restudied.

pfd4d73e8a.post: Adults in a Brazilian city described their own families, which were compared with a shared idea of a typical family. They also gave DNA and were followed for two years. Fitting that idea better went with fewer depressive symptoms, and the link was strongest for people with the A/A version of a serotonin receptor gene.

pfdb62dded.post: People who had never tried meditation were measured on how mindful they are in everyday life. They also had their sensitivity to pain measured. People who were more mindful had higher pain thresholds than people who were less mindful, meaning it took more to make something hurt.

pfede9747a.post: Parents answered online questions about their personality, their income and education, hard experiences from their own childhood, and how they treat their child. Mothers and fathers were analyzed separately. For mothers, how personality related to parenting depended on income and education; for fathers, it depended on childhood hardships.

pff307ce52.post: Adults in a large national survey were sorted into four groups: those who had ever had PTSD but not depression, both, depression only, or neither. Researchers then compared how many in each group had high blood pressure. High blood pressure was more common in both PTSD groups than in the depression-only group or the group with no mental disorder.

pff3c9c069.post: Heavy drinkers who also had trouble sleeping were randomly given one of two online programs. One was a self-paced program that teaches skills for better sleep. The other was a general health education program. Over the following months, the sleep program group had fewer insomnia symptoms and drank less than the education group.

pff4eb389c.post: Boys and girls in different grades were asked about peers whose behavior mental health professionals would see as signs of emotional disturbance. Their answers were compared with the judgments of clinicians. The children told apart milder and more serious problems in a way that closely matched the clinicians.

pffefd9240.post: People wrote about a time they treated someone badly. Then some put a hand in a bucket of ice water, and others put a hand in warm water while moving paper clips between boxes. People who held a hand in ice water felt less guilty afterward, and the drop was bigger than for the warm-water group.
